## Milestones: 1945–1952

**NOTE TO READERS**   
 “Milestones in the History of U.S. Foreign Relations” has been retired and is no longer maintained. For more information, please see [the full notice](/milestones).

# The Chinese Revolution of 1949

On October 1, 1949, Chinese Communist leader Mao Zedong declared the creation of the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The announcement ended the costly full-scale civil war between the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the Nationalist Party, or Kuomintang (KMT), which broke out immediately following World War II and had been preceded by on and off conflict between the two sides since the 1920’s. The creation of the PRC also completed the long process of governmental upheaval in China begun by the [Chinese Revolution of 1911](/milestones/1899-1913/chinese-rev). The “fall” of mainland China to communism in 1949 led the United States to suspend diplomatic ties with the PRC for decades.

![](https://static.history.state.gov/milestones/communists-beijing.jpg)

Communists entering Beijing in 1949.

The Chinese Communist Party, founded in 1921 in Shanghai, originally existed as a study group working within the confines of the First United Front with the Nationalist Party. Chinese Communists joined with the Nationalist Army in the Northern Expedition of 1926–27 to rid the nation of the warlords that prevented the formation of a strong central government. This collaboration lasted until the “White Terror” of 1927, when the Nationalists turned on the Communists, killing them or purging them from the party.

After the [Japanese invaded Manchuria in 1931](/milestones/1921-1936/mukden-incident), the Government of the Republic of China (ROC) faced the triple threat of Japanese invasion, Communist uprising, and warlord insurrections. Frustrated by the focus of the Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek on internal threats instead of the Japanese assault, a group of generals abducted Chiang in 1937 and forced him to reconsider cooperation with the Communist army. As with the first effort at cooperation between the Nationalist government and the CCP, this Second United Front was short-lived. The Nationalists expended needed resources on containing the Communists, rather than focusing entirely on Japan, while the Communists worked to strengthen their influence in rural society.

During World War II, popular support for the Communists increased. U.S. officials in China reported a dictatorial suppression of dissent in Nationalist-controlled areas. These undemocratic polices combined with wartime corruption made the Republic of China Government vulnerable to the Communist threat. The CCP, for its part, experienced success in its early efforts at land reform and was lauded by peasants for its unflagging efforts to fight against the Japanese invaders.

![](https://static.history.state.gov/milestones/chiang-kai-shek.jpg)

Chiang Kai-shek

Japanese surrender set the stage for the resurgence of civil war in China. Though only nominally democratic, the Nationalist Government of Chiang Kai-shek continued to receive U.S. support both as its former war ally and as the sole option for preventing Communist control of China. U.S. forces flew tens of thousands of Nationalist Chinese troops into Japanese-controlled territory and allowed them to accept the Japanese surrender. The Soviet Union, meanwhile, occupied Manchuria and only pulled out when Chinese Communist forces were in place to claim that territory.

In 1945, the leaders of the Nationalist and Communist parties, Chiang Kai-shek and Mao Zedong, met for a series of talks on the formation of a post-war government. Both agreed on the importance of democracy, a unified military, and equality for all Chinese political parties. The truce was tenuous, however, and, in spite of repeated efforts by U.S. General George Marshall to broker an agreement, by 1946 the two sides were fighting an all-out civil war. Years of mistrust between the two sides thwarted efforts to form a coalition government.

As the civil war gained strength from 1947 to 1949, eventual Communist victory seemed more and more likely. Although the Communists did not hold any major cities after World War II, they had strong grassroots support, superior military organization and morale, and large stocks of weapons seized from Japanese supplies in Manchuria. Years of corruption and mismanagement had eroded popular support for the Nationalist Government. Early in 1947, the ROC Government was already looking to the island province of Taiwan, off the coast of Fujian Province, as a potential point of retreat. Although officials in the Truman Administration were not convinced of the strategic importance to the United States of maintaining relations with Nationalist China, no one in the U.S. Government wanted to be charged with facilitating the “loss” of China to communism. Military and financial aid to the floundering Nationalists continued, though not at the level that Chiang Kai-shek would have liked. In October of 1949, after a string of military victories, Mao Zedong proclaimed the establishment of the PRC; Chiang and his forces fled to Taiwan to regroup and plan for their efforts to retake the mainland.

The ability of the PRC and the United States to find common ground in the wake of the establishment of the new Chinese state was hampered by both domestic politics and global tensions. In August of 1949, the Truman administration published the “China White Paper,” which explained past U.S. policy toward China based upon the principle that only Chinese forces could determine the outcome of their civil war. Unfortunately for Truman, this step failed to protect his administration from charges of having “lost” China. The unfinished nature of the revolution, leaving a broken and exiled but still vocal Nationalist Government and Army on Taiwan, only heightened the sense among U.S. anti-communists that the outcome of the struggle could be reversed. The outbreak of the Korean War, which pitted the PRC and the United States on opposite sides of an international conflict, ended any opportunity for accommodation between the PRC and the United States. Truman’s desire to prevent the Korean conflict from spreading south led to the U.S. policy of protecting the Chiang Kai-shek government on Taiwan.

For more than twenty years after the Chinese revolution of 1949, there were few contacts, limited trade and no diplomatic ties between the two countries. [Until the 1970s](/milestones/1969-1976), the United States continued to recognize the Republic of China, located on Taiwan, as China’s true government and supported that government’s holding the Chinese seat in the United Nations.

# The Chinese Civil War: a guide to the conflict and the rise of Mao Zedong

Who were the two sides of the civil war? Why was it fought in two phases? And who eventually came out on top? Emma Slattery Williams shares a quick guide on the 20th-century conflict that ripped a nation apart and led to the formation of the People's Republic of China...

* [Emma Slattery Williams](/author/emmawilliams/)

Published: January 26, 2022 at 8:49 AM

* [Share on facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://www.historyextra.com/period/20th-century/chinese-civil-war-china-chiang-kai-shek-mao-zedong-communism/)

### What was the Chinese Civil War?

The Chinese Civil War was a series of conflicts between the Communist Party of China and the country’s Nationalist government. The war is regarded as having been fought in two distinct stages: between 1927 and 1937, and then again between 1946 and 1949 (the latter a phase often referred to as the Chinese Communist Revolution).

Ad

Hostilities were largely halted between 1937 and 1945 as the two sides formed a begrudging alliance against Japan, which invaded China and then attempted to create a Pacific empire during [WW2](https://www.historyextra.com/period/second-world-war/timeline-important-dates-ww2-exact/).

### What was the political situation in China before the outbreak of the war?

After more than 2,000 years of imperial rule, China’s last dynasty – the Qing – was overthrown in 1912 and the country became a republic. The new president, Yuan Shikai, imposed a dictatorship and declared himself emperor, but his death in 1916 created a power vacuum that enabled local warlords to seize control of different regions.

In 1924, the Chinese Nationalist Party, or Kuomintang (KMT), which had aided the overthrow of the monarchy 12 years earlier, joined forces with the fledgling Communist Party of China (CPC). Together, they formed the First United Front in opposition to the warlords who were trying to take control of northern China. This would lead to the launch of an allied campaign in July 1926 known as the Northern Expedition, led by Chiang Kai-shek of the KMT and the newly formed National Revolutionary Army.

* **Read more | [China’s public image war](https://www.historyextra.com/period/20th-century/china-history-public-image-west/)**

### What was the Shanghai Massacre?

On 12 April 1927, during the Northern Expedition, Chiang Kai-shek ordered a violent purge of communists and other leftist groups within Shanghai. Thousands of CPC members were killed during the massacre, marking an end to the First United Front and widening the gulf between the ideological factions that had already emerged within the KMT.

Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek on horseback. In 1928, he became China’s de facto president (Photo by © CORBIS/Corbis via Getty Images)

Soon, the party split altogether, with Chiang forming a right-wing KMT government in Nanking and Wang Jingwei (who opposed the Shanghai killings) retaining control of the KMT’s left-wing administration in Wuhan.

### How did the civil war start?

In retaliation for the massacre and other communist murders, the CPC led an uprising in Nanchang on 1 August 1927, before going on to occupy the city. Although a counterattack saw the communists defeated, further uprisings and acts of guerrilla warfare continued to break out in opposition to the KMT, soon escalating into full-blown civil war.

One notable incident occurred on 7 September, when Mao Zedong – a founding member of the CPC – led a peasant revolt in his home province of Hunan. Although this, too, was crushed and Mao was forced to flee, the experience led him to believe that garnering communist support in China’s rural areas was key to defeating the KMT, where it had minimal influence.

* **Listen | [Graham Hutchings discusses his book *China 1949*, which explores the events of a tumultuous year that saw communist victory in the Chinese civil war and the birth of the People’s Republic of China](/membership/chaos-communism-chinas-1949-revolution/)**

### How did Chiang Kai-shek gain control of China?

Following the breakdown of the First United Front in 1927, China was in the unusual predicament of having three capitals: Beijing, which still was recognised by nations around the world as being the republic’s ‘true’ capital; Wuhan, which was the base of the CPC and Wang Jingwei’s KMT; and Nanking, the base of Chiang’s KMT.

However, after the right-wing KMT’s capture of Wuhan (July 1927) and Beijing (June 1928), Chiang – supported by landowners and businessmen – claimed to have united all of China. The Nationalist administration in Nanking was recognised as the country’s legitimate government, and in October, Chiang became the de facto president of the Republic of China.

Despite his victory, Chinese unity would not last. In 1930, a period of violent unrest broke out between the leader and some of his former allies, who challenged the legitimacy of his government and formed a coalition against him. Although Chiang again emerged triumphant, the incident left the Nationalist government on the brink of bankruptcy and drew attention to the party’s internal disputes.

To make matters worse for the KMT, China’s neighbour – Japan – was embarking on a period of expansion, and on 18 September 1931, some 40,000 Japanese troops marched into the Chinese region of Manchuria. Despite condemnation from the League of Nations, the Japanese installed a puppet government and placed China’s deposed emperor, Pu Yi, in charge.

Meanwhile, Mao established a state known as the Chinese Soviet Republic in the eastern province of Jiangxi. In a bid to crush it, the KMT undertook a series of five ‘encirclement’ campaigns that left their target surrounded and unable to escape. In order do this, Chiang was forced to assemble the largest army in the KMT’s history.

### What was the Long March?

On 16 October 1934, Mao’s Red Army broke through Nationalist lines and undertook a year-long retreat known as the [Long March](https://www.historyextra.com/period/20th-century/mao-communism-legend-long-march-mao-zedong-red-army/). The 100,000-strong group – which included soldiers as well as administrative personnel and civilians – trekked for some 6,000 miles, navigating snowy mountains and fighting opposing armies along the way.

Although only 10 per cent of the marchers survived the journey, they arrived at Yan’an, Shaanxi province, in October 1935, where Mao set about creating another communist state.

Around 100,000 people embarked on Mao Zedong’s ‘Long March’ in 1934, but only a fraction survived (Photo by Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

The feat cemented Mao as leader of the CPC, and the heroic efforts of the marchers led many people in China to rally behind the communist cause. Mao himself went on to declare that the Long March had been “a manifesto, a propaganda force... proclaiming to the world that the Red Army is an army of heroes”.

* **Read more | [Mao: the legend of the Long March](https://www.historyextra.com/period/20th-century/mao-communism-legend-long-march-mao-zedong-red-army/)**

### Why did the CPC and KMT unite again in 1937?

Taking advantage of the country’s internal struggles, Japan attempted to push further into Chinese territory. In a bid to beat back the Japanese advance, a Second United Front was formed between the KMT and the CPC, but only after Chiang was held hostage by two of his generals in December 1936 and forced into making peace with the communists.

By July 1937, Japan had invaded Beijing, but Mao sensed a new opportunity: by allowing the KMT to bear the brunt of the fighting, he hoped to recruit more people to the communist cause. Although the Nationalist forces put up a much stronger resistance than had been expected, events such as the Japanese attack on Shanghai in August 1937 took a heavy toll, forcing the KMT to abandon the city.

In December, the Chinese Nationalist capital of Nanking fell to Japan and the population suffered massacres and brutal attacks. In what would become known as the Rape of Nanking, thousands of surrendering soldiers and civilians were killed, with countless women raped.

The six-week atrocity shocked foreign observers and Christian missionaries in China, and hardened hostility towards Japan. Public opinion – especially in the United States – fell firmly on the side of China, which would have implications during the Second World War.

* **Read more | [Why December 1941 was the most important month of the Second World War](https://www.historyextra.com/period/second-world-war/pearl-harbor-hitler-america-most-important-decisive-month-ww2/)**

### How did the Second World War affect the conflict?

Having already signed a military pact with Germany and Italy, Japan formally entered the Second World War in December 1941 when it launched a surprise [attack on Pearl Harbor](https://www.historyextra.com/period/second-world-war/why-japan-attacked-pearl-harbor-empire-building-conflict-us/), the US naval base in Hawaii. In the wake of this destruction, it then set about expanding its empire across Asia and the Pacific.

Keen to halt Japan’s expansionist ambitions, the KMT and CPC continued to work together. However, the Red Army and the Nationalist forces fought much of the war separately, and still clashed with each other on occasion in a bid to assert their dominance.

After Japan’s surrender to the Allies in 1945, China reclaimed all the territories it had previously lost (including Manchuria), but it wouldn’t be long until domestic unrest reared its ugly head once again.

### What happened once the Second World War was over?

The Chinese Civil War resumed almost as soon as the Second World War had ended. Negotiations between the CPC and the Nationalists quickly broke down, and in July 1946, Chiang launched an attack on communist territory.

This time, victory was firmly on the side of the communists, who were greatly aided by China’s peasantry. Whereas Chiang was viewed as being a corrupt leader who did little to help the lives of the country’s poor, Mao had already won their support by paying off their debts and giving them land seized from their landlords.

Mao Zedong declares the birth of the People’s Republic of China on 1 October 1949 (Photo by Mondadori via Getty Images)

Furthermore, whereas the communists had suffered around 440,000 casualties during the war with Japan, the KMT had lost a staggering 3.2 million men. Cities thus fell with little resistance, and by June 1949, Beijing, Shanghai, Nanking and Tianjin had all been taken from Nationalist hands.

Following his historic triumph, Mao Zedong became president of the newly created People’s Republic of China on 1 October 1949 and remained in power until his death almost 27 years later. His rule – overshadowed by famines, massacres and the [purging of China’s cultural heritage](https://www.historyextra.com/period/20th-century/reign-of-the-red-terror/) – remains highly controversial.

* **Read more | [Reign of the red terror: Mao Zedong and the Cultural Revolution](https://www.historyextra.com/period/20th-century/reign-of-the-red-terror/)**

### How were ordinary citizens affected?

Atrocities against civilians were carried out by both sides, and some historians estimate that the total number of fatalities could be as high as 7.5 million. The land was ravaged by the conflict, so starvation and diseases were rife.

### When was peace declared?

No peace treaty or armistice has ever been signed between the two sides of the Chinese Civil War. In December 1949, Chiang fled to the island of Taiwan and established a rival government, declaring Taipei to be the capital of the Republic of China.

More than 70 years later, the issue remains complicated; although the People’s Republic of China views Taiwan as a breakaway province that must be retaken, many people on the island now regard it to be a separate nation altogether – even though independence has never been formally declared.

args.summary:
The Chinese Civil War was a series of conflicts between the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Nationalist government (Kuomintang/KMT), fought in two distinct stages: 1927–1937 and 1946–1949. Hostilities were largely halted between 1937 and 1945 when both sides formed a begrudging alliance against Japan during WWII.

After the Qing dynasty's overthrow in 1912, China became a republic but fell into warlord control. The First United Front (1924) between the KMT and CPC aimed to defeat northern warlords, but it ended after the 1927 Shanghai Massacre, where KMT leader Chiang Kai-shek ordered the killing of thousands of communists. This triggered the civil war, with Mao Zedong leading peasant revolts and believing rural support was key to defeating the KMT.

Chiang gained control of China by 1928, but internal disputes and Japanese expansion (invasion of Manchuria in 1931) weakened the country. Mao established the Chinese Soviet Republic in Jiangxi. The KMT's encirclement campaigns forced the CPC's famous Long March (1934–1935), a 6,000-mile retreat from which only about 10% of the 100,000 marchers survived. The march cemented Mao's leadership.

A Second United Front formed in 1937 after Japan invaded Beijing. During WWII, both sides fought Japan separately while occasionally clashing. After Japan's 1945 surrender, the civil war resumed. The CPC, aided by peasant support and Mao's land reforms, gained the upper hand. By June 1949, Beijing, Shanghai, Nanking, and Tianjin fell to communists. Mao declared the People's Republic of China on October 1, 1949.

Chiang fled to Taiwan in December 1949, establishing a rival government. No peace treaty has ever been signed. Estimated fatalities range as high as 7.5 million, with atrocities committed by both sides. The status of Taiwan remains contested—China views it as a breakaway province, while many on the island consider it a separate nation.

# The Collapse of Nationalist China: How Chiang Kai-shek Lost China’s Civil War

Author: **[Parks M. Coble](https://fairbank.fas.harvard.edu/person/parks-m-coble/)**, James L. Sellers Professor of History, University of Nebraska–Lincoln; Nonresident Associate, Fairbank Center for Chinese Studies

### About the book

When World War II ended Chiang Kai-shek seemed at the height of his power-the leader of Nationalist China, one of the victorious Allied Powers in 1945 and with the financial backing of the US. Yet less than four years later, he lost the China’s civil war against the communists. Offering an insightful chronological treatment of the years 1944–1949, Parks Coble addresses why Chiang was unable to win the war and control hyperinflation. Using newly available archival sources, he reveals the critical weakness of Chiang’s style of governing, the fundamental structural flaws in the Nationalist government, bitter personal rivalries and Chiang’s personal lack of interest in finance. This major work of revisionist scholarship will engage all those interested in the shaping of twentieth-century history.

ISBN 9781009297639

March 30, 2023 Cambridge University Press

270 Pages

>
> —Harold Tanner, The China Quarterly

# Who lost China?

* [Background](#background)
* [Key Question](#key-question)
* [Directions](#directions)
* [Materials](#materials)
* [Handouts](#handouts)

## Background

The 1931 Japanese invasion of Manchuria began a chain of events that led to the eventual communist overthrow of China in 1949. For years, the Nationalist government of Chiang Kai Shek had worked to suppress rebellions by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). The government was effective in defeating communist forces. The resulting period of retreat, commonly referred to as the Long March, marked the rise of Mao Ze Dong as a leader of the Communist movement in China.

In 1937, Nationalist forces, eager to drive the Japanese from Manchuria, began a series of engagements against them. The Japanese took this opportunity to expand their foothold in China and, within two years, had taken over most of the larger cities in eastern China. Japanese bombing of Chinese cities and atrocities against civilians led to an enormous loss of life. Driven out of the most prosperous parts of China, the government was unable to fund and support an organized resistance against the Japanese. As support for Chiang waned, the Nationalist government became increasingly ineffective and hostile towards the Chinese people.

Where Nationalist forces continued to be weakened from engagements with the Japanese, communist forces grew in size and support from the more rural parts of unoccupied China. Guerilla attacks by the CCP against the Japanese gave the perception that they were a more effective option. By the end of the war, the CCP enjoyed popularity in large parts of China.

By 1944 the United States was finally in a position to provide aid to China in the form of money and equipment. Trying to balance competing concerns of winning the war and avoiding communist gains in China the US government simultaneously provided most of its support to Nationalist forces and attempted to negotiate a peace agreement between them and the CCP. By the time the Japanese forces in China surrendered on September 2, 1945 the two groups were ready to resume a full-scale civil war.

In the context of the emerging post-WWII conflict between the Soviet Union and the United States, the Chinese Civil War presented a challenge to US politicians. When, on October 1, 1949, the People’s Republic of China was officially created plenty of blame went around. This inquiry presents several documents to explore the question, “Who lost China?”

These questions are not unique to this time period. While engaging in an active foreign policy after World War II United States’ leaders have faced difficult choices. Can the United States pick sides in a conflict with no ideal partner? What were the risks of not picking a side? Is the United States even capable of influencing the outcome of foreign conflicts? These questions ring as true today as they did in 1950.

Timeline of key events:

1921| Chinese Communist Party founded in Shanghai

1926-27 | Nationalist Party and Communist Party work together in the Northern Expedition to get rid of warlords in China

1927 | Nationalists turned on the Communists in the White Terror, attempting to purge this group from China.

1931 | Japanese Invasion of Manchuria

1945 | Nationalist forces flown into Manchuria to accept Japanese surrender. Nationalist and Communist forces sign a truce for plans for a coalition government to rule China after the war.

1946 | Nationalist and Communist forces are fighting an all-out civil war in China. George Marshall is sent to China to try to broker an agreement between the two sides.

1947 | Nationalist forces begin to look at Taiwan as a place of retreat in the event they lost the civil war.

August 1949 | Truman administration published the “China White Paper” outlining the administration’s policy towards China.

October 1, 1949 | Mao Ze Dong declares the creation of the People’s Republic of China

1950 | US becomes involved in Korean conflict, next door to China

## Key Question

Who lost China?

It explores the historical context and events leading to the Chinese Communist Party's overthrow of Nationalist China in 1949, examining the role of the United States in this outcome.

The background traces key events from Japan's 1931 invasion of Manchuria through the Long March, the rise of Mao Zedong, WWII Japanese occupation of Chinese cities, the weakening of Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government, and the CCP's growing rural support. The civil war resumed after Japan's September 2, 1945 surrender, and the People's Republic of China was declared on October 1, 1949.

The inquiry presents historical documents and asks students to consider: "Who lost China?" as well as broader questions about U.S. foreign policy, picking sides in conflicts, and influencing foreign outcomes. --- SOURCE 1: The Chinese Civil War 1945-1949 (Documentary) ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7slhD9PmxII

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a documentary transcript from Real Time History (published February 21, 2025) covering the Chinese Civil War from 1945-1949, examining the conflict between Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists (KMT) and Mao Zedong's Communists (CCP) following Japan's WWII surrender.

**Key Events & Timeline:**
- Post-WWII (1945): Japan surrenders; KMT (4.3M troops) vs CCP (900K troops). US supports Chiang with airlifts and 50,000 Marines. General Marshall mediates peace talks that fail.
- 1946: KMT launches General Offensive in June; captures 165 towns and 174,000 km², but fails to destroy main CCP armies.
- 1947: KMT Strongpoints Offensive captures Yan'an (CCP capital), but Mao deliberately abandons it. CCP begins counter-offensives. KMT fails to win quickly.
- 1948: CCP launches Liaoning-Shenyang Offensive, capturing Jinzhou, Changchun, and Shenyang (400,000 KMT losses). The Huaihai Campaign (Nov 1948-Jan 1949) becomes the largest post-WWII battle with 1.8M combatants.
- 1949: CCP captures Beijing (Jan 31), Nanjing, Shanghai (April-May). Mao proclaims People's Republic of China (Oct 1). Chiang flees to Taiwan (Dec 7).

**Why the CCP Won:**
- KMT poor strategy (overstretched forces, focus on cities), low morale, corruption, economic crisis (30% monthly inflation), and harsh discipline led to mass defections (40% desertion rate in training).
- CCP superior strategy (mobile warfare, retreat as tactical advantage, strict party control), land reform programs, captured enemy weapons/troops, and better morale.
- US shifted focus to Japan and stopped most aid to Chiang by 1947.
- Soviet Union provided limited help to CCP but was wary of a strong China.

**Casualties:** ~2M military casualties both sides, ~5M civilian deaths (including famine). Up to 1M landlords killed in CCP-led violence.

**Legacy:** The civil war never officially ended. The Korean War (1950) led the US to send the 7th Fleet to the Taiwan Strait, preventing a CCP invasion of Taiwan and preserving the KMT's Republic of China on the island.
</summary>

URL: https://pacificaffairs.ubc.ca/book-reviews/chinas-civil-war-a-social-history-1945-1949-by-diana-lary

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a book review from Pacific Affairs (published by UBC) of Diana Lary's "China's Civil War: A Social History, 1945-1949" (Cambridge University Press, 2015). The review, written by Matt Galway (UBC), examines Lary's approach to the Chinese Civil War through the lens of trauma theory and social history, moving beyond traditional Marxist and postmodern interpretations. The book uses biographies, memoirs, illustrations, and oral histories to highlight the "painful and divisive social impacts of the war" (12), giving voice to ordinary people who suffered. The eight-chapter volume covers the war chronologically—from the social background after 1927, through GMD instability and Communist resurgence, to the Communists' victory in 1949 and postwar outcomes in the 1950s, including class entrenchment, generational splits, and cross-Taiwan Strait interpretations of the conflict. The review notes two criticisms: Lary's biographical snapshots are too short and distracting, and her reliance on Chalmers Johnson's dated theory that nationalism alone explains peasant mobilization (citing recent scholarship by Chen Yungfa and Prasenatra Duara showing more complex factors). Overall, the review praises the book as a "long-overdue investigation" that breaks the mould of military history by emphasizing social dimensions of civil strife, while noting some issues detract from an otherwise excellent study.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Chinese Civil War was a conflict between the Kuomintang (KMT)-led Republic of China and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), fought intermittently from 1 August 1927 until the Communist victory and the KMT's retreat to Taiwan on 7 December 1949. The war is divided into two phases with an interlude: the first phase (1927–1937) began after the breakdown of the First United Front, which had been formed to defeat regional warlords. The KMT and CCP had allied in the Northern Expedition (1926-1927), but the alliance collapsed after Chiang Kai-shek's Shanghai Massacre of April 1927, in which communists were purged. The CCP launched uprisings including the Nanchang Uprising (1 August 1927) and the Autumn Harvest Uprising, leading to the creation of the Chinese Red Army. The KMT launched encirclement campaigns against communist-controlled "Soviet Zones" in southern China, forcing the CCP's Long March. The interlude (1937–1945) saw a Second United Front formed to fight the Japanese invasion. The second phase (1945–1949) resumed after Japan's defeat, with the Communists gaining the upper hand. The CCP proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949, while the ROC government retreated to Taiwan. A cross-strait standoff continues, with both sides claiming to be the legitimate government of all China, and no armistice or peace treaty has ever been signed. The background traces the collapse of the Qing dynasty, Sun Yat-sen's efforts, Soviet assistance, the formation of the First United Front, and the eventual split between the KMT's left and right wings.
</summary>

Key points include:

- The legacy of the Civil War persists in the CCP's coercive approach to governance, viewing politics as constant conflict.
- An irony noted: China's modern power rests on economics, not Mao's politics, and Taiwan's capitalist "tiger economy" became the unacknowledged model for China's post-Mao development.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Chinese Civil War (1945–49) was a military struggle between the Nationalist Kuomintang (KMT) under Chiang Kai-shek and the Communists (CCP) under Mao Zedong for control of China. The conflict concluded with a Communist victory.

After World War II ended in August 1945, the fragile peace between Nationalists and Communists collapsed. Japan's defeat triggered a race between both sides to control resources and territories in northern China and Manchuria. The U.S. transported Nationalist troops to key cities, while Communist forces occupied much of the hinterland.

Despite initial peace negotiations—including the Chongqing talks (Aug-Oct 1945) where Mao and Chiang agreed in principle to work for a united democratic China—fighting resumed. The U.S. Marshall Mission (Dec 1945) brokered a January 1946 armistice and agreements on government reorganization, constitutional assembly, and military integration. However, these agreements failed as renewed fighting broke out in Manchuria following Soviet withdrawal (March-April 1946). By late 1946, peace talks collapsed entirely.

Key factors in the Communist victory included: the CCP's land-reform program increasing peasant support; Nationalist ineptitude, corruption, and demoralization; and severe inflation in Nationalist-controlled areas. The Nationalists adopted a new constitution in December 1946 without Communist participation.

By 1947, the CCP gained ground in Manchuria. On October 1, 1949, Mao proclaimed the establishment of the People's Republic of China with its capital in Beijing. By the end of 1949, virtually all of mainland China was under Communist control. The Nationalist government re-established itself on Taiwan. Official Communist figures counted about 1.5 million dead and wounded among the People's Liberation Army.

Foreign involvement: The U.S. provided financial, military, and diplomatic support to the Nationalists. The Soviet Union initially supported the Nationalist government, took industrial equipment from Manchuria, but later recognized Mao's regime in 1949. After the Communist victory, China turned to the Soviet Union for guidance in transitioning to socialism.
</summary>

This is a historical article from the U.S. Department of State's Office of the Historian (from the "Milestones" series) documenting the Chinese Revolution of 1949. On October 1, 1949, Mao Zedong declared the creation of the People's Republic of China (PRC), ending the civil war between the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the Nationalist Party (Kuomintang/KMT). The conflict had roots in the 1920s, with brief periods of cooperation (the First and Second United Fronts) interspersed with violent conflict.

During World War II, popular support shifted toward the Communists due to Nationalist corruption, undemocratic policies, and successful Communist land reform efforts. After Japan's surrender, full-scale civil war resumed. Despite U.S. support for Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government (including flying troops into Japanese-controlled territory), the Communists gained strength through grassroots support, superior military organization, and weapons seized from Japanese supplies in Manchuria.

By 1947, the Nationalist government was already looking to Taiwan as a potential retreat. The Truman administration continued military and financial aid to the Nationalists but was unable to prevent the Communist victory. In October 1949, Mao proclaimed the PRC, and Chiang fled to Taiwan.

The establishment of the PRC led to a suspension of U.S.-PRC diplomatic ties for decades. The Truman administration's "China White Paper" (August 1949) failed to protect it from charges of having "lost" China. The Korean War further ended any chance of accommodation. For over twenty years, the U.S. recognized the Republic of China on Taiwan as China's legitimate government.

URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7slhD9PmxII

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a documentary transcript from Real Time History (published February 21, 2025) covering the Chinese Civil War from 1945-1949, examining the conflict between Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists (KMT) and Mao Zedong's Communists (CCP) following Japan's WWII surrender.

**Key Events & Timeline:**
- Post-WWII (1945): Japan surrenders; KMT (4.3M troops) vs CCP (900K troops). US supports Chiang with airlifts and 50,000 Marines. General Marshall mediates peace talks that fail.
- 1946: KMT launches General Offensive in June; captures 165 towns and 174,000 km², but fails to destroy main CCP armies.
- 1947: KMT Strongpoints Offensive captures Yan'an (CCP capital), but Mao deliberately abandons it. CCP begins counter-offensives. KMT fails to win quickly.
- 1948: CCP launches Liaoning-Shenyang Offensive, capturing Jinzhou, Changchun, and Shenyang (400,000 KMT losses). The Huaihai Campaign (Nov 1948-Jan 1949) becomes the largest post-WWII battle with 1.8M combatants.
- 1949: CCP captures Beijing (Jan 31), Nanjing, Shanghai (April-May). Mao proclaims People's Republic of China (Oct 1). Chiang flees to Taiwan (Dec 7).

**Why the CCP Won:**
- KMT poor strategy (overstretched forces, focus on cities), low morale, corruption, economic crisis (30% monthly inflation), and harsh discipline led to mass defections (40% desertion rate in training).
- CCP superior strategy (mobile warfare, retreat as tactical advantage, strict party control), land reform programs, captured enemy weapons/troops, and better morale.
- US shifted focus to Japan and stopped most aid to Chiang by 1947.
- Soviet Union provided limited help to CCP but was wary of a strong China.

**Casualties:** ~2M military casualties both sides, ~5M civilian deaths (including famine). Up to 1M landlords killed in CCP-led violence.

**Legacy:** The civil war never officially ended. The Korean War (1950) led the US to send the 7th Fleet to the Taiwan Strait, preventing a CCP invasion of Taiwan and preserving the KMT's Republic of China on the island.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a book review from Pacific Affairs (published by UBC) of Diana Lary's "China's Civil War: A Social History, 1945-1949" (Cambridge University Press, 2015). The review, written by Matt Galway (UBC), examines Lary's approach to the Chinese Civil War through the lens of trauma theory and social history, moving beyond traditional Marxist and postmodern interpretations. The book uses biographies, memoirs, illustrations, and oral histories to highlight the "painful and divisive social impacts of the war" (12), giving voice to ordinary people who suffered. The eight-chapter volume covers the war chronologically—from the social background after 1927, through GMD instability and Communist resurgence, to the Communists' victory in 1949 and postwar outcomes in the 1950s, including class entrenchment, generational splits, and cross-Taiwan Strait interpretations of the conflict. The review notes two criticisms: Lary's biographical snapshots are too short and distracting, and her reliance on Chalmers Johnson's dated theory that nationalism alone explains peasant mobilization (citing recent scholarship by Chen Yungfa and Prasenatra Duara showing more complex factors). Overall, the review praises the book as a "long-overdue investigation" that breaks the mould of military history by emphasizing social dimensions of civil strife, while noting some issues detract from an otherwise excellent study.

The Chinese Civil War was a series of conflicts between the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Nationalist government (Kuomintang/KMT), fought in two distinct stages: 1927–1937 and 1946–1949. Hostilities were largely halted between 1937 and 1945 when both sides formed a begrudging alliance against Japan during WWII.

After the Qing dynasty's overthrow in 1912, China became a republic but fell into warlord control. The First United Front (1924) between the KMT and CPC aimed to defeat northern warlords, but it ended after the 1927 Shanghai Massacre, where KMT leader Chiang Kai-shek ordered the killing of thousands of communists. This triggered the civil war, with Mao Zedong leading peasant revolts and believing rural support was key to defeating the KMT.

Chiang gained control of China by 1928, but internal disputes and Japanese expansion (invasion of Manchuria in 1931) weakened the country. Mao established the Chinese Soviet Republic in Jiangxi. The KMT's encirclement campaigns forced the CPC's famous Long March (1934–1935), a 6,000-mile retreat from which only about 10% of the 100,000 marchers survived. The march cemented Mao's leadership.

A Second United Front formed in 1937 after Japan invaded Beijing. During WWII, both sides fought Japan separately while occasionally clashing. After Japan's 1945 surrender, the civil war resumed. The CPC, aided by peasant support and Mao's land reforms, gained the upper hand. By June 1949, Beijing, Shanghai, Nanking, and Tianjin fell to communists. Mao declared the People's Republic of China on October 1, 1949.

Chiang fled to Taiwan in December 1949, establishing a rival government. No peace treaty has ever been signed. Estimated fatalities range as high as 7.5 million, with atrocities committed by both sides. The status of Taiwan remains contested—China views it as a breakaway province, while many on the island consider it a separate nation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Collaboration in Japanese-occupied China (1937-1945): Old and New Questions | Occupation Studies ---
URL: https://fasos-research.nl/occupationstudies/collaboration-in-japanese-occupied-china-1937-1945-old-and-new-questions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by David Serfass (Inalco-IFRAE, Paris) surveys the historiography of collaboration in Japanese-occupied China (1937-1945), focusing on the collaboration regimes established after Japan's invasion of Chinese provinces from July 1937 to October 1938. Key collaboration governments included the Provisional Government in Beijing (Dec. 1937), the Reformed Government in Nanjing (Mar. 1938), and most notably the Reorganized National Government (RNG) chaired by former Premier Wang Jingwei (Mar. 1940), which claimed legitimacy as the successor to the pre-war National Government. Over 200 million people lived under Japanese occupation.

The historiographical debate revolves around three questions: Who were the collaborators? Why did they collaborate? How was collaboration conducted? These questions have been approached from two opposing directions: one viewing collaboration as a historical anomaly to be denounced, and another contextualizing it within broader historical developments.

**Who were collaborators?** The term "hanjian" (traitors) has been politically charged, with the CPC historically using it to delegitimize the KMT. Western historians like John Hunter Boyle (1972) and Timothy Brook (coining "collaborationist nationalism") have offered more nuanced assessments, while Chinese historians have moved from class-based denunciations to more complex analyses post-1980s.

**Why collaborate?** Explanations range from teleological (looking for warning signs in collaborators' pasts) to circumstantial (contextual choices). Political factors include anti-communism, Asianism, and KMT internal rivalries, while sociological factors include studying in Japan or Japanese marriages. Chinese historians have shifted from class-based explanations to psychological determinism and more recently to complex causal analyses.

**How was collaboration conducted?** Scholarship has moved from viewing collaboration regimes as mere "puppets" to recognizing their autonomy and internal negotiations. Historians now examine the concrete functioning of pro-Japanese institutions and the collaborators' agency vis-à-vis Japanese occupiers. Brook argues collaboration regimes should be studied as part of China's modern state trajectory.

**New research perspectives** include: cultural history (visual culture, music), spatial expansion beyond the Lower-Yangzi region and North China, trans-war approaches (post-1945 continuities), prosopography of middle/low-level administration, study of the Japanese adviser system, puppet armies, and connections within Japan's broader colonial empire. The author calls for bridging gaps between studies of occupied and free China, and between occupation studies and other historical fields.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Altogether, more than two hundred million people were brought under the direct or indirect rule of the Japanese authorities.", "Timothy Brook went further by coining the term 'collaborationist nationalism'. He thus makes the point that pro-Japanese collaboration deserves to be studied as one side of the Chinese elites' common effort to 'save the nation'.", "Against a tendency among earlier Chinese historians to address the former as historical anomalies, Timothy Brook placed them as an integral part of China's modern state trajectory by arguing that 'our disdain for forced ideology produces its opposite, confirmation of the natural legitimacy of state sovereignty' (Brook 2005, p. 223).", "Future research on Japanese-occupied China should not only further explore collaboration in all its aspects, but also attempt to better bridge the gap with other historical fields and broader questions emanating from the comparative field of occupation studies."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The webpage is the Wikipedia article on the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945), a major conflict in East Asia that was part of the Pacific Theater of World War II. The war began with the Marco Polo Bridge Incident on July 7, 1937, and concluded with Japan's surrender on September 2, 1945, resulting in a Chinese victory. The conflict involved China (Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek and Communists under Mao Zedong, with a United Front against Japan) fighting against the Empire of Japan and its puppet states (Manchukuo, Wang Jingwei regime, Mengjiang).

Key background includes Japanese expansion, the Warlord Era, Nationalist reunification, and the start of the Chinese Civil War. Pre-war events included the 1931 invasion of Manchuria and sporadic Japanese encroachments. The war progressed through phases: 1937 outbreak (Marco Polo Bridge, Battle of Shanghai, Fall of Nanjing and the Nanjing Massacre); 1938 strategic retreat (Xuzhou, Wuhan, Yellow River flood); 1939–1941 stalemate (Chinese counter-offensives, Japan's Three Alls Policy, United Front collapse); 1942–1943 Allied entry (foreign aid, Burma campaign); 1944 renewed Japanese offensives (Operation Ichi-Go); and 1945 conclusion (final Chinese offensives, Japanese surrender).

Casualties were enormous: Chinese military casualties of approximately 3.85 million, Japanese military casualties of 1.5~ million, and 12,000,000+ civilian deaths. The war involved widespread use of guerrilla tactics, chemical and biological warfare by Japan. The aftermath saw the resumption of the Chinese Civil War. The legacy includes commemorations, controversy over historical revisionism, and implications for the political status of Taiwan.

URL: https://www.usmcu.edu/Outreach/Marine-Corps-University-Press/MCU-Journal/JAMS-vol-11-no-2/Same-Water-Different-Dreams

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Marine Corps University Press (JAMS, vol. 11, no. 2) by Andrew Rhodes examines the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95 and its enduring lessons for contemporary naval warfare, particularly regarding Chinese strategic thinking. The war was a contest for control of Korea, where Japan's Imperial Navy destroyed China's Beiyang Fleet despite China having modern warships. Key battles included the Battle of Pungdo Island (July 1894), the Battle of Pyongyang, and the pivotal Battle of the Yalu (September 17, 1894), where Japan prevailed due to superior tactics, quick-firing guns, and Chinese command failures. The war ended with the Treaty of Shimonoseki, ceding Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula to Japan.

The author analyzes three consistent themes from recent Chinese publications about the war's lessons: (1) the need to inculcate "maritime consciousness" (haiyang yishi) in the Chinese people, as Qing society had no connection to the sea; (2) the importance of building strong institutions to sustain seapower, contrasting Japan's unified Meiji-era institutions with China's fractured, corrupt Qing system; and (3) the imperative to employ the navy actively and aggressively in combat, rather than the Qing's passive defensive strategy that ceded sea control. Chinese authors criticize the Qing policy of "war avoidance" and argue the Beiyang Fleet should have taken the fight to the enemy.

The article notes that American officers like Philo N. McGiffin and Alfred Thayer Mahan analyzed the war at the time, but it has since been neglected in Western scholarship. The author argues that understanding how Chinese strategists interpret this history is essential for American planners, as the PLAN of today is larger than the U.S. Navy and its officers have absorbed lessons that would lead them to sortie their fleet aggressively in a future conflict, not remain in a defensive posture. The article concludes that the third lesson—active employment of the fleet in combat—remains untested for the modern PLAN, making it a critical area for U.S. wargaming and scenario development.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a conference summary of the "Review and Prospect of the Study of the History of China's War of Resistance Against Japan" symposium, held on April 12, 2015, at Renmin University of China. The event was co-organized by Renmin University's Institute of CPC History and Theory and the CASS Institute of Modern History's Revolutionary History Research Office, bringing together over 100 scholars from major Chinese universities and research institutions.

**Part 1: Recent Advances in Research**
The symposium noted that the study of the War of Resistance Against Japan has become an academic hotspot. Key advances include: (1) rich, diverse research output with hundreds of books and thousands of papers annually; (2) extensive archival materials from both Chinese and international sources (including Japan, the US, UK, France, Germany, and Russia); (3) growing international academic exchange, particularly among China, Japan, and South Korea. Scholars emphasized that the war should be viewed as a pivotal turning point in China's national rejuvenation and as the Eastern main battlefield of the global anti-fascist war. The study of the war was divided into two periods: pre-1995 (focused on exposing Japanese atrocities) and post-1995 (expanded to themes of national rejuvenation). Debates on the roles of the CPC and KMT, Japanese war crimes (including the "comfort women" issue, the Nanjing Massacre, and the Tokyo Trials), and war memory were also discussed.

**Part 2: Problems in Current Research**
Scholars identified several issues: (1) inadequate use of foreign sources and limited international perspectives; (2) interference from nationalist sentiment and political considerations, particularly in popular/sensationalist writing; (3) weak research on actual military/war history (e.g., guerrilla warfare, battlefield strategy); (4) insufficient academic study of occupied areas and puppet regimes, which remains at a superficial, condemnatory level.

**Part 3: Consensus for Future Development**
Scholars agreed on four directions: (1) greater use of overseas archives and local Chinese county/municipal archives; (2) strengthening theoretical and methodological frameworks, borrowing from Western and social science approaches; (3) combining macro-narrative with micro-empirical research, and top-down with bottom-up perspectives; (4) balancing national historiography with a global historical perspective to promote more academic and internationalized study of the war.
</summary>

URL: https://www.krzzjn.com/uploadfile/2020/1207/20201207100620254.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a conference summary published in the journal "抗日战争研究" (Studies of China's Resistance War Against Japan), 2019 Issue No. 4, reporting on the "Seventy Years of Resistance War Studies: Retrospect and Prospect" academic symposium held at Nankai University from November 30 to December 1, 2019. The conference brought together over 40 scholars to review 70 years of academic research on China's War of Resistance Against Japan (1937-1945), since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949.

Key organizational details: The symposium was co-hosted by Nankai University's History Department, the editorial board of "Studies of China's Resistance War Against Japan," and the War of Resistance Memorial Network. It was chaired by Gao Shihua (editor-in-chief of the journal), with opening remarks by Wang Jianlang (Director of the Institute of Modern History, CASS), Tang Zhixuan (Deputy Editor of the Memorial Network), and Jiang Pei (Dean of Nankai History Department).

The symposium covered six sessions organized around thematic areas:

**1. Overall and Conceptual Issues:**
- Zang Yunhu (Peking University) analyzed the "hot and cold" cycles of resistance war studies, noting that before the 1980s the field was "cold," but has since become "gradually hot," though many areas remain under-researched (e.g., the "14-year resistance war" concept, China's wartime economy, society, and culture, occupied territories, Japanese invasion studies).
- Chen Qianping (Nanjing University) proposed a three-stage periodization for the 14-year war: (1) partial resistance before the Marco Polo Bridge Incident (July 1937); (2) China's independent full-scale resistance from July 1937 to Pearl Harbor; (3) international resistance after Pearl Harbor—the most critical stage, which laid the foundation for China's victory and postwar international status.
- Li Jinzheng (Nankai University) discussed the difficulty of writing a comprehensive history of the war, noting three challenges: insufficient attention to foundational social, economic, and cultural forces; the need to address both the anti-Japanese struggle and the CCP-KMT contradictions; and the relative neglect of KMT rear-area resistance.
- Wu Zhijun (CCP History Research editorial board) called for scholars to go beyond the war itself and examine how historians view, study, and represent the war, placing it in broader political, social, and cultural contexts.
- Zhang Sheng (Nanjing University) argued that historical research cannot avoid "fragments" but should not become fragmented; micro-level research can serve larger questions, but fragmentation can lead to historical nihilism.
- Bian Xiuyue (CASS) examined the usage of terms like "comprehensive resistance" and "national resistance," cautioning against rigid politicization of these terms.

**2. CCP (Chinese Communist Party) Resistance:**
- Zhang Yi (Shanghai University of Finance and Economics) reviewed 21st-century scholarship on CCP mass mobilization, noting three shifts: from traditional party history to social and cultural history; from "grand narrative" to "micro-narrative"; and from single to multiple sources. However, insufficient use of Japanese-language materials hampers a full understanding from the Japanese perspective.
- Li Lifeng (Nanjing University) analyzed the CCP's rural political mobilization, identifying two consistent approaches: interest-based mobilization and identity/emotion-based mobilization.
- Li Bingkui (Peking University) noted that "mass movements" remain under-studied, and called for comparative studies across CCP base areas, KMT areas, occupied territories, and overseas Chinese communities.
- Zheng Lizhu (Hebei University) reviewed 70 years of scholarship on the Jin-Cha-Ji (Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei) base area, noting that social history approaches have flourished since 2000.
- Huang Daoxuan (CASS) discussed the May 1938 CCP decision to advance into the North China plain as a turning point, linking it to Mao Zedong's "On Protracted War."
- Zhang Baijia (CCP Central Committee History and Literature Research Institute) urged greater use of foreign observers' records and noted that China's research on war trauma lags behind international WWII studies, while Sino-Japanese war reconciliation remains an urgent issue.
- Li Mingnan (Nankai University) traced how the CCP's revolutionary experience shaped its postwar perceptions and policies toward Japan.
- Lu Xijun (Daito Bunka University, Japan) divided Japanese scholarship on wartime CCP history into two periods: 1945-1979 dominated by "revolution-centered historiography," and post-1980s "relativization" that moved beyond binary good/evil frameworks.

**3. Japanese Invasion of China:**
- Qi Jianmin (Nagasaki Prefectural University, Japan) traced the shift in Japanese research from "Tenno-system fascism theory" to "total war system theory," noting that the latter, emerging after the Cold War, tends to downplay war responsibility and even legitimize wartime policies by linking them to postwar development.
- Liu Yuebing (Nankai University) analyzed the ideological logic of Japan's modern invasion of China, focusing on the kokutai (national polity) theory and Nihon seishin (Japanese spirit) theory.
- Tang Liguo (Peking University) examined Japan's "thought war" (ideological warfare) as a propaganda campaign and a framework for understanding how Japanese elites, intellectuals, and the public accepted the war.
- Wang Meiping (Nankai University) reviewed three periods of postwar Japanese scholarship on the opium invasion policy (1985 and 2000 as dividing lines).
- Xiao Hongsong (Hebei University) noted that Chinese scholarship on wartime opium issues has produced over 80 articles and 11 books, but foreign-language sources remain scarce.
- Ji Chen (Sun Yat-sen University, Zhuhai) examined the compilation of the official Japanese war history of the First Sino-Japanese War (1894-95), noting that after 1903 its editorial policy shifted to beautify Japan's war initiation, avoid military critique, and reduce length, with lasting influence on later official war histories.
- Guo Xunchun (Nankai University) reviewed domestic and Japanese research on modern Japanese military systems.
- Song Zhiyong (Nankai University) traced three periods in Japanese scholarship on the Tokyo Trials, noting that political rightward shifts since the 1990s have significantly affected research.
- Yin Yanjun (Kanto Gakuin University, Japan) discussed disagreements between Chinese and Japanese scholars on whether the Marco Polo Bridge Incident was planned, concluding that while the timing and location may have been contingent, Japan's invasion of China was inevitable.

**4. Other Topics:**
- Zhu Hanguo (Beijing Normal University) discussed Wang Guilin's contributions to resistance war studies, including his views on the "one battlefield vs. two battlefields" debate, the "eight-year vs. fourteen-year war" question, and the nature of Chiang Kai-shek's group.
- Jiang Pei (Nankai University) traced Wei Hongyun's evolving research from military campaigns to fiscal, economic, and social history, with a growing emphasis on international perspectives.
- Zhao Qingyun (CASS) examined the exchanges between Japanese leftist historian Inoue Kiyoshi and Chinese academia.
- Su Shengxiong (Academia Sinica, Taipei) noted that military history research in Taiwan was dominated by the military for the first 40 years, then shifted to academia, with a move from traditional to "new military history" emphasizing war-society relations.
- Qi Xiaolin (CCP Central Party School) advocated for studying war history through material factors (food, ammunition, medicine, communications) from an international perspective.
- Guo Yang (Nanjing University) reviewed 70 years of scholarship on KMT political warfare, calling for new perspectives on party-army relations.
- Li Bin (Hunan Academy of Social Sciences) discussed Hunan's resistance war studies.
- Zeng Chongbi (Chongqing Technology and Business University) reviewed local fiscal studies during the war.
- He Jiangfeng (Nankai University) re-examined the "He-Umezu Agreement" (1935) controversy.

In the final discussion, Gao Shihua concluded that the field of resistance war studies, as a mature discipline, should engage in self-reflection and maintain a sense of crisis. He urged younger scholars to master at least one foreign language and to strengthen use of Japanese sources and research.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Wang Jianlang pointed out that among all periods of modern Chinese history, resistance war studies is the most popular, and the recent National Social Science Fund 'Special Project on War of Resistance Studies' with nearly 30 approved projects has further boosted its热度, yet beneath the popularity there remain many insufficiently studied areas.", "Zang Yunhu argued that before the 1980s—the first 40 years of resistance war studies—the overall research situation was 'cold'; since the 1980s, it has entered a 'gradually hot' state and reached a climax, but still exhibits 'hot within cold' and 'cold within heat'.", "Lu Xijun divided Japanese scholarship on wartime CCP history into two periods: 1945-1979 dominated by 'revolution-centered historiography,' and the post-1980s 'relativization' era that overcomes binary good/evil frameworks.", "Gao Shihua concluded that the field of resistance war studies, as a mature discipline, should have the capacity for self-summary and self-reflection, and must maintain a sense of crisis; the younger generation should master at least one foreign language and strengthen their grasp of Japanese research information and use of Japanese materials."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: 贺江枫、叶子锐 | 日记与中国抗日战争史学术研讨会综述 ---
URL: http://jds.cass.cn/xscg/xslw/202403/t20240312_5737918.shtml

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The webpage is a conference summary published in *抗日战争研究* (2023年第4期) by贺江枫 and 叶子锐, reviewing the "Diaries and the History of China's War of Resistance Against Japan Academic Symposium" held November 3-5, 2023, at Nankai University. The symposium was co-organized by Nankai University's History Department, the Center for Chinese and Foreign Civilizations, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) Institute of Modern History's War of Resistance Research Office, and the journal *抗日战争研究*. Over 30 scholars from leading Chinese universities and research institutes participated, presenting 20 papers across five sessions.

**Key Themes:**

1. **Diaries and Anti-Japanese Base Areas (Revolutionary Base Research):** Papers examined CCP cadre diaries (e.g., Gao Lu) to explore rural investigation, party-building, and the evolution of the party-state system. Emphasis was placed on using diaries to understand policy-making, organization, and daily life in base areas.

2. **Diaries and Nationalist-Controlled Areas (Guomindang/Guotongqu):** Papers utilized diaries of Chiang Kai-shek, Chen Bulei, Chen Kewen, and Zhang Xueliang to analyze high-level politics, military strategy (e.g., the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign), diplomacy (Sino-German relations in 1940), and the publication of Chiang's *China's Destiny*.

3. **Diaries and Occupied Areas (Lunxianqu):** Papers examined ordinary people's diaries (e.g., engineer Sun Shoushan, village intellectual Lü Shunxiang, Peking opera actor Xun Huisheng) to reveal daily life, mentalities of fear and survival, and local military integration under Japanese occupation.

4. **Diaries and Wartime Intellectuals:** Papers focused on the diaries of Zheng Tianting, Mei Yiqi, and other scholars to examine the restoration of Peking University after the war, field investigations by scholars in the rear areas, and the spread of wartime information.

5. **Foreign-Language Diaries:** Papers explored diaries of Western residents (e.g., Bertrand Beitler in Shanghai) and Japanese Prime Minister Hara Takashi's diary to provide international perspectives on the war and Sino-Japanese diplomacy.

**Roundtable Discussion:** Scholars debated the academic value of diaries (richness, continuity, ability to restore human agency), methodological approaches (caution about privacy, authenticity, and the need to corroborate with archives), and limitations (fragmentation, homogenization, and the need to distinguish between individual and public dimensions). The consensus was that diaries are crucial for deepening War of Resistance research but must be used critically and in combination with other sources.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Diary as a type of historical material has irreplaceable significance for deepening the study of the history of the War of Resistance, said CASS researcher Wang Jianlang and Professor Jiang Pei in their opening remarks., Diaries can restore the 'human' subject that has long been buried in historical research, noted Professor Jiang Pei., The use of diaries should avoid homogenization and pay attention to the commonalities and differences presented in diaries from different regions and individuals, argued Professor Zhang Junfeng., Diaries should be cross-referenced with archival materials, and emotional expressions in diaries should be stripped as much as possible, suggested Associate Researcher He Jiangfeng., People's limitations determine the limitations of diaries; in the current era of explosive growth in historical materials, more attention should be paid to the interpretation of historical materials, stated Professor Li Xiang.
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://weread.qq.com/web/bookDetail/a1a32140811e8a97eg011789

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a book listing for "当代中国抗日战争史研究" (Research on the History of the War of Resistance Against Japan in Contemporary China), edited by Du Jidong and Wu Minchao, published in August 2025. The book is a comprehensive research survey covering the history of the War of Resistance against Japan (Second Sino-Japanese War) within mainland China, excluding Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, and foreign studies. It is structured in three parts: (1) overviewing the development of the topic over 70 years by stages; (2) introducing important themes, developmental context, and innovative research; and (3) identifying existing problems and offering forward-looking thoughts. --- SOURCE 13: 中国历史研究院 ---
URL: http://hrczh.cass.cn/sxqy/zgs/202502/t20250228_5853389.shtml

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The webpage announces the publication of "The History of China's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression: Wartime Politics" (Volume 3), authored by Wang Chaoguang, a researcher at the Institute of World History, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. This volume is part of an eight-volume comprehensive history of China's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, published by the Institute of Modern History. The book examines the political dimensions of China's nationwide war of resistance (1937-1945), emphasizing that the war was a pivotal moment for China's national rejuvenation. 

Key themes include: the国民党 (Nationalist Party/KMT) as the ruling party proposing "war of resistance and national reconstruction" while facing organizational deficiencies and corruption; the中国共产党 (Chinese Communist Party/CCP) implementing New Democratic policies in base areas and mobilizing the masses; and the complex KMT-CCP relationship of cooperation and conflict throughout the war. The volume argues that the KMT's leadership declined while the CCP's grew, a shift that shaped postwar Chinese politics. The book covers chapters on the outbreak of all-out resistance, KMT's wartime governance, multiple dimensions of wartime politics, CCP's base area building, fluctuating KMT-CCP relations, and late-war political developments.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Chinese people, with their tenacious historical heritage, unruffled spiritual temperament, and generous sacrifice, ultimately defeated the Japanese aggressors and achieved a complete victory in the War of Resistance, thus establishing a monument for the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation since modern times.", "The center of wartime Chinese politics was how to fully resist Japanese aggression, how to fight to the end, and strive for China's complete victory in the War of Resistance; the protagonists were the Chinese Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party.", "The Nationalist Party's detachment from the people, organizational laxity, emphasis on words over deeds, and rampant corruption contrasted sharply with the Communist Party's mobilization of the masses, organizational strengthening, pragmatism, and vigorous governance.", "The rise and fall of leadership between the Kuomintang and Communist Party not only concerned the development of wartime Chinese politics but also laid the groundwork for the direction of postwar Chinese politics.", "The research on the history of China's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression is a cause that should be passed down through generations."
</key_excerpts>

Approximately 1.39 billion people, or 17% of the global population, speak one of the [varieties of Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varieties_of_Chinese "Varieties of Chinese") as their [first language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_language "First language").[[1]](#cite_note-e28-3)

The different Chinese language varieties together form the largest branch of the [Sino-Tibetan languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Tibetan_languages "Sino-Tibetan languages"). While the [Chinese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_government "Chinese government") defines all spoken Chinese varieties as merely diverse [dialects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialect "Dialect") of a single language, the frequent lack of [mutual intelligibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_intelligibility "Mutual intelligibility"), especially among those outside of the dominant [northern varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_Chinese "Mandarin Chinese"), has led [linguists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguist "Linguist") to consider them as separate languages within a [language family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_family "Language family").[[g]](#cite_note-10) Investigation of the [historical relationships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_linguistics "Historical linguistics") among the varieties of Chinese is ongoing. Currently, most classifications posit 7 to 13 main regional groups based on phonetic developments from [Middle Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Chinese "Middle Chinese"), of which the most spoken by far is [Mandarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_Chinese "Mandarin Chinese") with 66%, or around 800 million speakers, followed by [Min](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Min_Chinese "Min Chinese") (75 million, e.g., [Hokkien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hokkien "Hokkien") and [Teochew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teochew_Min "Teochew Min")), [Wu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wu_Chinese "Wu Chinese") (74 million, e.g., [Shanghainese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghainese "Shanghainese")) and [Yue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yue_Chinese "Yue Chinese") (68 million, e.g., [Cantonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese "Cantonese")).[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChinese_Academy_of_Social_Sciences20123,_125-11) These groups are unintelligible to each other, and many of their subgroups are unintelligible with other subgroups within the same branch (e.g. [Northern Min](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Min "Northern Min") vs. [Southern Min](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Min "Southern Min")). There are, however, transitional areas where varieties from different branches share enough features for some limited intelligibility, including [New Xiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Xiang "New Xiang") with [Southwestern Mandarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_Mandarin "Southwestern Mandarin"), [Xuanzhou Wu Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xuanzhou_Wu_Chinese "Xuanzhou Wu Chinese") with [Lower Yangtze Mandarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Yangtze_Mandarin "Lower Yangtze Mandarin"), [Jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_Chinese "Jin Chinese") with [Central Plains Mandarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Plains_Mandarin "Central Plains Mandarin") and certain divergent dialects of [Hakka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hakka_Chinese "Hakka Chinese") with [Gan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gan_Chinese "Gan Chinese"). All varieties of Chinese are [tonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tone_(linguistics) "Tone (linguistics)") at least to some degree, and are largely [analytic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_language "Analytic language").

The Chinese language is [transcribed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcription_(linguistics) "Transcription (linguistics)") via a [writing system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writing_system "Writing system") consisting of [logographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logograph "Logograph") [characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_characters "Chinese characters"), historically in the [grammatical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammatical "Grammatical") form of [Literary Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_Chinese "Literary Chinese"). The earliest attested [written Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Written_Chinese "Written Chinese") consists of the [oracle bone inscriptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_bone_inscriptions "Oracle bone inscriptions") created during the [Shang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty "Shang dynasty") c. 1250 BCE. The phonetic categories of [Old Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chinese "Old Chinese") can be reconstructed from the rhymes of ancient [Chinese poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_poetry "Chinese poetry"). During the [Northern and Southern dynasties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_and_Southern_dynasties "Northern and Southern dynasties"), Middle Chinese went through several [sound changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_change "Sound change") and split into several varieties following prolonged geographic and political separation. The *[Qieyun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qieyun "Qieyun")*, a [rhyme dictionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyme_dictionary "Rhyme dictionary"), recorded a compromise between the pronunciations of different regions. The royal courts of the Ming and early [Qing dynasties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasties "Qing dynasties") operated using a [koiné language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koiné_language "Koiné language") known as *[Guanhua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_(late_imperial_lingua_franca) "Mandarin (late imperial lingua franca)")*, based on the [Nanjing dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_dialect "Nanjing dialect") of Mandarin.

[Standard Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Chinese "Standard Chinese"), a [standard language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_language "Standard language") based on the [Beijing dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_dialect "Beijing dialect") and first officially adopted in the 1930s, is the current [official language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_language "Official language") of both the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") ([Mainland China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China")) and the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China "Republic of China") (Taiwan), one of the [four official languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Singapore "Languages of Singapore") of [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore"), and one of the [six official languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_languages_of_the_United_Nations "Official languages of the United Nations") of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_N

Approximately 1.39 billion people (17% of the global population) speak a variety of Chinese as their first language. Chinese varieties form the largest branch of the Sino-Tibetan language family. While the Chinese government considers all spoken varieties as dialects of a single language, linguists often classify them as separate languages due to lack of mutual intelligibility, especially among non-northern varieties. The major regional groups include Mandarin (66%, ~800 million speakers), Min (75 million, e.g., Hokkien), Wu (74 million, e.g., Shanghainese), and Yue (68 million, e.g., Cantonese), among others. All varieties are tonal and largely analytic. The writing system uses logographic Chinese characters, with the earliest attested written Chinese from oracle bone inscriptions of the Shang dynasty (c. 1250 BCE). Standard Chinese, based on the Beijing dialect, was adopted in the 1930s and is the official language of Mainland China, Taiwan, one of Singapore's four official languages, and one of the six official languages of the United Nations.
