***The Rape of Nanking: The Forgotten Holocaust of World War II*** is a [bestselling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bestselling "Bestselling") 1997 [non-fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fiction "Non-fiction") book written by [Iris Chang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iris_Chang "Iris Chang") about the 1937–1938 [Nanjing Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre "Nanjing Massacre")—the [mass murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_murder "Mass murder") and the [mass rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wartime_sexual_violence "Wartime sexual violence") of Chinese civilians which was committed by the [Imperial Japanese Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Japanese_Army "Imperial Japanese Army") in [Nanjing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing "Nanjing") (Nanking), the capital of the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912–1949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)"), immediately after the [Battle of Nanjing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Nanjing "Battle of Nanjing") during the [Second Sino-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War "Second Sino-Japanese War"). It describes the events which lead up to the Nanjing Massacre, provides graphic details of the war crimes and the atrocities which were committed by Japanese troops, and it lambasts the [Japanese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_government "Japanese government") for its [refusal to acknowledge the atrocities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre_denial "Nanjing Massacre denial"). It also criticizes the Japanese people for their ignorance about the massacre. It is one of the first major English-language books to introduce the Nanjing Massacre to [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world") and [Eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_world "Eastern world") readers alike, and it has been translated into several languages.[[1]](#cite_note-1) The book significantly renewed public interest in [Japanese wartime conduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_war_crimes "Japanese war crimes") in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea "Korea"), [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") (including the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines")) and the [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific "Pacific").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

The book received acclaim and criticism by the public and academics. It has been praised as a work that "shows more clearly than any previous account" the extent and brutality of the episode,[[3]](#cite_note-KirbyForward-3) while elements of Chang's analysis of the motivations for the events, [Japanese culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Japan "Culture of Japan"), and her calculations of the total number of people who were killed and raped were criticized as inaccurate because of her lack of training as a historian.[[4]](#cite_note-Fogel-4) Chang's research on the book was credited with the finding of the diaries of [John Rabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rabe "John Rabe") and [Minnie Vautrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnie_Vautrin "Minnie Vautrin"), both of whom played important roles in the [Nanking Safety Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanking_Safety_Zone "Nanking Safety Zone"), a designated area in Nanjing that protected Chinese civilians during the Nanjing Massacre.[[5]](#cite_note-SFGate2005-04-17-5)

The book prompted [AOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL "AOL") executive [Ted Leonsis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Leonsis "Ted Leonsis") to fund and produce *[Nanking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanking_(2007_film) "Nanking (2007 film)")*, a 2007 [documentary film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_film "Documentary film") about the massacre.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

## Background

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

### Inspiration

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Inspiration")]

When she was a child, Chang's parents told her that during the [Nanjing Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre "Nanjing Massacre"), the Japanese "sliced babies not just in half but in thirds and fourths." Her parents and their families had escaped from [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") by moving to [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan") and after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), they moved to the United States. In the introduction of *The Rape of Nanking,* she wrote that throughout her childhood, the Nanjing Massacre "remained buried in the back of [her] mind as a metaphor for unspeakable evil." When she searched the local public libraries in her school and found nothing, she wondered why no one had written a book about it.[[7]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking7-8-7)

The subject of the Nanjing Massacre entered Chang's life again almost two decades later when she learned that film producers had completed documentary films about it. One of the film producers was Shao Tzuping, who helped produce *Magee's Testament*, a film that contains footage of the Nanjing Massacre, shot by the [missionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missionary "Missionary") [John Magee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Magee_(missionary) "John Magee (missionary)").[[8]](#cite_note-Princeton-8) The other producer was Nancy Tong, who, together with [Christine Choy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Choy "Christine Choy"), produced and co-directed *In The Name of the Emperor*,[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] a film containing a series of interviews with Chinese, American, and Japanese citizens.[[8]](#cite_note-Princeton-8) Chang began talking to Shao and Tong, and soon she was connected to a network of activists who felt the need to document and publicize the Nanjing Massacre.[[9]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking8-9-9): 8–9

In December 1994, she attended a conference on the Nanjing Massacre, held in [Cupertino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupertino "Cupertino"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), and what she saw and heard at the conference motivated her to write her 1997 book*.*[[10]](#cite_note-Penguin-10) As she wrote in the book's introduction, while she was at the conference:

> I was suddenly in a panic that this terrifying disrespect for death and dying, this reversion in human social evolution, would be reduced to a footnote of history, treated like a harmless glitch in a computer program that might or might not again cause a problem, unless someone forced the world to remember it.[[9]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking8-9-9): 10

### Research

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Research")]

Chang spent two years conducting research for the book.[[5]](#cite_note-SFGate2005-04-17-5) She found source materials in the US, including diaries, films, and photographs of missionaries, journalists, and military officers who were in Nanjing at the time of the massacre.[[9]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking8-9-9): 11 Additionally, she traveled to Nanjing to interview survivors of the Nanjing Massacre and to read Chinese accounts and confessions by Japanese army veterans.[[11]](#cite_note-SFGate1998-11) Also, she incorporated the most recent work on the subject by Chinese and Chinese-American historians by including many disturbing photographs and a myriad of translated documents.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Before its publication, the book was reviewed by [Rana Mitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rana_Mitter "Rana Mitter") and Christian Jessen-Klingenberg of the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"); [Carol Gluck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Gluck "Carol Gluck") of [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"); and [William C. Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._Kirby "William C. Kirby") of [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University").[[13]](#cite_note-13) At the time of writing, the Japanese government classified Japan's World War 2 archives, making archival records unavailable to investigators.[[14]](#cite_note-Alan_Rosenbaum-14)

#### The diaries

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: The diaries")]

Chang's research led her to make what one *[San Francisco Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Chronicle "San Francisco Chronicle")* article called "Significant Discoveries" on the subject of the Nanjing Massacre, in the forms of the diaries of two Westerners who were in Nanjing leading efforts to save lives during the Japanese invasion.[[5]](#cite_note-SFGate2005-04-17-5) The diaries documented the events of the Nanjing Massacre from the perspectives of their writers, and provided detailed accounts of atrocities that they saw, as well as information surrounding the circumstances of the [Nanking Safety Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanking_Safety_Zone "Nanking Safety Zone").

One diary was written by [John Rabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rabe "John Rabe"), a [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans "Germans") [Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party "Nazi Party") member who was the leader of the Nanking Safety Zone, a [demilitarized zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demilitarized_zone "Demilitarized zone") in Nanjing that Rabe and other Westerners set up to protect Chinese civilians.[[15]](#cite_note-15) Rabe's diary is over 800 pages, and contains one of the most detailed accounts of the Nanjing Massacre.[[16]](#cite_note-16) Translated into English, it was published in 1998 by [Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_House "Random House") as *[The Good Man of Nanking: The Diaries of John Rabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Good_Man_of_Nanking:_The_Diaries_of_John_Rabe "The Good Man of Nanking: The Diaries of John Rabe")*.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

The other diary was written by belonged to [Minnie Vautrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnie_Vautrin "Minnie Vautrin"), the American missionary who saved the lives of about 10,000 women and children when she provided them with shelter in [Ginling College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginling_College "Ginling College").[[18]](#cite_note-Vautrin-18) Vautrin's diary recounts her personal experience and feelings on the Nanjing Massacre; in it, an entry reads, "There probably is no crime that has not been committed in this city today."[[19]](#cite_note-19) It was used as source material by Hua-ling Hu for a biography of Vautrin and her role during the Nanjing Massacre, entitled *[American Goddess at the Rape of Nanking: The Courage of Minnie Vautrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Goddess_at_the_Rape_of_Nanking:_The_Courage_of_Minnie_Vautrin "American Goddess at the Rape of Nanking: The Courage of Minnie Vautrin")*.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

Chang dubbed Rabe the "[Oskar Schindler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_Schindler "Oskar Schindler") of Nanking" and she dubbed Vautrin the "[Anne Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Frank "Anne Frank") of Nanking."[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[5]](#cite_note-SFGate2005-04-17-5)

## Contents

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Contents")]

*The Rape of Nanking* is divided into three main parts. The first part uses a technique—what Chang calls the "[Rashomon perspective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashomon_(film) "Rashomon (film)")"—to narrate the events of the massacre from three different perspectives: that of the Japanese military, that of the Chinese victims, and that of the Westerners who tried to help Chinese civilians. The second part describes the postwar reaction to the massacre, especially the reactions of the American and European governments. The third part of the book examines the circumstances that, Chang believed, have kept knowledge of the massacre out of the public's consciousness for decades after the war.[[9]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking8-9-9): 14–15

### Atrocities

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Atrocities")]

The book contains detailed depictions of the killing, torture, and rape that occurred during the Nanjing Massacre. Chang listed and described the kinds of torture that were visited upon the residents of the city, including [live burials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_burial "Live burial"), [mutilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutilation "Mutilation"), "[death by fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_by_fire "Death by fire")," "[death by ice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freezing_to_death "Freezing to death")," and "death by dogs." Based on the testimony of a survivor of the massacre, Chang also describes a killing contest amongst a group of Japanese soldiers to determine who could kill the fastest.[[9]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking8-9-9): 83–88 On the rape that occurred during the massacre, Chang wrote that "certainly it was one of the greatest mass rapes in world history." She estimates that the number of women raped ranged from 20,000 to as many as 80,000,[[22]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking89-22) and states that women from all classes were raped, including [Buddhist nuns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist_nun "Buddhist nun").[[23]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking90-23) Furthermore, rape occurred in all locations and at all hours,[[24]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking90-91-24) and both very young and very old women were raped.[[25]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking91a-25) Not even pregnant women were spared, Chang wrote, and that after gang rape, Japanese soldiers "sometimes slashed open the bellies of pregnant women and ripped out the [fetuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fetus "Fetus") for amusement."[[26]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking91b-26) Not all rape victims were women, according to the book, Chinese men were sodomized and forced to perform repulsive sexual acts.[[27]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking95a-27) Some were forced to commit incest—fathers to rape their own daughters, brothers their sisters, sons their mothers.[[28]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking95b-28)

### Death toll

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Death toll")]

Chang wrote about the death toll estimates which were given by different sources:[[9]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking8-9-9): 100

* Chinese military specialist Liu Fang-chu proposed a figure of 430,000; officials at the [Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre_Memorial_Hall "Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall") and the procurator of the District Court of Nanjing in 1946 stated at least 300,000 were killed;
* the [International Military Tribunal for the Far East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Military_Tribunal_for_the_Far_East "International Military Tribunal for the Far East") (IMTFE) judges concluded that more than 260,000 people were killed;
* Japanese historian [Akira Fujiwara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akira_Fujiwara "Akira Fujiwara") mentioned at least 200,000;
* [John Rabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rabe "John Rabe"), who "never conducted a systematic count and left Nanking in February," estimated 50,000 to 60,000; and
* Japanese historian [Ikuhiko Hata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ikuhiko_Hata "Ikuhiko Hata") argued the number killed was between 38,000 and 42,000.

The book discusses the research of Sun Zhaiwei, a historian at the Jiangsu Academy of Social Sciences. In his 1990 paper, "The Nanking Massacre and the Nanking Population", Sun estimated that the total number of people who were killed in the massacre was 377,400. By using Chinese burial records, he calculated that the number of dead exceeded the figure of 227,400. He then added estimates which totaled 150,000 based on estimates which were given by Japanese Imperial Army Major Ohta Hisao in a confessional report about the Japanese army's efforts to dispose of dead bodies, arriving at the sum of 377,400 dead.[[9]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking8-9-9): 101

Chang wrote that there is "compelling evidence" that the Japanese themselves, at the time, believed that the death toll may have been as high as 300,000. She cited a message that [Japan's foreign minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan's_foreign_minister "Japan's foreign minister") [Kōki Hirota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kōki_Hirota "Kōki Hirota") relayed to his contacts in [Washington, DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_DC "Washington, DC") in the first month of the massacre on January 17, 1938. The message acknowledged that "not less than three hundred thousand Chinese civilians [were] slaughtered, many cases in cold blood."[[9]](#cite_note-RapeOfNanking8-9-9): 103–4

## Reception

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Acclaim

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Acclaim")]

More than half a million copies of *The Rape of Nanking* were sold when it was first published in the US, and according to *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")*, it generally received critical acclaim.[[29]](#cite_note-NewYorkTimes-29) The book remained on the [*New York Times'* Best Seller list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "New York Times Best Seller list") for 10 weeks and sold more than 125,000 copies in four months.[[11]](#cite_note-SFGate1998-11) Several leading historians said they believe that Chang's revelation of Japanese wartime crimes and the country's postwar attempts to cover up and distort history will help raise public awareness of the incident.[[30]](#cite_note-once-30)

Chang became an instant celebrity in the US:[[31]](#cite_note-TimesOnline-31) she was awarded honorary degrees;[[32]](#cite_note-SFGate2004-11-11-32) invited to give lectures and to discuss the Nanjing Massacre on shows such as *[Good Morning America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Morning_America "Good Morning America")*, *[Nightline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightline "Nightline")*, and *[The NewsHour with Jim Lehrer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_NewsHour_with_Jim_Lehrer "The NewsHour with Jim Lehrer")*; profiled by *The New York Times*; and was featured on the cover of *[Reader's Digest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reader's_Digest "Reader's Digest")*.[[10]](#cite_note-Penguin-10) Moreover, [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton") invited her to the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"); the American historian [Stephen E. Ambrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_E._Ambrose "Stephen E. Ambrose") described her as "maybe the best young historian we've got;"[[31]](#cite_note-TimesOnline-31) and the [Organization of Chinese Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_of_Chinese_Americans "Organization of Chinese Americans") named her National Woman of the Year.[[32]](#cite_note-SFGate2004-11-11-32) The book's popularity prompted a lengthy book tour, with Chang visiting 65 cities in over a year and a half.[[5]](#cite_note-SFGate2005-04-17-5)

The book also received praise from news media. *[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")* wrote that it was the "first comprehensive examination of the destruction of this Chinese imperial city," and that Chang "skillfully excavated from oblivion the terrible events that took place." *[The Atlantic Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic_Monthly "The Atlantic Monthly")* described the book as "a crushing indictment of the Japanese army's behavior." The *[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")* called it "a powerful new work of history and moral inquiry" and stated that "Chang takes great care to establish an accurate accounting of the dimensions of the violence." *[The Philadelphia Inquirer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Philadelphia_Inquirer "The Philadelphia Inquirer")* wrote that it was a "compelling account of a horrendous episode that, until recently, has been largely forgotten."[[33]](#cite_note-MediaPraise-33)

According to William C. Kirby, Professor of History at Harvard University, Chang "shows more clearly than any previous account just what [the Japanese] did," and that she "draws connections between the slaughter in Europe and in Asia of millions of innocents during World War II."[[3]](#cite_note-KirbyForward-3) [Ross Terrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Terrill "Ross Terrill"), an associate in research at the [Fairbank Center for East Asian Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairbank_Center_for_East_Asian_Research "Fairbank Center for East Asian Research") at Harvard,[[34]](#cite_note-34) wrote that the book is "scholarly, an exciting investigation and a work of passion."[[35]](#cite_note-Quotes-35) Beatrice S. Bartlett, [Emeritus Professor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emeritus_Professor "Emeritus Professor") of History at [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"),[[36]](#cite_note-36) wrote, "Iris Chang's research on the Nanking holocaust yields a new and expanded telling of this World War II atrocity and reflects thorough research."[[35]](#cite_note-Quotes-35) [Frederic Wakeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_Wakeman "Frederic Wakeman"), director of the Institute of East Asian Studies at the [University of California, Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley"), wrote that the book was "Heartbreaking ... An utterly compelling book. The descriptions of the atrocities raise fundamental questions not only about imperial Japanese militarism but the psychology of the torturers, rapists, and murderers."[[35]](#cite_note-Quotes-35)

### Criticism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Criticism")]

Chang's critics alleged that she made an inappropriate and facile association between mass murder and Japanese culture, which included Japanese martial competitions and *[bushido](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bushido "Bushido")*; that her book contained incorrect historical dates and names because of her lack of training as a historian; that her personal feelings were evident in the book, making it lack intellectual rigor; that certain passages of her book were plagiarized; and that she placed an undue amount of attention to the actions of right-wing Japanese politicians and groups who refuse to acknowledge Japan's wartime crimes, while ignoring the contributions made by Japanese historians and groups who are preserving the memory of the massacre.[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-Kennedy-38)[[39]](#cite_note-39)[[40]](#cite_note-Jeans-40) Robert Entenmann, professor of history at [St. Olaf College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Olaf_College "St. Olaf College"), disagreed with her description of the massacre.[[41]](#cite_note-41) Entenmann opined that her explanations on why the massacre occurred were inadequate. Disagreements notwithstanding, he acknowledged that her book will help preserve the memory of the atrocity.[[42]](#cite_note-42)

Sonni Efron of the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* opined that the bitter row over Iris Chang's book may leave Westerners with the misimpression that little has been written in Japan about the Nanjing Massacre, when in fact the [National Diet Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Diet_Library "National Diet Library") holds at least 42 books about the Nanjing massacre and Japan's wartime misdeeds, 21 of which were written by liberals investigating Japan's wartime atrocities. In addition, Efron noted that geriatric Japanese soldiers have published their memoirs and have been giving speeches and interviews in increasing numbers, recounting the atrocities they committed or witnessed. After years of government-enforced denial, Japanese middle school textbooks now carry accounts of the Nanjing massacre as accepted truth. According to Efron, Japanese liberals alleged that the mistakes found in her book could undermine their endeavors, which include bringing the knowledge of the massacre to the Japanese public and pressuring the Japanese government into apologizing and atoning for the massacre.[[30]](#cite_note-once-30)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Baoshan1937-Asahi-01.jpg/250px-Baoshan1937-Asahi-01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baoshan1937-Asahi-01.jpg)

The original version of a photograph used by Chang—the accuracy of the caption in the book is disputed[[11]](#cite_note-SFGate1998-11)

*[San Francisco Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Chronicle "San Francisco Chronicle")* staff writer Charles Burress wrote that Chang's quote of a secret telegram sent by Japan's foreign minister in 1938 was incorrectly cited as "compelling evidence" that Japanese troops killed at least 300,000 Chinese civilians in Nanjing.[[11]](#cite_note-SFGate1998-11) According to Burress, the figure of 300,000 Chinese civilians killed actually came from a message sent by a British reporter, concerning deaths not only in Nanjing but in other places as well. Additionally, Burress questioned her motivation for writing the book—whether she wrote it as an activist or as a historian, stating that the book "draws its emotional impetus" from her conviction to not let the Nanjing Massacre be forgotten by the world.[[11]](#cite_note-SFGate1998-11)

Burress also cited [Ikuhiko Hata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ikuhiko_Hata "Ikuhiko Hata"), a Japanese history professor at [Nihon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihon_University "Nihon University"), who alleged that 11 photos in the book were misrepresented or fake. One particular photo shows women and children walking across a bridge with Japanese soldiers, and captioned as "The Japanese rounded up thousands of women. Most were gang-raped or forced into military prostitution." Hata stated that the photo originally appeared in 1937 in a Japanese newspaper as part of a series of photos that showed peaceful scenes of Chinese villagers under Japanese occupation.[[11]](#cite_note-SFGate1998-11) He alleged that since she did not conduct research in Japan, she incorrectly portrayed Japan's postwar attitudes towards the atrocity.[[11]](#cite_note-SFGate1998-11)

Chang responded to Burress' criticism in a letter written to the *San Francisco Chronicle*, but the letter was not published by the newspaper.[[43]](#cite_note-43) In the letter, she offered criticism of her own concerning Burress's article. She said Hata is considered as an untrustworthy scholar because of his regular contributions to ultra right-wing Japanese publishing companies such as [Bungeishunjū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bungeishunjū "Bungeishunjū"), which published an article that promoted [Holocaust denial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_denial "Holocaust denial") and another that accused Chang, the [MacArthur Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Foundation "MacArthur Foundation") and [Rupert Murdoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupert_Murdoch "Rupert Murdoch") of being part of a conspiracy organized by the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party").[[44]](#cite_note-ChangLetter-44) In regards to his allegations of her misrepresentation of photos and captions, she wrote that Hata provided insufficient evidence to support his suggestion that the photos proved a peaceful Japanese occupation.[[44]](#cite_note-ChangLetter-44)

In reference to the photo that shows women and children walking across a bridge with Japanese soldiers, she wrote:

> "The Japanese, like the Nazis, relied on deception to make mass executions and mass rapes more manageable. The hapless Chinese men, women and children rounded up by the Japanese were usually kept ignorant about their fate until it was too late to escape. In Nanking, women were guided to "marketplaces" to buy ducks and chicken, only to find platoons of soldiers waiting to rape them. Men were assured of food, shelter and safety by Japanese soldiers, only to be lured to remote areas and used for bayonet practice or decapitation contests."[[44]](#cite_note-ChangLetter-44)

She wrote that her book dealt with the "horror of the Japanese invasion of China," and that the caption reading "The Japanese rounded up thousands of women. Most were gang-raped or forced into military prostitution" contained two statements of indisputable fact.[[44]](#cite_note-ChangLetter-44) Chang also issued a rejoinder to Burress's argument that she incorrectly cited a telegram sent by Japan's foreign minister. She wrote that while the original figure of 300,000 Chinese civilian deaths in Nanjing was reported by a British reporter, this figure was cited in a message that Japan's foreign minister sent to his contacts in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Chang argued that figure's use by a high-ranking Japanese government official was evidence that the Japanese government recognized 300,000 as the number of Chinese civilian deaths. Finally, she criticized Burress for his "nitpick" of small details in order to draw attention away from the scope and magnitude of the Nanjing Massacre, writing that such was a "common tactic" of Holocaust deniers.[[44]](#cite_note-ChangLetter-44) In an interview, Chang challenged her critics by saying:

> "If the Japanese Foreign Ministry and the rest of the Japanese government truly care about historical truth, then they should open all their wartime archives to the rest of the world … They shouldn’t mind inviting an international task force of historians – historians from the U.S., China, Japan, Korea, and other countries – to review all the high-level Japanese records from that era and publish them for general and scholarly consumptions. Trust me, if the newly released archival records disprove any of the facts in my book, I would be the first person to acknowledge this in the next edition of *The Rape of Nanking*. Moreover, I would help the Japanese government publicize the new facts to the world media and find prestigious publishers in the U.S. to translate the documents into English."[[14]](#cite_note-Alan_Rosenbaum-14)

### Reaction in Japan

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Reaction in Japan")]

*The Rape of Nanking* has caused controversy in Japan.[[45]](#cite_note-45) In 1999 Fujiwara said that:

> “A campaign to deny the Nanking massacre itself by presenting the weaknesses of Iris Chang’s book is being developed. The massacre denial groups have been using these kinds of tactics to maintain there was no massacre by presenting the contradictions in testimony quoted or by the use of inappropriate photos. Yet it is impossible to deny the occurrence of the incident itself because of these few mistakes. It is an illogical jump in reasoning to deny that the Nanking massacre ever happened by attacking her book.”[[30]](#cite_note-once-30)

Associate Professor David Askew of [Ritsumeikan Asia Pacific University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritsumeikan_Asia_Pacific_University "Ritsumeikan Asia Pacific University") said that Chang's book ignited an interest in Japan about the massacre, increasing the amount of publications about the massacre in Japan. He opined that a unified Japanese view of the massacre doesn't exist because of the internal debates and contentions surrounding the massacre, and that the different views can be categorized into mutually exclusive thought groups. He alleged that some aspects of her book undermined the argument put forth by the "Great Massacre School of thought," which advocates for the validity of the findings at the [Tokyo Trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Trials "Tokyo Trials") and concludes that there were at least 200,000 casualties and at least 20,000 rape cases, and is considered to be the most sophisticated and credible thought group in Japan.[[46]](#cite_note-Askew-46)

In an attempt to prevent her Japanese publisher from releasing a Japanese translation of her book, right-wing Japanese groups threatened and pilloried Chang, her publisher and Japanese historians.[[29]](#cite_note-NewYorkTimes-29)[[30]](#cite_note-once-30)[[47]](#cite_note-47)[[48]](#cite_note-Hall-48) A Japanese literary agency informed her that several Japanese historians declined to review the translation; one professor backed out because of pressure placed on his family from "an unknown organization"; and her publisher said he was risking his life by publishing her book.[[29]](#cite_note-NewYorkTimes-29)[[30]](#cite_note-once-30) According to Japan scholar Ivan P. Hall, revisionist historians in Japan organized a committee of right-wing scholars to condemn the book with repeated appearances at the [Foreign Correspondents' Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Correspondents'_Club "Foreign Correspondents' Club") in Tokyo and throughout Japan.[[48]](#cite_note-Hall-48) Her Japanese publisher requested her to edit the book for the changes the right-wing Japanese scholars wanted made, which included deleting photographs, altering maps, and publishing a rebuttal to her book.[[48]](#cite_note-Hall-48) According to the email correspondence between Chang and Soni Efron of the Los Angeles Times, Chang defended the veracity of her research.[[30]](#cite_note-once-30) She said that she corrected 10 errors, including incorrect dates and misspelled names.[[30]](#cite_note-once-30) She rejected the publisher's attempt to annotate about 65 items in the book, stating that the suggested changes were additional details, interpretations or assertions by right-wing critics for which no evidence was provided.[[30]](#cite_note-once-30) She wrote,

> “I can assure you that virtually none of these errors had anything to do with the historical description of the Nanking massacre itself.”[[30]](#cite_note-once-30)

Since the editorial requests were against the publishing contract between Chang and her publisher, she decided to withdraw the Japanese publication of her book and criticized her publisher for capitulating to right-wing threats.[[48]](#cite_note-Hall-48)[[30]](#cite_note-once-30) A Japanese translation of her book was not published and circulated in Japan until December 2007.[[49]](#cite_note-49)[[50]](#cite_note-50)

## Chang's death

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Chang's death")]

After publishing the book, Chang received hate mail, primarily from Japanese [ultranationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultranationalists "Ultranationalists"),[[5]](#cite_note-SFGate2005-04-17-5) and threatening notes on her car and also believed her phone was tapped. Her mother said the book "made Iris sad". Suffering from [depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_depression "Clinical depression"), Chang was diagnosed with [brief reactive psychosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brief_reactive_psychosis "Brief reactive psychosis") in August 2004. She began taking medications to stabilize her mood.[[5]](#cite_note-SFGate2005-04-17-5) She wrote:

> I can never shake my belief that I was being recruited, and later persecuted, by forces more powerful than I could have imagined. Whether it was the [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIA "CIA") or some other organization I will never know. As long as I am alive, these forces will never stop hounding me.[[5]](#cite_note-SFGate2005-04-17-5)

Chang committed suicide on November 9, 2004.[[5]](#cite_note-SFGate2005-04-17-5) A memorial service was held in China by Nanjing Massacre survivors coinciding with her funeral in [Los Altos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Altos,_California "Los Altos, California"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"). The [Memorial Hall of the Victims in the Nanjing Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre_Memorial_Hall "Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall"), a memorial site in Nanjing built to commemorate the victims of the Nanjing Massacre,[[51]](#cite_note-51) added a wing dedicated to her in 2005.[[52]](#cite_note-SFGate2004-11-20-52)

In the US, a Chinese garden in [Norfolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk,_Virginia "Norfolk, Virginia"), [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia"), which contains a memorial to [Minnie Vautrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnie_Vautrin "Minnie Vautrin"), added a memorial dedicated to Chang, including her as the latest victim of the Nanjing Massacre, and drawing parallels between Chang and Vautrin, who also took her own life.[[52]](#cite_note-SFGate2004-11-20-52) Vautrin exhausted herself trying to protect women and children during the Nanjing Massacre and subsequently during the Japanese occupation of Nanjing, finally suffering a nervous breakdown in 1940. She returned to the US for medical treatment and committed suicide a year later.[[18]](#cite_note-Vautrin-18)

## Editions

args.summary:
The Rape of Nanking: The Forgotten Holocaust of World War II is a bestselling 1997 non-fiction book by Iris Chang about the 1937-1938 Nanjing Massacre, where the Imperial Japanese Army committed mass murder and mass rape of Chinese civilians after the Battle of Nanjing. It was one of the first major English-language books on the subject and has been translated into several languages. 

Chang was inspired to write the book after her parents told her about the massacre in her childhood and she found little information in libraries. She spent two years researching, finding the diaries of John Rabe (a German Nazi Party member who led the Nanking Safety Zone) and Minnie Vautrin (an American missionary who saved about 10,000 women and children). The book is divided into three parts: narrating events from Japanese, Chinese, and Western perspectives; describing postwar reactions; and examining why knowledge of the massacre remained hidden. It details atrocities including killing, torture, and rape, estimating 20,000 to 80,000 women were raped and citing death toll estimates ranging from 38,000 to 430,000.

The book was a commercial and critical success, selling over half a million copies and spending 10 weeks on the New York Times Best Seller list. However, it faced criticism from some historians who questioned Chang's analysis of Japanese culture, her death toll calculations, and accuracy due to her lack of formal historian training. The book caused significant controversy in Japan, with right-wing groups threatening Chang and her publisher, ultimately causing the Japanese translation to be delayed until 2007. Chang received hate mail and threats from Japanese ultranationalists, suffered from depression and psychosis, and committed suicide on November 9, 2004.

args.key_excerpts: Iris Chang was an American author and historian whose work brought global attention to one of the most devastating and often overlooked wartime events of the 20th century., She wrote a powerful book documenting the atrocities that took place in Nanjing in 1937 during the Second Sino Japanese War, where hundreds of thousands of civilians and prisoners of war are believed to have died., In 2004, at the age of 36, Iris Chang died, leaving behind a legacy of influential historical work that continues to be read and debated today., Her story is often remembered as both a major contribution to historical awareness and a reminder of the human cost carried by those who document it.
args.summary: This is a Facebook post from the page "Top 10s" (dated April 12) about Iris Chang, the American author and historian. Chang wrote a powerful book documenting the Nanjing Massacre of 1937 during the Second Sino-Japanese War, where hundreds of thousands of civilians and prisoners of war are believed to have died. Her book brought global attention to this overlooked wartime atrocity. However, the emotional toll of researching and writing about mass suffering severely impacted her mental health. In 2004, at age 36, Iris Chang died. The post notes her legacy as both a major contribution to historical awareness and a reminder of the human cost carried by those who document atrocities. The post generated 935 reactions, 63 comments, and 88 shares. Notable comments include a user expressing heartbreak that it cost her life, another suggesting conspiracy theories around her death, and a visitor to Nanjing noting the museum there is "phenomenal."

Most [women in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_China "Women in China") were profoundly impacted by the [Second Sino-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War "Second Sino-Japanese War") (also referred to in China as the War of Resistance), in which the [Empire of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Japan "Empire of Japan") fought the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912–1949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)") starting in 1937, primarily due to the [Marco Polo Bridge Incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Polo_Bridge_incident "Marco Polo Bridge incident") on July 7, 1937.[[1]](#cite_note-1) On September 2, 1945, Japan formally surrendered. This war resulted in the deaths of approximately 20 million people, mostly the civilians in China.

Women's experiences during the war depended on a variety of factors, including class, place of origin, and social connections. While some groups of women in China were in a position to contribute to the resistance efforts, poor women in urban and rural areas fought every day to keep themselves and their families alive. The war's impact on women also varied by location, whether they stayed in regions controlled by the [Nationalist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Nationalist_Party "Chinese Nationalist Party"), the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP), or the Japanese.

While thousands of women in [eastern China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_China "East China") fled their homes for inland regions to escape Japanese occupation and the violence that came with it, women also stayed behind in occupied areas.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHershatter2019190-2) The Nationalist government relocated several times throughout the war, from [Nanjing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing "Nanjing") to [Wuhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuhan "Wuhan"), and after the [fall of Wuhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Wuhan "Battle of Wuhan"), they established a wartime capital in [Chongqing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chongqing "Chongqing"). Refugees who fled to Chongqing from the lower reaches of the [Yangtze River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangtze_River "Yangtze River") in the east were referred to by locals as "downriver people" (Chinese: 下江人).[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201018-3) Many women also migrated to [Yan'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yan'an "Yan'an"), the CCP's headquarters during the war, and other CCP [revolutionary base areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_base_area "Revolutionary base area") in [northern regions of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_China "North China").

## Women's contributions to the war effort

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Women's contributions to the war effort")]

Women contributed to the Second Sino-Japanese war in various capacities, such as in medical work, education, women's organizations, and on the battlefield. Women's work during the war was vitally important and helped China make it through the war.

### Medical work

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Medical work")]

Women in China supported injured soldiers in CCP and Nationalist bases alike, working as nurses, doctors, and midwives during the war. While women had worked as caregivers before, women during the war provided medical care in public, which marked a shift in gender roles. Not only were women working outside of the home, but they were also making physical contact with male strangers. The war prompted the feminization of the nursing profession in China.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes20183-4) There were roughly 60,000 women that served as nurses in the Army Corps. Getting paid wasn't something that began happening until 1944, when Congress decided to fix the law; this granted temporary commissions with full pay and privileges to the nurses. With these women breaking barriers, it didn't mean they received equal pay; most nurses worked for $111 a month.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Soldiers in China needed medical care for battle wounds, as well as for lethal diseases such as [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera") and [malaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaria "Malaria").[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201898–99-6) Nurses were in high demand for the state, and the number of registered nurses increased dramatically throughout the war, as did the number of nursing schools.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201855,_106-7) Nurses in Chongqing performed various medical tasks, such as administering vaccines, in hospitals and on the street.[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201858-8)

Nursing schools in Chongqing recruited young, educated, and unmarried women to enroll during the war. While women attended nursing schools during the war, Chinese provincial governments integrated nursing classes into high school curriculums. In 1937, high school girls in Hubei started taking compulsory nursing classes. In 1940, female high school graduates in Hunan and Sichuan were required to work as nurses, either for the military or for rural public health.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes2018108-9)

Women such as [Zhou Meiyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Meiyu "Zhou Meiyu") helped professionalize the nursing industry and raise its status.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201871-10)[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHershatter2019184-11) While some nurses were paid, other women helped soldiers on a volunteer basis. Many women felt fulfilled working as nurses and accepted to work for low pay.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201873-12)

Women joined the Nationalist expeditionary army for the [Burma campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burma_campaign "Burma campaign") as nurses, office staff and interpreters.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13): 101

### Fundraising and relief work

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Fundraising and relief work")]

Middle-class and upper-class women across China participated in various fundraising activities and led organizations to provide relief for soldiers, refugees, orphans, among other groups. Some of the services women in Chongqing organizations provided were clothing drives and soup kitchens. Volunteers in orphanages taught children a number of songs and plays with anti-Japanese sentiment alongside public health lessons.[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201865-14)

Dozens of women's organizations registered with local governments across the country. Three important nationally recognized organizations during the war, which all relocated to Chongqing, were the "National Association of Chinese Women for the Cheering and Comforting of the Officers and Soldiers of the War of Self-Defense and Resistance against Japan", the "Wartime Child Welfare Protection Association", and the "Women’s Directorial Committee of [New Life Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Life_Movement "New Life Movement") Promotion Federation".[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201020–21-15) Prominent women such as [Song Meiling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soong_Mei-ling "Soong Mei-ling"), [Deng Yingchao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Yingchao "Deng Yingchao"), [Shi Liang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Liang "Shi Liang"), and [Li Dequan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Dequan "Li Dequan") cooperated to lead these organizations.[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201021-16)

The leaders of women's organizations in Chongqing created multiple job opportunities for hundreds of refugee women in the Songji experimental zone, located in [Yongchuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongchuan,_Chongqing "Yongchuan, Chongqing"). After this project was launched, refugee women worked at a textile factory, library, farm, and schools, among other places in Songji.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201097-17)

### Teachers and students

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Teachers and students")]

Many urban, educated women from the east fled to Chongqing and taught in schools. They often integrated the war into their lessons, explaining why Chinese people should care and participate in the war effort. Refugee teachers at an elementary school in Chongqing taught students patriotic war songs and gave students essay assignments about the war. They also prompted young students to give speeches about the war to public audiences at neighboring markets.[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201040-18)

Women and girls continued to attend school and college if their families could afford it. Due to the war, many leading educational institutions and preeminent teachers relocated to Chongqing, which meant local students received a better education than they otherwise would have.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201052-19) In addition to giving speeches, students in Chongqing contributed to the war effort by teaching lessons to peasants about the war, writing articles for wall bulletins, producing shoes and other goods for soldiers, and putting on performances at markets to spread awareness about the war.[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201042–43,_139-20)

Many high school girls and women college students volunteered to write letters for illiterate soldiers. These volunteers provided emotional support for soldiers, formed friendships, and boosted their morale through entertainment.[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes20181–2,_82-21)

In 1939, [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong") proposed creating a women's university where the CCP could develop female cadres.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWang202570–71-22) The Chinese Women's University was inaugurated on 20 July of that year in [Yan'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yan'an_Soviet "Yan'an Soviet"), and Mao's inauguration speech emphasized the role of women in resisting the Japanese invasion of China.[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWang202571-23) Mao stated, "The day all women in China rise up is the moment of China's revolutionary victory!"[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWang202571-23)

### Soldiers

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Soldiers")]

Some women in the CCP-controlled front-line base areas joined armies to fight against Japanese soldiers, including the [Eighth Route Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighth_Route_Army "Eighth Route Army") and the [New Fourth Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Fourth_Army "New Fourth Army"). Some women participated in fighting, but more often, women were told to support the bases in other ways.[[24]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHershatter2019207-24)

In May 1938, the women's battalion of Zhejiang formed with Nationalist leadership.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13): 100 Its more than 200 soldiers fought behind the Japanese lines.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13): 100

In 1933, Guangxi established a military training program in public high schools for male and female students.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13): 100 In 1934, it was extended to students in middle school.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13): 100 After full-scale war broke out, Guangxi formed the women students army, which traveled on foot from Guangxi to Wuhan, doing [propaganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propaganda_in_the_Republic_of_China "Propaganda in the Republic of China") work through drama performances and public rallies.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13): 100–101 Under General [Li Zongren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Zongren "Li Zongren"), the Guangxi women students army also rescued wounded soldiers and fought when necessary.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13): 101

## War's impact on women

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: War's impact on women")]

The war impacted women across China in striking ways. The household, gender roles, and women's occupations changed during the war. While often victims of murder and horrific acts of violence, women in China used various survival strategies to cope with the war's impact and fight for survival.**[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13)**

### Refugees and migration

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Refugees and migration")]

Many women in wartime China migrated to different regions, either to escape Japanese soldiers and bombing or disasters such as floods and famine. Many women also migrated to escape the Japanese soldiers enslaving them for sex as [comfort women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comfort_women "Comfort women"). With many of the Chinese women being forced to relocate and others migrating for their safety, this made it difficult accurately quantify them and track their contributions to the war.[[25]](#cite_note-25) However, leaving one's home was not a smooth process for many women. Refugee mothers were responsible for looking after their children, which made it harder to make ends meet along the way to their next destination.[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMuscolino2014151-26) Additionally, it was dangerous for women to leave their homes as they were sexually vulnerable to soldiers and bandits. Some women got pregnant on the way to their next destination.[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201058-27)

For poor women in Chongqing, the mass arrival of refugees in their hometowns drove up prices, making it even more difficult to cover basic needs.[[28]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201084-28) Women from peasant families in Chongqing could barely make ends meet before the war, so they took on more jobs that sometimes put their lives at risk.

Wealthy, well-connected women in Chongqing had the means to relocate during the war. Amid the [Chongqing bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Chongqing "Bombing of Chongqing"), wealthy women moved out of Sichuan temporarily and returned home afterward.[[29]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201083-29)

#### 1938 Yellow River Flood

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1938 Yellow River Flood")]

A man-made disaster causing to slow down the Japanese advance and to create more time for relocation for the government to Chongqing. The [National Revolutionary Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Revolutionary_Army "National Revolutionary Army") (NRA) did this by breaching the Yellow River dikes;[[30]](#cite_note-30) breaching essentially means the intentional removal of flood defense structures, allowing the river to flow freely.[[31]](#cite_note-31) Women in [Henan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henan "Henan") who were displaced and affected by the [1938 Yellow River flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1938_Yellow_River_flood "1938 Yellow River flood") resorted to various survival strategies to stay alive during the war. Some women migrated to Nationalist-controlled regions of Henan, while others stayed behind in the flooded, occupied region. Women flood victims who stayed behind made a living by selling salt.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMuscolino201478-32) Women who fled worked jobs in domestic service and textile arts, and many resorted to begging and prostitution.[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMuscolino201470–71-33)[[34]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChen2012147-34) In some instances, families were forced to give their daughters away to another family or sell their daughters into prostitution.[[35]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMuscolino2014170-35)

### Sexual violence

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Sexual violence")]

Women were subject to sexual violence throughout the Second Sino-Japanese War. While many women in occupied areas decided to stay indoors to avoid contact with Japanese soldiers, some braved the threat of leaving their houses. In many instances, women did not have a choice.[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELary201068-36)

Across China, various situations and places were dangerous for women to go during the war, because of increased chances of being raped or assaulted. For instance, it was dangerous for women in Chongqing to dump garbage outside of the city, yet some women from poor peasant families did so to make a living.[[28]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201084-28)

Refugee women who fled their homes risked sexual assault and violence on the way to their next destination. In one instance, a refugee woman was forced to satisfy a man's sexual desires to protect her family and gain connections in a new city.[[37]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201057–58-37)

#### Nanjing Massacre

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Nanjing Massacre")]

On December 13, 1937, Japanese soldiers invaded Nanjing, the capital of China at the time. Women of all ages in Nanjing were sexually assaulted, raped, and murdered by Japanese soldiers in the [Nanjing Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre "Nanjing Massacre"). Women fled their homes and sought refuge in public spaces such as colleges.[[38]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMitter2013131-38) One woman resorted to covering herself in excrement to reduce the chances of being raped.[[39]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMitter2013132–133-39) In the first month of Japanese soldiers occupying the capital, estimates suggest there were 20,000 instances of rape.[[40]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMitter2013134-40) Rape victims who survived were traumatized and did not want to speak about their experiences after the war ended.[[41]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHershatter2019181-41) Many woman choose avoid speaking about their sexual violence experiences primarily to not relive that traumatic time, feel shame or blame their self, and sadly to also avoid the feeling of not being believed.[[42]](#cite_note-42)

#### Comfort women

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Comfort women")]

Thousands of girls in China were forced to work in military brothels as sex slaves, also known as [comfort women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comfort_women "Comfort women").[[43]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELary201025-43) While estimates vary, scholars agree that the number of women enslaved as comfort women numbered over 200,000.[[44]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELary2010100-44)**[[45]](#cite_note-:02-45)**: 153 Women resorted to various tactics to make themselves less attractive and protect themselves. Some women in occupied regions wore unflattering clothing or covered their faces in ash.[[46]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHershatter2019188-46)

The [Tokyo war crimes trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Military_Tribunal_for_the_Far_East "International Military Tribunal for the Far East") did not address the enslavement of women for sex by the Japanese army, given that rape was not viewed as a war crime.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13): 154

### Social and economic impact

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Social and economic impact")]

Due to a number of men leaving home to either work or fight, the structure of the household and gender roles shifted dramatically in various regions of China.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

#### The household

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: The household")]

The war tore many women's families apart. Refugee women were often permanently separated from their extended families.[[47]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELary201092–93-47) While refugee women lost their support systems, their mental health became impacted heavily with the separation. Many refugees experienced anxiety, depression, stress, physical health changes, appetite changes, and helplessness.[[48]](#cite_note-48) However, they also gained certain freedoms living away from family, such as choosing one's own husband rather than having an arranged marriage.[[49]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELary201098-49)

Many women became widows during the war and often did not remarry. The likelihood of a woman remarrying depended on whether she had children and other family members to care for. The best outcome, if a woman was on her own, was marrying a poor man.[[50]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELary20105-50)

Women filed for divorce throughout the war, frequently because their husbands abandoned them.[[51]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHershatter2019187-51) Women also ran away from their husbands during the war without facing legal repercussions.[[46]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHershatter2019188-46) Other women stayed with their husbands despite being separated by the war. Some husbands sent their wives money when they were away, because they depended on his paycheck. However, the war disrupted the postal service in places like Chongqing, which meant that women struggled to meet basic needs and had to find alternate ways of getting money.[[52]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi201063-52)

#### Labor and gender roles

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Labor and gender roles")]

With fewer men at home during the war, women took on different kinds of work to provide for their families, such as farming. It became increasingly common for women, especially poor women, to work in the fields during the war. Young girls worked in the fields as well. However, agricultural work involved several risks for women, including the shame of working outside and the threat of being surrounded by bandits and soldiers.[[53]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMuscolino2014154-53)

Women's occupations often varied by region. Women in Japan-occupied Shanghai, for instance, worked in stores, [cotton mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton_mill "Cotton mill"), as models, and opera singers among other jobs.[[54]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHershatter2019186–187-54) In CCP [revolutionary base areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_base_area "Revolutionary base area"), such as Yan’an, women contributed to the self-sufficiency and independence of the bases by farming and making goods like shoes and clothing.[[55]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHershatter2019189-55) The CCP bases relied heavily on women's labor for economic production. Women's participation in politics in CCP base areas varied. Some gained political experience at a village level, whereas in regions like Wuxiang, women did not participate in politics at all.[[56]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELary201097-56)[[57]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodman2000929-57)

The war prompted the feminization of several industries, such as agriculture and nursing. By providing for their families by working out of the house, women disrupted gender norms and transformed gender roles. After the war, women in China continued working. They no longer had to rely solely on male family members to stay afloat.[[58]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELary201099-58)

## Media coverage and depictions of wartime women

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Media coverage and depictions of wartime women")]

In various mediums, such as [cartoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoon "Cartoon"), women in China during the war were depicted as victims of sexual violence and murder to inspire Chinese people to keep fighting.[[59]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHershatter2019182-59) However, women were also depicted as strong and resilient. During the war, stories about famous heroines resurfaced in China. For instance, [Hua Mulan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hua_Mulan "Hua Mulan") became a central figure in plays, cartoons, poetry, and movies. In 1939, a movie called *[Mulan Joins the Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulan_Joins_the_Army_(1939_film) "Mulan Joins the Army (1939 film)")* (木兰从军) was released*,* in which the story of Mulan was rewritten to show her taking action against the "foreign invaders" (which mirrored China's current situation against the Japanese) and included not-so-subtle parallels to events that happened in the Second Sino-Japanese War.[[58]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELary201099-58) Inspired from the 1939 film, Disney created an animated version title Mulan is 1998. This further showed representation and female empowerment while staring an Asian-American woman.[[60]](#cite_note-60) This story continues to inspire young girls to challenge the status quo and be bold.[[61]](#cite_note-61)

To commemorate [International Women's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Women's_Day "International Women's Day") in 1940, the [Yan'an Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yan'an_Soviet "Yan'an Soviet") organized performances of plays showcasing heroic women, including *Mother Yue Tattooing Characters*, *Liang Hongyu*, and *Qiu Jin*.[[62]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWang202570-62) The selection of plays was intended to encourage the people, particularly women, in opposing the Japanese invasion of China.[[62]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWang202570-62)

### Song Meiling

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Chinese_women_in_the_Second_Sino-Japanese_War&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Song Meiling")]

[Song Meiling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soong_Mei-ling "Soong Mei-ling"), the First Lady of the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912–1949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)") and wife of [Chiang Kai-shek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiang_Kai-shek "Chiang Kai-shek"), was the most prominent woman in China during the war. She traveled to the United States on multiple occasions and spoke in front of Congress to ask for increased aid. She frequently appeared in the press in China and overseas, demonstrating how women should support the war effort. She also took an active involvement in fundraising and caring for "warphans" or war orphans, to ensure China received donations overseas.[[63]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201862–63-63) Meiling was fluent in English and of the Christian faith, which allowed her to create a deeper connection with the United States and represent China effectively.[[64]](#cite_note-64) Song Meiling was beloved by Americans, much more than her husband Chiang Kai-shek.[[63]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201862–63-63)

args.summary:
This Wikipedia article examines the experiences of Chinese women during the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945), also known as the War of Resistance. The war resulted in approximately 20 million deaths, mostly civilians. Women's experiences varied greatly depending on class, location, and social connections.

**Women's Contributions:**
- **Medical work:** About 60,000 women served as nurses. The war prompted the feminization of nursing in China. Nursing schools recruited young, educated, unmarried women, and provincial governments integrated nursing classes into high school curriculums. Women like Zhou Meiyu helped professionalize the field.
- **Fundraising and relief:** Middle- and upper-class women led organizations providing clothing, soup kitchens, and orphanage services. Key organizations were led by prominent figures including Song Meiling (Madame Chiang Kai-shek), Deng Yingchao, and Shi Liang.
- **Teachers and students:** Educated women from eastern China taught in relocated schools, integrating war lessons into curricula. Students wrote letters to illiterate soldiers, produced goods, and spread propaganda. In 1939, Mao Zedong inaugurated the Chinese Women's University in Yan'an.
- **Soldiers:** Some women fought in CCP-led armies (Eighth Route Army, New Fourth Army) and Nationalist-led units such as the Zhejiang women's battalion (over 200 soldiers) and the Guangxi women students army.

**War's Impact:**
- **Refugees and migration:** Millions of women fled eastern China to inland regions like Chongqing and Yan'an. The 1938 Yellow River Flood, a man-made disaster by the National Revolutionary Army, displaced many women in Henan who resorted to selling salt, domestic service, begging, or prostitution.
- **Sexual violence:** Widespread rape occurred throughout the war. During the Nanjing Massacre (beginning December 13, 1937), there were an estimated 20,000 instances of rape in the first month alone. Over 200,000 Chinese women were forced into sexual slavery as "comfort women" by the Japanese military. The Tokyo war crimes trials did not address this enslavement.
- **Social and economic impact:** The war disrupted households, with women becoming widows, filing for divorce, or gaining new freedoms. Women entered farming and other labor roles, feminizing agriculture. In CCP base areas, women's labor was crucial for economic production.

**Media and Depictions:**
Women were depicted both as victims and as heroic figures. The story of Hua Mulan was revived in a 1939 film ("Mulan Joins the Army") and later inspired Disney's 1998 animated film. Song Meiling, the First Lady, was the most prominent wartime woman, traveling to the US to speak before Congress and appearing in media to rally support.

## Abstract

The Second Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945) occupies an integral position in the memory politics of the People's Republic of China (PRC). In recent years, dominant representations of the war create a memory discourse which portrays the heroic triumph of the Chinese people led by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) over Japan. This article shows how the war has been remembered from the victory of the Communist revolution in 1949 to the present in the PRC. It contributes to the debate on the effectiveness and limitations of the monopoly of war memory by the CCP.

Appearance

From Simple English Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Flashingsecond.gif/250px-Flashingsecond.gif?utm_source=simple.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flashingsecond.gif)

A light flashing once per second.

The **second** (symbol: **s**), is a [unit](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Units_of_measurement "Units of measurement") of [time](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time "Time"). There are 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, and 24 hours in a day. This tradition dates back to the [Babylonians](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon "Babylon").

In science, a second is the time it takes for a [caesium](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesium "Caesium") [atom](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom "Atom") to vibrate 9,192,631,770 (around 9 billion) times. Scientists measure the second this way because the length of a day changes all the time. For example, when the [dinosaurs](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur "Dinosaur") lived, a day was about an hour shorter.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Vibrations of [atoms](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom "Atom") on the other hand always take the same time. This **atomic second** is also called the [SI](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI "SI") second.

[Metric prefixes](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units#Prefixes "International System of Units") are frequently combined with the word *second* to denote subdivisions of the second, *e.g.*, the [millisecond](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millisecond "Millisecond") (one thousandth of a second) and [nanosecond](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanosecond "Nanosecond") (one billionth of a second). Though SI prefixes may also be used to form multiples of the second (such as “kilosecond”, or one thousand seconds), such units are rarely used in practice. More commonly encountered, non-SI units of time such as the [minute](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute "Minute"), [hour](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hour "Hour"), and [day](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day "Day") increase by multiples of 60 and 24 (rather than by powers of ten as in the SI system).

One heartbeat of an [adult](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult "Adult") at rest, will last about one second.

## International second

[[change](/w/index.php?title=Second&veaction=edit&section=1 "Change section: International second") | [change source](/w/index.php?title=Second&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: International second")]

Under the [International System of Units](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units "International System of Units"), the second is currently defined as the duration of 9,192,631,770 [periods](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_(physics) "Period (physics)") of the radiation [corresponding](https://simple.wiktionary.org/wiki/correspond "wikt:correspond") to the [transition](https://simple.wiktionary.org/wiki/transition "wikt:transition") between the two [hyperfine levels](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperfine_structure?action=edit&redlink=1 "Hyperfine structure (not yet started)") of the [ground state](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ground_state "Ground state") of the [caesium](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesium "Caesium")-133 [atom](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom "Atom").[[2]](#cite_note-USNO-2) This definition refers to a caesium atom at rest at a [temperature](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature "Temperature") of 0 kelvins (−273.15 degrees Celsius; −459.67 degrees Fahrenheit) ([absolute zero](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_zero "Absolute zero")). The ground state is defined at zero [magnetic field](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_field "Magnetic field").[[2]](#cite_note-USNO-2) The second thus defined is equivalent to the [ephemeris](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephemeris "Ephemeris") second.

The international standard symbol for a second is **s** (see [ISO 31-1](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_31-1?action=edit&redlink=1 "ISO 31-1 (not yet started)"))

## Equivalence to other units of time

[[change](/w/index.php?title=Second&veaction=edit&section=2 "Change section: Equivalence to other units of time") | [change source](/w/index.php?title=Second&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section's source code: Equivalence to other units of time")]

1 international second is equal to:

* 1/60 [minute](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute "Minute") (1 minute is equal to 60 seconds)
* 1/3,600 [hour](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hour "Hour") (1 hour is equal to 3,600 seconds)
* 1/86,400 [day](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day "Day") (1 day, in the sense of non-SI units accepted for use with the International System of Units, is equal to 86,400 seconds)

There are 31,536,000 seconds in a [common year](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_year "Common year"), 31,622,400 seconds in a [leap year](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_year "Leap year"), and 31,557,600 seconds in a [Julian year](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_year_(astronomy) "Julian year (astronomy)")

## Historical origin

[[change](/w/index.php?title=Second&veaction=edit&section=3 "Change section: Historical origin") | [change source](/w/index.php?title=Second&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section's source code: Historical origin")]

Originally, the second was known as a "second minute", meaning the second minute (i.e. small) division of an hour. The first division was known as a "prime minute" and is equivalent to the [minute](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute "Minute") we know today. Third and fourth minutes were sometimes used in calculations.

The factor of 60 comes from the [Babylonians](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon "Babylon") who used a [sexagesimal](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexagesimal "Sexagesimal") (base-60) [numeral system](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numeral_system "Numeral system"). However, the Babylonians did not subdivide their time units sexagesimally (except for the day). The [hour](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hour "Hour") had been defined by the [ancient Egyptians](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt "Ancient Egypt") as either 1/12 of daytime or 1/12 of nighttime, hence both varied with the seasons. Greek astronomers, for example [Hipparchus](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hipparchus "Hipparchus") and [Ptolemy](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy "Ptolemy"), defined the hour as 1/24 of a mean [solar day](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time "Solar time"). Sexagesimally subdividing this mean solar hour made the second 1/86,400 of a mean solar day.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

## SI multiples

[[change](/w/index.php?title=Second&veaction=edit&section=4 "Change section: SI multiples") | [change source](/w/index.php?title=Second&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section's source code: SI multiples")]

Main article: [Metric time](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_time "Metric time")

SI prefixes are commonly used for times shorter than one second, but rarely for multiples of a second. Instead, certain [non-SI units are permitted for use in SI](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-SI_units_mentioned_in_the_SI?action=edit&redlink=1 "Non-SI units mentioned in the SI (not yet started)"): [minutes](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute "Minute"), [hours](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hour "Hour"), [days](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day "Day"), and in astronomy [Julian days](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day "Julian day").[[4]](#cite_note-IAU-4)
