# Gail Hershatter Discusses Her Book "The Gender Of Memory: Rural Women And China's Collective Past"
## USC U.S.-China Institute
16500 subscribers
23 likes

### Description
1497 views
Posted: 9 Jun 2016
About the Book

What can we learn about the Chinese revolution by placing a doubly marginalized group—rural women—at the center of the inquiry? In this book, Gail Hershatter explores changes in the lives of seventy-two elderly women in rural Shaanxi province during the revolutionary decades of the 1950s and 1960s. Interweaving these women’s life histories with insightful analysis, Hershatter shows how Party-state policy became local and personal, and how it affected women’s agricultural work, domestic routines, activism, marriage, childbirth, and parenting—even their notions of virtue and respectability. The women narrate their pasts from the vantage point of the present and highlight their enduring virtues, important achievements, and most deeply harbored grievances. In showing what memories can tell us about gender as an axis of power, difference, and collectivity in 1950s rural China and the present, Hershatter powerfully examines the nature of socialism and how gender figured in its creation.

About the Author 

Gail Hershatter teaches history at the University of California, Santa Cruz, where she also heads the East Asian Studies program. One of the profession’s most accomplished scholars, Hershatter was president of the Association for Asian Studies in 2011-2012. She’s received numerous research and teaching awards. She’s also written Women in China's Long Twentieth Century, Personal Voices: Chinese Women in the 1980s (with Emily Honig), Dangerous Pleasures: Prostitution and Modernity in 20th-Century Shanghai, and The Workers of Tianjin, 1900-1949.

1 comments
### Transcript:
Hi I'm Gail Hershatter. I teach Chinese
history at University of California Santa Cruz and I'm here to talk about my
book "The Gender of Memory: Rural Women and China's Collective Past". I teach
modern Chinese history to undergrads. Every time i would get to the 1950s,
there was nothing good to give them to read. There was all of this great stuff
about the war against Japan and then there was all of this great stuff about
the 1960s and in between there was just a list of government campaigns: land
reform, marriage law, mutual aid teams, cooperatives, Great Leap Forward, Great
Leap famine. As a list it's like the Congressional Record, it's not that
interesting. And I was interested in what's the connection between the
government says something up here and something happens on the ground. For me
it was more of a historical interest. I wanted material to teach and I wanted to
understand what had happened to socialism once it hit the ground and how
people who were very removed from power, because they were far from Beijing, they
were in pretty remote villages in Shanxi province but mostly not
in the suburbs of Xian. What was the connection between what the state said
in Beijing and what they understood as having happened and what was the
connection of the state's big policy objectives about women and what actually
happened to women. So I understood these people to be far from power in the sense
that they were farmers, rural people and they were women. People ask me why I did
this in Shanxi. I did it in Shanxi because there was someone in Shanxi
who had good contacts in the countryside. It's not that Shanxi is the only
place or even the most representative place but it's a place.
There ought to be people doing this in lots of places. One of the ways that it
wasn't hard, was it wasn't hard to get people to talk. They were dying to talk,
they were waiting for someone to ask them. They were really eager to tell
their stories and I suspect that in many cases their families and their neighbors
either were sick of hearing these stories or already knew bare outlines and didn't
want to go any further with it because it was about things that had happened
almost half a century before. 1949 is a big event when we teach the history. Many
of the women I talked to didn't register 1949 at all. You'd say what happened in
1949, they'd say well China was liberated. What happened here? I don't remember,
nothing happened here. For them the changes that came with land reform, the
marriage law, rural collectivization, were a very long process and they happened
unevenly. But often the thing that brought home to people the fact that
something had changed, especially if they were kids or young women at the time, was
the arrival of work teams of people from outside who were there to organize for
various policy objectives. And often these people weren't big faraway
high-ranking or even military people. Sometimes they were young women who had
just recently graduated from middle school themselves, who got mobilized to
go out and mobilize young women in the villages to come and participate in land
reform. It had to do with reorganizing work. Women in these regions, these are
very poor agricultural regions, had always done a lot of agricultural labor.
Often they did it because the men had to go elsewhere to look for work or the men
ran off so they wouldn't be conscripted into the nationalist army or the men
died. And women were left doing a lot of the farming but it was considered
dangerous, it exposed them to sexual assault, it was considered shameful
because it showed how poor your family was and now they were being mobilized to
do agricultural labor but not in small vulnerable women in the family left at
home formations but rather organized with everybody else all of the other
young women in the village. The marriage law arrived at the same time that the
state was trying to promote land reform and the land reform was a very contested complicated process. And sometimes if it looked
like marriage reform was going to just make life in the villages too
complicated because it engendered so much conflict among families, the state
or by which I mean the local completely overburdened cadres put it on the back
burner. The reason it engendered so much conflict is people were afraid that
their daughters-in-law for whom they had paid good money would walk. Taking that
entire investment in the bride-price with them. One of the things I talk about
in the book is the difference between what I call campaign time, that is
organized by those campaigns that by which we organize time, the most familiar
signposts and domestic time but you could also say personal time or
emotional time or time organized around the family and they're quite different
but they help to constitute each other. For instance when we asked about the
Great Leap Forward, a campaign that everybody knows about, they all
understood us but they would answer back and say oh the time when we ate in the
dining halls, oh the time when we panned for iron ore, oh the time when the men
were off smelting steel. And for them the thing that stood out the most was the
thing that really reorganized daily household life, which was that they ate
in the dining halls. I don't want to make it sound as though this is just a the
state puts loose all of these policy prescriptions and they're all wonderful
and the only thing that happens is there's a lag time. Sometimes the
collision of campaign time and domestic time highlights exactly what went wrong,
not what went right. But you can't assume that these two things are going along in
tandem. You always have to ask what's the state up to, how does that get translated
on the local level and then what do people remember because it remains
important to them as they remember four decades later. I would put it this way, a
lot of the success of the collective years, a lot of the state's strategy of
what some people have called primitive socialist accumulation, of laying the
basis for certain kind of industrialization and the kind of rapid
economic development that took place in the
reform era, a lot of that was underwritten by resources sucked out of
the countryside by state policies. And a lot of that increase in productivity and
freeing up men to do other kinds of work by bringing women into basic agriculture,
a lot of that labor was done by precisely this generation of women. You
could say they underwrote the reforms, farmers in general and women in
particular. So I think what surprised me is just how complicated these different
temporalities are. That you can't just teach the temporality of state events.
You can, but you're going to miss most of what is interesting there and I think to
get it most of what is interesting you got to go talk to people and my most
fervent hope right now because it's really too late to talk to the group
that I talked to, is that people will get out there and talk to their grandparents
about the 60s, 70s, 80s and get some of this firsthand experience and
reflection recorded. And later when people have questions that have not yet
arisen historically or politically, they will have that material to go back to,
because it doesn't hang around until we realize it's important. It passes from
the scene.

args.summary: Gail Hershatter discusses her book "The Gender of Memory: Rural Women and China's Collective Past," which examines the lives of 72 elderly women in rural Shaanxi province during the revolutionary decades of the 1950s and 1960s. The book explores how Party-state policy became local and personal, affecting women's agricultural work, domestic routines, marriage, childbirth, parenting, and notions of virtue. Hershatter explains that she wrote the book because there was insufficient material for teaching about the 1950s beyond a list of government campaigns. She wanted to understand the connection between state policy in Beijing and what happened on the ground for rural women far from power. The research was conducted in Shaanxi due to existing contacts there. Hershatter found that women were eager to share their stories but often didn't register 1949 as a significant event. Key concepts include the distinction between "campaign time" (organized around state campaigns) and "domestic time" (personal/emotional time organized around family). For example, women remembered the Great Leap Forward through daily life changes like eating in communal dining halls rather than through state narratives. Hershatter argues that the generation of women who did agricultural labor during the collective years underwrote China's later economic reforms. She urges people to interview their grandparents about the 1960s-80s to preserve firsthand accounts before they are lost.

The past is never dead. It's not even past

[Not Even Past](https://notevenpast.org/)

# The Gender of Memory: Rural Women and China’s Collective Past, by Gail Hershatter (2011)

By [Jing Zhai](http://www.utexas.edu/cola/history/graduate/gradstudents/profile.php?id=jz8774)

Seventy-two ordinary women, living in four different villages in central and southern Shaanxi Province, mostly born during the 1920s or 1930s, witnessed the rise of the new Communist regime in 1949 and experienced dramatic life transformations as a result. During the 1950s and 1960s, a few of them were national or regional labor models. Some were local activists, village-level officials, or midwives. And the others were just ordinary village women who did not involve themselves in local politics. Although the national or regional labor models might get the precious chance of going to Beijing and even meeting Chairman Mao, these women’s life experiences were mostly confined to their villages. Few of them had the habit of keeping a diary or recording their observations. And in official documents, their personal life stories were rarely discussed. If not for the interviews conducted by Gail Hershatter and Gao Xiaoxian from 1996 through 2006, aging and death would have surely silenced these women’s memory.

[![The Gender of Memory](https://notevenpast.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/The-Gender-of-Memory-196x300.jpg)](https://notevenpast.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/The-Gender-of-Memory.jpg)This book focuses on the memories of rural women who lived through the momentous events of the 1950s. It attempts to recount their life stories not only as historical witnesses, but mostly importantly as women. By tracing the social roles that rural women assumed across their lifetimes, the book reveals changes taking place in women’s field work, domestic labor, childbearing, and marriage. Hershatter successfully brings out the beauty, vibrancy and pain in these women’s rich life experiences. The author asks, “If we placed a doubly marginalized group — rural women — at the center of an inquiry about the 1950s, what might we learn about the effects of Party-state policy and its permutations and appropriations at the local level?”

Usually, memoirs, diaries and interviews that contain people’s memory are used as important clues for historical facts. However, Hershatter’s book is striking for its study of memory itself, based on the large number of interviews she and her collaborator were able to carry out. The distance between memory and the “true” story seems to not be an obstacle for the author and she is fully aware of today’s influences on recollecting the past. Instead, she analyzes the context in which individual memory is generated, especially the subjects’ special experiences as rural women and girls. The stories we hear from women reflect a more distant relationship from politics than that of men. Taking timekeeping as an example, compared with rural men who were familiar with using official time to organize their daily life, women relied on domestic events to remember things. The zodiac, the date of their marriage, and the birthdates of their children formed the system of timekeeping that they used to frame their memories. Memory here is gendered memory.

This book challenges the conventional narrative on the 1950s that is usually focused on changing political campaigns. Many events that people experienced are outside the narrative frame punctuated by campaigns such as land reforms, collectivization, and the Great Leap Forward. By following the life stories of women in farming communities far from the center of state control, these women’s conception of time produced a much more continuous narrative compared with official histories.

[![Chinese workers in front of the open hearth furnace, September 1958. Via Wikimedia Commons](https://notevenpast.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/Chinese-workers-in-front-of-the-open-hearth-furnace-September-1958.-Via-Wikimedia-Commons-640x476.jpg)](https://notevenpast.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/Chinese-workers-in-front-of-the-open-hearth-furnace-September-1958.-Via-Wikimedia-Commons.jpg)

Chinese workers in front of the open hearth furnace, September 1958. Via Wikimedia Commons

Memories of Chinese rural women also questioned the unified narrative in the academic study of gender. For example Chaofeng had been a *tongyangxi*, a “child raised to be a daughter-in-law.” But she experienced painful uncertainties when she decided to divorce her husband during the New Marriage Law Campaign due to her close relations with her mother-in-law. Her experience argues against the traditional analysis of gender reform, regardless of the guilt of *tongyangxi* or the absolute legitimacy of marriage freedom. This book questions the limitations of a lot feminist scholars’ opinion and brings out the question about recording the perspective and the experience of ordinary women. Is gender such a coherent and unified genre that feminists can easily represent the experience of women from a lower society stratum?

As a work about China’s collective past, Hershatter’s book sheds light on the cultural and social history of the 1950s China. But even if you are just simply searching for some enchanting stories, Hershatter’s book is a great place to start.

Gail Hershatter *[The Gender of Memory: Rural Women and China’s Collective Press](http://www.ucpress.edu/book.php?isbn=9780520267701)* (University of California Press, 2011)

args.summary: This webpage is a book review of Gail Hershatter's "The Gender of Memory: Rural Women and China's Collective Past" (2011), published on the academic history blog Not Even Past (University of Texas at Austin). The review, written by Jing Zhai, describes how Hershatter conducted interviews with 72 ordinary rural women from four villages in central and southern Shaanxi Province, mostly born in the 1920s-1930s, who lived through the Communist rise in 1949 and the transformative events of the 1950s (land reforms, collectivization, Great Leap Forward). The book focuses on these women's memories not just as historical witnesses but as women, examining changes in field work, domestic labor, childbearing, and marriage. Rather than treating memory as a transparent window to historical facts, Hershatter studies memory itself—analyzing how individual memory is generated and how rural women's gendered experiences shaped their recollection. For example, women used domestic events (zodiac signs, marriage dates, children's birthdates) rather than official timekeeping to frame memories. The book challenges conventional political-campaign-focused narratives and unified feminist scholarship, arguing that experiences of women like Chaofeng—a former tongyangxi (child bride) who faced painful uncertainties in divorce—complicate simple narratives about gender reform. The review concludes that the book sheds light on China's cultural and social history of the 1950s while also offering engaging personal stories.

--- SOURCE 1: Collaboration in Japanese-occupied China (1937-1945): Old and New Questions | Occupation Studies ---
URL: https://fasos-research.nl/occupationstudies/collaboration-in-japanese-occupied-china-1937-1945-old-and-new-questions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by David Serfass (Inalco-IFRAE, Paris) surveys the historiography of collaboration in Japanese-occupied China (1937-1945), focusing on the collaboration regimes established after Japan's invasion of Chinese provinces from July 1937 to October 1938. Key collaboration governments included the Provisional Government in Beijing (Dec. 1937), the Reformed Government in Nanjing (Mar. 1938), and most notably the Reorganized National Government (RNG) chaired by former Premier Wang Jingwei (Mar. 1940), which claimed legitimacy as the successor to the pre-war National Government. Over 200 million people lived under Japanese occupation.

The historiographical debate revolves around three questions: Who were the collaborators? Why did they collaborate? How was collaboration conducted? These questions have been approached from two opposing directions: one viewing collaboration as a historical anomaly to be denounced, and another contextualizing it within broader historical developments.

**Who were collaborators?** The term "hanjian" (traitors) has been politically charged, with the CPC historically using it to delegitimize the KMT. Western historians like John Hunter Boyle (1972) and Timothy Brook (coining "collaborationist nationalism") have offered more nuanced assessments, while Chinese historians have moved from class-based denunciations to more complex analyses post-1980s.

**Why collaborate?** Explanations range from teleological (looking for warning signs in collaborators' pasts) to circumstantial (contextual choices). Political factors include anti-communism, Asianism, and KMT internal rivalries, while sociological factors include studying in Japan or Japanese marriages. Chinese historians have shifted from class-based explanations to psychological determinism and more recently to complex causal analyses.

**How was collaboration conducted?** Scholarship has moved from viewing collaboration regimes as mere "puppets" to recognizing their autonomy and internal negotiations. Historians now examine the concrete functioning of pro-Japanese institutions and the collaborators' agency vis-à-vis Japanese occupiers. Brook argues collaboration regimes should be studied as part of China's modern state trajectory.

**New research perspectives** include: cultural history (visual culture, music), spatial expansion beyond the Lower-Yangzi region and North China, trans-war approaches (post-1945 continuities), prosopography of middle/low-level administration, study of the Japanese adviser system, puppet armies, and connections within Japan's broader colonial empire. The author calls for bridging gaps between studies of occupied and free China, and between occupation studies and other historical fields.
</summary>

He thus makes the point that pro-Japanese collaboration deserves to be studied as one side of the Chinese elites' common effort to 'save the nation'.", "Against a tendency among earlier Chinese historians to address the former as historical anomalies, Timothy Brook placed them as an integral part of China's modern state trajectory by arguing that 'our disdain for forced ideology produces its opposite, confirmation of the natural legitimacy of state sovereignty' (Brook 2005, p. 223).", "Future research on Japanese-occupied China should not only further explore collaboration in all its aspects, but also attempt to better bridge the gap with other historical fields and broader questions emanating from the comparative field of occupation studies."

--- SOURCE 6: Second Sino-Japanese War ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The webpage is the Wikipedia article on the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945), a major conflict in East Asia that was part of the Pacific Theater of World War II. The war began with the Marco Polo Bridge Incident on July 7, 1937, and concluded with Japan's surrender on September 2, 1945, resulting in a Chinese victory. The conflict involved China (Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek and Communists under Mao Zedong, with a United Front against Japan) fighting against the Empire of Japan and its puppet states (Manchukuo, Wang Jingwei regime, Mengjiang).

Key background includes Japanese expansion, the Warlord Era, Nationalist reunification, and the start of the Chinese Civil War. Pre-war events included the 1931 invasion of Manchuria and sporadic Japanese encroachments. The war progressed through phases: 1937 outbreak (Marco Polo Bridge, Battle of Shanghai, Fall of Nanjing and the Nanjing Massacre); 1938 strategic retreat (Xuzhou, Wuhan, Yellow River flood); 1939–1941 stalemate (Chinese counter-offensives, Japan's Three Alls Policy, United Front collapse); 1942–1943 Allied entry (foreign aid, Burma campaign); 1944 renewed Japanese offensives (Operation Ichi-Go); and 1945 conclusion (final Chinese offensives, Japanese surrender).

Casualties were enormous: Chinese military casualties of approximately 3.85 million, Japanese military casualties of 1.5~ million, and 12,000,000+ civilian deaths. The war involved widespread use of guerrilla tactics, chemical and biological warfare by Japan. The aftermath saw the resumption of the Chinese Civil War. The legacy includes commemorations, controversy over historical revisionism, and implications for the political status of Taiwan.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Same Water Different Dreams ---
URL: https://www.usmcu.edu/Outreach/Marine-Corps-University-Press/MCU-Journal/JAMS-vol-11-no-2/Same-Water-Different-Dreams

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Marine Corps University Press (JAMS, vol. 11, no. 2) by Andrew Rhodes examines the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95 and its enduring lessons for contemporary naval warfare, particularly regarding Chinese strategic thinking. The war was a contest for control of Korea, where Japan's Imperial Navy destroyed China's Beiyang Fleet despite China having modern warships. Key battles included the Battle of Pungdo Island (July 1894), the Battle of Pyongyang, and the pivotal Battle of the Yalu (September 17, 1894), where Japan prevailed due to superior tactics, quick-firing guns, and Chinese command failures. The war ended with the Treaty of Shimonoseki, ceding Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula to Japan.

The author analyzes three consistent themes from recent Chinese publications about the war's lessons: (1) the need to inculcate "maritime consciousness" (haiyang yishi) in the Chinese people, as Qing society had no connection to the sea; (2) the importance of building strong institutions to sustain seapower, contrasting Japan's unified Meiji-era institutions with China's fractured, corrupt Qing system; and (3) the imperative to employ the navy actively and aggressively in combat, rather than the Qing's passive defensive strategy that ceded sea control. Chinese authors criticize the Qing policy of "war avoidance" and argue the Beiyang Fleet should have taken the fight to the enemy.

The article notes that American officers like Philo N. McGiffin and Alfred Thayer Mahan analyzed the war at the time, but it has since been neglected in Western scholarship. The author argues that understanding how Chinese strategists interpret this history is essential for American planners, as the PLAN of today is larger than the U.S. Navy and its officers have absorbed lessons that would lead them to sortie their fleet aggressively in a future conflict, not remain in a defensive posture. The article concludes that the third lesson—active employment of the fleet in combat—remains untested for the modern PLAN, making it a critical area for U.S. wargaming and scenario development.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 remains a cautionary tale full of salient lessons for future conflict." "Chinese authors assess that the future requires that China inculcate an awareness of the maritime domain in its people, that it build institutions that can sustain seapower, and that, at the operational level, it actively seeks to contest and gain sea control far from shore." "Wu Shengli... called on his officers to study the lessons of the Sino-Japanese War as a conflict 'in which both sides' navies were central, and in which victory was won through naval battles.'" "The consensus of the authors cited here suggests that, if they were in command in a future conflict, they would not restrain the fleet behind a geographic line... they would seek to sail the fleet far from shore to take the fight to a superior adversary and contest control of the sea early in a conflict." "The PLAN of 2020 is better built, equipped, and manned than the Beiyang Fleet of 1894, but it remains an open question whether the PLAN would live up to high international expectations or, like the Beiyang Fleet, prove a grave disappointment when meeting a peer competitor in combat."

--- SOURCE 9: “中国抗日战争史研究的回顾与前瞻研讨会”综述 ---
URL: http://jxyyj.ruc.edu.cn/CN/abstract/abstract15555.shtml

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a conference summary of the "Review and Prospect of the Study of the History of China's War of Resistance Against Japan" symposium, held on April 12, 2015, at Renmin University of China. The event was co-organized by Renmin University's Institute of CPC History and Theory and the CASS Institute of Modern History's Revolutionary History Research Office, bringing together over 100 scholars from major Chinese universities and research institutions.

**Part 1: Recent Advances in Research**
The symposium noted that the study of the War of Resistance Against Japan has become an academic hotspot. Key advances include: (1) rich, diverse research output with hundreds of books and thousands of papers annually; (2) extensive archival materials from both Chinese and international sources (including Japan, the US, UK, France, Germany, and Russia); (3) growing international academic exchange, particularly among China, Japan, and South Korea. Scholars emphasized that the war should be viewed as a pivotal turning point in China's national rejuvenation and as the Eastern main battlefield of the global anti-fascist war. The study of the war was divided into two periods: pre-1995 (focused on exposing Japanese atrocities) and post-1995 (expanded to themes of national rejuvenation). Debates on the roles of the CPC and KMT, Japanese war crimes (including the "comfort women" issue, the Nanjing Massacre, and the Tokyo Trials), and war memory were also discussed.

**Part 2: Problems in Current Research**
Scholars identified several issues: (1) inadequate use of foreign sources and limited international perspectives; (2) interference from nationalist sentiment and political considerations, particularly in popular/sensationalist writing; (3) weak research on actual military/war history (e.g., guerrilla warfare, battlefield strategy); (4) insufficient academic study of occupied areas and puppet regimes, which remains at a superficial, condemnatory level.

**Part 3: Consensus for Future Development**
Scholars agreed on four directions: (1) greater use of overseas archives and local Chinese county/municipal archives; (2) strengthening theoretical and methodological frameworks, borrowing from Western and social science approaches; (3) combining macro-narrative with micro-empirical research, and top-down with bottom-up perspectives; (4) balancing national historiography with a global historical perspective to promote more academic and internationalized study of the war.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: [PDF] “抗战研究七十年:回顾与展望” 学术讨论会综述 ---
URL: https://www.krzzjn.com/uploadfile/2020/1207/20201207100620254.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a conference summary published in the journal "抗日战争研究" (Studies of China's Resistance War Against Japan), 2019 Issue No. 4, reporting on the "Seventy Years of Resistance War Studies: Retrospect and Prospect" academic symposium held at Nankai University from November 30 to December 1, 2019. The conference brought together over 40 scholars to review 70 years of academic research on China's War of Resistance Against Japan (1937-1945), since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949.

Key organizational details: The symposium was co-hosted by Nankai University's History Department, the editorial board of "Studies of China's Resistance War Against Japan," and the War of Resistance Memorial Network. It was chaired by Gao Shihua (editor-in-chief of the journal), with opening remarks by Wang Jianlang (Director of the Institute of Modern History, CASS), Tang Zhixuan (Deputy Editor of the Memorial Network), and Jiang Pei (Dean of Nankai History Department).

The symposium covered six sessions organized around thematic areas:

**1. Overall and Conceptual Issues:**
- Zang Yunhu (Peking University) analyzed the "hot and cold" cycles of resistance war studies, noting that before the 1980s the field was "cold," but has since become "gradually hot," though many areas remain under-researched (e.g., the "14-year resistance war" concept, China's wartime economy, society, and culture, occupied territories, Japanese invasion studies).
- Chen Qianping (Nanjing University) proposed a three-stage periodization for the 14-year war: (1) partial resistance before the Marco Polo Bridge Incident (July 1937); (2) China's independent full-scale resistance from July 1937 to Pearl Harbor; (3) international resistance after Pearl Harbor—the most critical stage, which laid the foundation for China's victory and postwar international status.
- Li Jinzheng (Nankai University) discussed the difficulty of writing a comprehensive history of the war, noting three challenges: insufficient attention to foundational social, economic, and cultural forces; the need to address both the anti-Japanese struggle and the CCP-KMT contradictions; and the relative neglect of KMT rear-area resistance.
- Wu Zhijun (CCP History Research editorial board) called for scholars to go beyond the war itself and examine how historians view, study, and represent the war, placing it in broader political, social, and cultural contexts.
- Zhang Sheng (Nanjing University) argued that historical research cannot avoid "fragments" but should not become fragmented; micro-level research can serve larger questions, but fragmentation can lead to historical nihilism.
- Bian Xiuyue (CASS) examined the usage of terms like "comprehensive resistance" and "national resistance," cautioning against rigid politicization of these terms.

**2. CCP (Chinese Communist Party) Resistance:**
- Zhang Yi (Shanghai University of Finance and Economics) reviewed 21st-century scholarship on CCP mass mobilization, noting three shifts: from traditional party history to social and cultural history; from "grand narrative" to "micro-narrative"; and from single to multiple sources. However, insufficient use of Japanese-language materials hampers a full understanding from the Japanese perspective.
- Li Lifeng (Nanjing University) analyzed the CCP's rural political mobilization, identifying two consistent approaches: interest-based mobilization and identity/emotion-based mobilization.
- Li Bingkui (Peking University) noted that "mass movements" remain under-studied, and called for comparative studies across CCP base areas, KMT areas, occupied territories, and overseas Chinese communities.
- Zheng Lizhu (Hebei University) reviewed 70 years of scholarship on the Jin-Cha-Ji (Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei) base area, noting that social history approaches have flourished since 2000.
- Huang Daoxuan (CASS) discussed the May 1938 CCP decision to advance into the North China plain as a turning point, linking it to Mao Zedong's "On Protracted War."
- Zhang Baijia (CCP Central Committee History and Literature Research Institute) urged greater use of foreign observers' records and noted that China's research on war trauma lags behind international WWII studies, while Sino-Japanese war reconciliation remains an urgent issue.
- Li Mingnan (Nankai University) traced how the CCP's revolutionary experience shaped its postwar perceptions and policies toward Japan.
- Lu Xijun (Daito Bunka University, Japan) divided Japanese scholarship on wartime CCP history into two periods: 1945-1979 dominated by "revolution-centered historiography," and post-1980s "relativization" that moved beyond binary good/evil frameworks.

**3. Japanese Invasion of China:**
- Qi Jianmin (Nagasaki Prefectural University, Japan) traced the shift in Japanese research from "Tenno-system fascism theory" to "total war system theory," noting that the latter, emerging after the Cold War, tends to downplay war responsibility and even legitimize wartime policies by linking them to postwar development.
- Liu Yuebing (Nankai University) analyzed the ideological logic of Japan's modern invasion of China, focusing on the kokutai (national polity) theory and Nihon seishin (Japanese spirit) theory.
- Tang Liguo (Peking University) examined Japan's "thought war" (ideological warfare) as a propaganda campaign and a framework for understanding how Japanese elites, intellectuals, and the public accepted the war.
- Wang Meiping (Nankai University) reviewed three periods of postwar Japanese scholarship on the opium invasion policy (1985 and 2000 as dividing lines).
- Xiao Hongsong (Hebei University) noted that Chinese scholarship on wartime opium issues has produced over 80 articles and 11 books, but foreign-language sources remain scarce.
- Ji Chen (Sun Yat-sen University, Zhuhai) examined the compilation of the official Japanese war history of the First Sino-Japanese War (1894-95), noting that after 1903 its editorial policy shifted to beautify Japan's war initiation, avoid military critique, and reduce length, with lasting influence on later official war histories.
- Guo Xunchun (Nankai University) reviewed domestic and Japanese research on modern Japanese military systems.
- Song Zhiyong (Nankai University) traced three periods in Japanese scholarship on the Tokyo Trials, noting that political rightward shifts since the 1990s have significantly affected research.
- Yin Yanjun (Kanto Gakuin University, Japan) discussed disagreements between Chinese and Japanese scholars on whether the Marco Polo Bridge Incident was planned, concluding that while the timing and location may have been contingent, Japan's invasion of China was inevitable.

**4. Other Topics:**
- Zhu Hanguo (Beijing Normal University) discussed Wang Guilin's contributions to resistance war studies, including his views on the "one battlefield vs. two battlefields" debate, the "eight-year vs. fourteen-year war" question, and the nature of Chiang Kai-shek's group.
- Jiang Pei (Nankai University) traced Wei Hongyun's evolving research from military campaigns to fiscal, economic, and social history, with a growing emphasis on international perspectives.
- Zhao Qingyun (CASS) examined the exchanges between Japanese leftist historian Inoue Kiyoshi and Chinese academia.
- Su Shengxiong (Academia Sinica, Taipei) noted that military history research in Taiwan was dominated by the military for the first 40 years, then shifted to academia, with a move from traditional to "new military history" emphasizing war-society relations.
- Qi Xiaolin (CCP Central Party School) advocated for studying war history through material factors (food, ammunition, medicine, communications) from an international perspective.
- Guo Yang (Nanjing University) reviewed 70 years of scholarship on KMT political warfare, calling for new perspectives on party-army relations.
- Li Bin (Hunan Academy of Social Sciences) discussed Hunan's resistance war studies.
- Zeng Chongbi (Chongqing Technology and Business University) reviewed local fiscal studies during the war.
- He Jiangfeng (Nankai University) re-examined the "He-Umezu Agreement" (1935) controversy.

In the final discussion, Gao Shihua concluded that the field of resistance war studies, as a mature discipline, should engage in self-reflection and maintain a sense of crisis. He urged younger scholars to master at least one foreign language and to strengthen use of Japanese sources and research.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Wang Jianlang pointed out that among all periods of modern Chinese history, resistance war studies is the most popular, and the recent National Social Science Fund 'Special Project on War of Resistance Studies' with nearly 30 approved projects has further boosted its热度, yet beneath the popularity there remain many insufficiently studied areas.", "Zang Yunhu argued that before the 1980s—the first 40 years of resistance war studies—the overall research situation was 'cold'; since the 1980s, it has entered a 'gradually hot' state and reached a climax, but still exhibits 'hot within cold' and 'cold within heat'.", "Lu Xijun divided Japanese scholarship on wartime CCP history into two periods: 1945-1979 dominated by 'revolution-centered historiography,' and the post-1980s 'relativization' era that overcomes binary good/evil frameworks.", "Gao Shihua concluded that the field of resistance war studies, as a mature discipline, should have the capacity for self-summary and self-reflection, and must maintain a sense of crisis; the younger generation should master at least one foreign language and strengthen their grasp of Japanese research information and use of Japanese materials."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The webpage is a conference summary published in *抗日战争研究* (2023年第4期) by贺江枫 and 叶子锐, reviewing the "Diaries and the History of China's War of Resistance Against Japan Academic Symposium" held November 3-5, 2023, at Nankai University. The symposium was co-organized by Nankai University's History Department, the Center for Chinese and Foreign Civilizations, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) Institute of Modern History's War of Resistance Research Office, and the journal *抗日战争研究*. Over 30 scholars from leading Chinese universities and research institutes participated, presenting 20 papers across five sessions.

**Key Themes:**

1. **Diaries and Anti-Japanese Base Areas (Revolutionary Base Research):** Papers examined CCP cadre diaries (e.g., Gao Lu) to explore rural investigation, party-building, and the evolution of the party-state system. Emphasis was placed on using diaries to understand policy-making, organization, and daily life in base areas.

2. **Diaries and Nationalist-Controlled Areas (Guomindang/Guotongqu):** Papers utilized diaries of Chiang Kai-shek, Chen Bulei, Chen Kewen, and Zhang Xueliang to analyze high-level politics, military strategy (e.g., the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign), diplomacy (Sino-German relations in 1940), and the publication of Chiang's *China's Destiny*.

3. **Diaries and Occupied Areas (Lunxianqu):** Papers examined ordinary people's diaries (e.g., engineer Sun Shoushan, village intellectual Lü Shunxiang, Peking opera actor Xun Huisheng) to reveal daily life, mentalities of fear and survival, and local military integration under Japanese occupation.

4. **Diaries and Wartime Intellectuals:** Papers focused on the diaries of Zheng Tianting, Mei Yiqi, and other scholars to examine the restoration of Peking University after the war, field investigations by scholars in the rear areas, and the spread of wartime information.

5. **Foreign-Language Diaries:** Papers explored diaries of Western residents (e.g., Bertrand Beitler in Shanghai) and Japanese Prime Minister Hara Takashi's diary to provide international perspectives on the war and Sino-Japanese diplomacy.

**Roundtable Discussion:** Scholars debated the academic value of diaries (richness, continuity, ability to restore human agency), methodological approaches (caution about privacy, authenticity, and the need to corroborate with archives), and limitations (fragmentation, homogenization, and the need to distinguish between individual and public dimensions). The consensus was that diaries are crucial for deepening War of Resistance research but must be used critically and in combination with other sources.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Diary as a type of historical material has irreplaceable significance for deepening the study of the history of the War of Resistance, said CASS researcher Wang Jianlang and Professor Jiang Pei in their opening remarks., Diaries can restore the 'human' subject that has long been buried in historical research, noted Professor Jiang Pei., The use of diaries should avoid homogenization and pay attention to the commonalities and differences presented in diaries from different regions and individuals, argued Professor Zhang Junfeng., Diaries should be cross-referenced with archival materials, and emotional expressions in diaries should be stripped as much as possible, suggested Associate Researcher He Jiangfeng., People's limitations determine the limitations of diaries; in the current era of explosive growth in historical materials, more attention should be paid to the interpretation of historical materials, stated Professor Li Xiang.

--- SOURCE 1: Forgotten Ally: China's World War II - With Rana Mitter ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wpBmOlUjDUo

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a transcript of a WW2TV YouTube episode (posted Dec 4, 2022) featuring historian Rana Mitter discussing his book "Forgotten Ally: China's World War II, 1937-1945" (UK title: "China's War with Japan, 1937-1945: The Struggle for Survival"). Mitter, a professor at Oxford University specializing in modern Chinese history, explores China's role in WWII, arguing it has been largely overlooked in Western historiography.

**Key points covered:**

- **Scale of the war**: 10+ million Chinese deaths (including ~4 million from the Henan famine attributable to the Japanese invasion), 80-100 million refugees, and 8 years of continuous conflict (1937-1945), making it WWII's longest theater.

- **Strategic importance**: China pinned down over 500,000 Japanese troops for 4.5 years before Pearl Harbor. Mitter argues that China's decision to keep fighting in 1938 (when many diplomats thought it should surrender) was crucial to the global war — if China had capitulated, Japan could have redirected forces toward the Soviet Union or British India.

- **Wang Jingwei**: Mitter discusses the controversial collaborator who set up a Japanese-sponsored regime in Nanjing in 1940. Unlike French collaborators, Wang argued he was the true patriot restoring peace, and his widow's trial drew public sympathy. He remains a taboo subject in China.

- **Reassessment of Chiang Kai-shek and Nationalist forces**: Recent scholarship has partially rehabilitated the Nationalist (Guomindang) war effort. Chiang was "playing a weak hand quite well" — holding down Japanese forces from the southwest, conducting major battles (Tai'erzhuang, Changsha, Shanghai, Hengyang), and pursuing a strategy of protracted war until foreign assistance arrived.

- **General Stilwell**: Mitter critiques the American commander, noting that newly available diaries show Chiang Kai-shek's perspective — Stilwell was reckless with Chinese troops and his account was self-serving. The "Vinegar Joe" myth has been substantially revised.

- **Social history**: The experience of refugees, survival under occupation, and the massive movement to Chongqing (wartime capital) are areas where recent archival research has transformed understanding.

- **Future research**: Mitter calls for more access to Chinese archives (especially on collaboration and Communist decision-making), and more social history of the war, particularly on Chongqing as a wartime capital.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Bear in mind that this is, whatever else you think about it, in terms of scale, an absolutely massive part of the Second World War. We still don't know the exact number of casualties. Perhaps we never will do... but you know, it's certainly realistic to say that many millions, 10 or more million people died as a result of the war.", "In 1938, an awful lot of observers, including many British and American diplomats, thought that China, a year into the war, was so heavily battered, so much on the brink of defeat that it ought to to do a deal. And if it had done so, think about actually what the aftermath would be... that would have freed up all those troops or freed up large numbers of them anyway to turn their attention elsewhere, maybe towards Soviet Union, maybe towards British India.", "Chiang Kai-shek was playing a weak hand quite well. In other words, he had, you know, a large, poor, agrarian country. He was not fully in charge of it even when he was the president of generalissimo president of China.", "The Chinese communist guerrilla resistance does remain very important for the harassment of the Japanese, but in terms of set piece battles, it's now widely acknowledged that... essentially all the big battles of China's World War II experience... have to be undertaken by nationalist troops, nationalist armies.", "For a very long time, I would say from the 1950s through to 70s, Mao's China did not acknowledge that Chiang Kai-shek's nationalists had been actually the major part of that resistance... But from the 1980s onwards, there has been a wider and a more objective examination of the war from within China itself."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Forgotten Ally: China's World War II 1937-1945 (Rana Mitter) ---
URL: https://jeffrich.substack.com/p/forgotten-ally-chinas-world-war-ii

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the "Burning Archive" substack by Jeff Rich reviews Rana Mitter's book *Forgotten Ally: China's World War II 1937-1945* (2013), as part of a World History Tour of China. The key argument is that China's role in WWII is largely forgotten in the West, despite China suffering 14-20 million deaths and fighting since 1937. The review highlights the paradox of China emerging from the war as a sovereign nation and a founding "Big Four" member of the UN, while simultaneously being devastated and internally divided. Chiang Kai-shek described the Allied powers (USA, UK, USSR) as "a kidnapper, a hooligan, and a bully." The review details the terrible price of war: catastrophic bombing, the Nanjing Massacre, the deliberate destruction of Yellow River dams by Nationalist forces (causing 500,000-900,000 deaths and 5 million refugees), and the internal polarization and violence against collaborators. Mitter personalizes the story through three leaders: Chiang Kai-shek, Mao Zedong, and Wang Jingwei (who led a collaborationist government), each representing a different path to a modern Chinese state. The review also discusses Mitter's later work *China's Good War* (2020), which argues that China is now rewiring "circuits of memory" of WWII to assert its role as a creator of the post-war order and challenge the US narrative of liberation. The article concludes that to understand the present, we must acknowledge China's suffering and resistance in WWII.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: The Rape of Nanking (book) - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rape_of_Nanking_(book)

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Rape of Nanking: The Forgotten Holocaust of World War II is a bestselling 1997 non-fiction book by Iris Chang about the 1937-1938 Nanjing Massacre, where the Imperial Japanese Army committed mass murder and mass rape of Chinese civilians after the Battle of Nanjing. It was one of the first major English-language books on the subject and has been translated into several languages. 

Chang was inspired to write the book after her parents told her about the massacre in her childhood and she found little information in libraries. She spent two years researching, finding the diaries of John Rabe (a German Nazi Party member who led the Nanking Safety Zone) and Minnie Vautrin (an American missionary who saved about 10,000 women and children). The book is divided into three parts: narrating events from Japanese, Chinese, and Western perspectives; describing postwar reactions; and examining why knowledge of the massacre remained hidden. It details atrocities including killing, torture, and rape, estimating 20,000 to 80,000 women were raped and citing death toll estimates ranging from 38,000 to 430,000.

The book was a commercial and critical success, selling over half a million copies and spending 10 weeks on the New York Times Best Seller list. However, it faced criticism from some historians who questioned Chang's analysis of Japanese culture, her death toll calculations, and accuracy due to her lack of formal historian training. The book caused significant controversy in Japan, with right-wing groups threatening Chang and her publisher, ultimately causing the Japanese translation to be delayed until 2007. Chang received hate mail and threats from Japanese ultranationalists, suffered from depression and psychosis, and committed suicide on November 9, 2004.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a book review from Pacific Affairs (published by UBC) of Diana Lary's "China's Civil War: A Social History, 1945-1949" (Cambridge University Press, 2015). The review, written by Matt Galway (UBC), examines Lary's approach to the Chinese Civil War through the lens of trauma theory and social history, moving beyond traditional Marxist and postmodern interpretations. The book uses biographies, memoirs, illustrations, and oral histories to highlight the "painful and divisive social impacts of the war" (12), giving voice to ordinary people who suffered. The eight-chapter volume covers the war chronologically—from the social background after 1927, through GMD instability and Communist resurgence, to the Communists' victory in 1949 and postwar outcomes in the 1950s, including class entrenchment, generational splits, and cross-Taiwan Strait interpretations of the conflict. The review notes two criticisms: Lary's biographical snapshots are too short and distracting, and her reliance on Chalmers Johnson's dated theory that nationalism alone explains peasant mobilization (citing recent scholarship by Chen Yungfa and Prasenatra Duara showing more complex factors). Overall, the review praises the book as a "long-overdue investigation" that breaks the mould of military history by emphasizing social dimensions of civil strife, while noting some issues detract from an otherwise excellent study.
</summary>

<summary>
# 南京大屠杀 - 维基百科条目摘要

**南京大屠杀**（日语：南京大虐殺）是1937年12月13日至1938年2月期间，大日本帝国在攻占中华民国首都南京后，对当地平民与战俘实施的大规模屠杀、强奸、纵火、抢劫等一系列战争罪行。

## 背景与时间线
- 1937年8月13日：日军进攻上海（淞沪会战），中国军队顽强抵抗三个月
- 11月20日：蒋介石任命唐生智为南京卫戍司令官
- 12月1日：日本天皇下令华中方面军进攻南京
- 12月8日：日军全面占领南京外围阵地
- 12月12日：南京卫戍司令部下令撤退，但撤退命令混乱，导致大量军民伤亡
- 12月13日：南京沦陷，大屠杀开始
- 持续6周以上，直至1938年2月

## 主要事件

### 屠杀
- 日军在攻占南京时俘虏数万中国官兵，在高层授意下集体屠杀
- 手段包括集体枪杀、活埋、机枪扫射、刺刀捅戮、焚尸灭迹
- 据统计，被集体屠杀者达19万人以上，加上零散屠杀，总计达30万人以上
- 远东国际军事法庭认定：大屠杀前2-3天内南京城内有1.2万平民被杀害，超过20万人遇害
- 南京军事法庭查证日军集体屠杀28案，19万余人受害

### 强奸与性虐待
- 约2万至8万名中国妇女遭日军强奸
- 受害者从10岁幼女到70岁老妇，多数遭奸杀
- 远东国际军事法庭认定，在大屠杀第一个月内约2万中国妇女遭日军强奸
- 日军军官纵容、鼓动强奸作为鼓舞士气的工具

### 劫掠与纵火
- 日军抢劫商店、住宅、机关、仓库，甚至各国使馆
- 南京城三分之一建筑被纵火烧毁
- 城内外23.8%建筑被焚毁，63.0%遭劫掠，合计88.5%遭破坏
- 损失古物26,584件、字画7,720幅、书籍45,979册

## 人道救助
- **南京安全区**：由约翰·拉贝等20多位西方人士建立，占地约3.86平方公里，最多收容难民约25万人
- 其他避难所包括栖霞寺、江南水泥厂等
- 安全区于1938年2月被日军强行解散

## 遇难者人数
- 东京审判认定：20万人以上遇难
- 中国官方认定：30万人遇难
- 联合国教科文组织世界记忆名录估计：至少30万中国人遇难
- 慈善团体掩埋尸体记录：8家慈善团体共埋尸19.8万具

## 战后审判与争议
- 远东国际军事法庭和南京军事法庭对日本战犯进行审判
- 松井石根、谷寿夫等被判处死刑
- 日本国内存在对死亡人数和事件性质的争议，但几乎无人完全否认事件发生
- 围绕大屠杀的争议仍是中日关系的主要障碍
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 30: 汪海涛 | 《抗日战争研究》30年论文主题探密 ---
URL: http://jds.cass.cn/xscg/ybwz/202302/t20230209_5587050.shtml

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a detailed academic article by Wang Haitao (汪海涛) published on the website of the Institute of Modern History, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS). The article analyzes the thematic evolution of papers published in the journal *The Journal of Studies of China's Resistance War Against Japan* (《抗日战争研究》) over its 30-year history (1991-2021). The author systematically categorizes nearly 1,200 articles into 16 major themes to help researchers understand the field's development, research hotspots, and remaining gaps.

Key findings from the analysis include:

1. **Overview of the Journal**: The journal was founded in 1991 as a leading publication for the study of China's War of Resistance Against Japan. Initial classification systems (1991-2010) grouped articles into categories such as general overview, Japan's invasion of China, politics, military, economy, society, culture, foreign relations, and war legacy issues. Later classifications became more simplified.

2. **Quantitative Analysis (1991-2010)**: According to scholar Zhang Zhiyi (2011), 1,026 papers were published in the first 20 years. Among 197 papers with identifiable author age data, "socio-economic-cultural-education" topics comprised 23.38%, "political-military" 22.73%, "Japan's invasion of China" 22.08%, "war legacy issues" 13.64%, "foreign relations" 8.44%, and "biographical studies" 7.8%.

3. **16-Category Breakdown**: 
   - **Review/Summary Articles (147)**: Early focus on major events (e.g., September 18 Incident, Marco Polo Bridge Incident), later shifted to regional and specialized topics, including international perspectives and cross-strait collaboration.
   - **Japan's Invasion of China (123)**: Covered policy/theory, specific atrocities (bombings, biological/chemical warfare), economic plunder, and organizational structures (e.g., units like Unit 1855, the South Manchuria Railway).
   - **Biographies/Groups (114)**: Most-studied figures: Chiang Kai-shek (16 articles), Wang Jingwei (4), Song Ziwen (4), Song Qingling (4), Zhang Wentian (4), Zhang Xueliang (3), Yan Xishan (3), Hu Shi (3), Chen Cheng (3).
   - **Foreign Relations (113)**: Most studied foreign nations: US (33), UK (20), Soviet Union (17), League of Nations (8), Germany (5), Italy (3), Burma (3).
   - **Politics (120)**: Subdivided into CPC, KMT, other parties, pre-war politics, local governance, and puppet regimes.
   - **Military History (141)**: Major battles (e.g., Battle of Shanghai: 7 articles, Hundred Regiments Offensive: 6), strategy, logistics, air/naval forces, and the distinction between "frontline" and "enemy rear" battlefields.
   - **Economics (97)**: Finance, taxation, banking, salt, grain/oil, textiles, trade, rural economy, enterprises, and mining.
   - **Base Areas & Occupied Territories (105)**: Most studied base areas: Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia (17 articles), followed by Jin-Cha-Ji and North China (9 each). Growing focus on CPC internal cadre rectification and social history.
   - **Nanjing Massacre (56)**: Mostly focused on debates and significance, with fewer on specific details; shifted to specialized journal *Japanese Invasion of China and Nanjing Massacre Studies* after 2008.
   - **Culture & Education (96)**: Puppet regimes' enslaving education, KMT education, base area education, journalism/publishing, wartime literature/arts, and intellectual trends.
   - **Sociology (54)**: Social issues, famine/refugee problems, migration, women, and modernization.
   - **National Defense Mobilization (59)**: Military industry, conscription, military grain supply, and air defense.

4. **Notable Observations**: 
   - The field has shifted from broad macro-narratives to more specialized, micro-level topics.
   - There is a recognized need for more international perspectives, especially using Japanese primary sources.
   - Traditional military/war history has declined relative to socio-cultural approaches.
   - By 2021, a consensus had emerged that the leadership of the war was shared between the CPC and KMT, as proposed by Liu Danian.

The article also provides links to related databases and institutions, including the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, the National Social Sciences Database, and the "Database of the War of Resistance Against Japan and Modern Sino-Japanese Relations."
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: The Fruits of 28 years of Investigation into the “Comfort Women ---
URL: https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/5DD450FEFCFBE39C98D422CA893A7295/S1557466021037980a.pdf/reconstructing-the-history-of-the-comfort-women-system-the-fruits-of-28-years-of-investigation-into-the-comfort-women-issue-in-china.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic article by Professor Su Zhiliang of Shanghai Normal University, published in The Asia-Pacific Journal | Japan Focus (March 2021), reconstructs the history of the Japanese military's "comfort women" system—a system of sexual slavery operated during World War II. The article traces 28 years of investigation into the issue in China and beyond.

**Key Points:**

- **Origins and Timeline:** The comfort women system began in January 1932 in Shanghai, when Japanese marine commanders designated businesses as comfort stations (e.g., Dai-ichi Salon). It expanded rapidly after the July 1937 Marco Polo Bridge Incident and lasted until August 1945, covering 22 provinces in China and extending across the Pacific and Southeast Asia.

- **Government/Military Involvement:** The Japanese state—including the Ministries of Foreign Affairs, Home Affairs, Justice, police, and military—was directly involved in establishing and managing comfort stations. Documents from the Jilin Provincial Archives show the Kwantung Army spent 532,000 yen on "purchasing comfort women" in just four months (1944-1945). Funds were treated as public military money.

- **Scale:** At least 172 comfort stations in Shanghai, 70 in Nanjing, 67 in Hainan confirmed. In Zhenjiang, 109 comfort women served 15,000 soldiers (a ratio of 1 woman to 137 men); over ten days, one woman serviced an average of 82 men.

- **Survivor Numbers:** Confirmed survivors identified include: Chinese mainland (250), South Korea (239), North Korea (209), Indonesia (several hundred), Philippines (over 100), Taiwan (around 50), Japan (around ten), Netherlands (several). At time of writing, only 18 identified victims remained on the Chinese mainland.

- **International Consensus:** UN Human Rights Commission (1996, via Radhika Coomaraswamy) recommended Japan acknowledge legal responsibility, compensate victims, release documents, formally apologize, include history in textbooks, and punish war crimes. The US, Canada, Netherlands, EU, Philippines, South Korea, and others have issued condemnatory resolutions.

- **Memory and Commemoration:** August 14 is International "Comfort Women" Commemoration Day. Museums exist in Korea, China, Taiwan, Japan, Philippines, Netherlands, US, and Canada. In 2016, a joint application for UNESCO Memory of the World Register inscription ("Voices of the Comfort Women") was submitted by 11 countries/regions but faced Japanese government opposition.

- **Forced Recruitment:** The article refutes Japanese rightist claims that women were not compelled, presenting extensive documentary evidence of women being forced or deceived into sexual slavery. Examples include women detained in blockhouses in Shanxi and captured on Hainan Island.

The translator's introduction (Edward Vickers) notes the political context of Chinese scholarship on this issue, observing that while Su Zhiliang documents the system extensively, the Chinese Communist Party limits discussion of broader feminist or transnational critiques that might implicate contemporary attitudes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The history of the comfort women system begins in January 1932 in Shanghai. At that time, the commanders of a special unit of the Japanese marines designated a number of businesses run by local overseas Japanese as comfort stations.", "Rather than talking simply of 'links' between the Japanese government and military, and the comfort women system, it is thus more accurate to see them as its 'midwives'.", "Amongst 109 comfort women, there were 48 Japanese, 36 Koreans and 25 Chinese. Meanwhile, the 109 comfort women in Zhenjiang had to serve 15,000 soldiers – a ratio of one woman to 137 men.", "In December 2015, the Japanese and South Korean Governments hurriedly concluded an agreement 'irrevocably' resolving the comfort women issue, but its blatant insincerity aroused strident opposition from victims and from the Korean public.", "The Japanese military's comfort women system – a war crime involving the sexual enslavement of women – like the Nazi Holocaust of the Jews or the Nanjing Massacre, is an instance of inhuman wartime violence that should be carved into the memory of humanity and used to instruct future generations, in order to guard against the repetition of such violence."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: [PDF] JF Special Issue: 'The Comfort Women as Public History' - UCL Discovery ---
URL: https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10127536/3/Frost_1.%20CW%20INTRO%20FROSTVICKERS02_09%202.m.%20finally%20final%200210.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This introductory essay to a special issue of Japan Focus analyzes the "heritagization" of the "comfort women" issue since the early 2000s, examining how the focus of activism has shifted from litigation and reparations toward commemoration and heritage-making. The authors (Mark R. Frost and Edward Vickers) trace the political, cultural, and historiographical background to ongoing disputes over comfort women, including the post-Cold War democratization of South Korea that enabled the issue to surface in 1991 when Kim Hak-Sun launched the first legal case. The essay examines how the Japanese government issued apologies in 1993 and 1995 and established the Asian Women's Fund, but these measures were deemed inadequate by many activists. Since the late 1990s, Japanese rightists have denied military involvement, while the scholarly consensus outside Japan generally acknowledges the system existed as a genuine atrocity, though debate continues regarding its relationship with licensed prostitution.

The essay critically examines the turn toward UNESCO's Memory of the World Register as a forum for "heritage diplomacy," with rival East Asian actors competing for global approval. The authors note that Holocaust commemoration has become a paradigm influencing comfort women heritage-making, but question whether heritagization necessarily fosters reconciliation, arguing that "when done badly, the drive to commemorate a contentious issue as public history can exacerbate rather than resolve division and hatred." The essay examines how comfort women commemoration has become entangled with transnational feminism, diaspora activism in the US, and global identity politics, including connections to the #MeToo movement. The authors conclude by emphasizing the need for representation of comfort women as public history to pay "due regard to nuance and complexity," particularly regarding the depiction of victims versus perpetrators, the transnational dimension of the system, and its relationship with broader histories of gender politics and sexual subjugation of women.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"When done badly, the drive to commemorate a contentious issue as public history can exacerbate rather than resolve division and hatred.", "we therefore emphasise the need for representation of comfort women as public history to pay due regard to nuance and complexity, for example regarding the depiction of victims versus perpetrators; the transnational dimension of the system; and its relationship with the broader history of gender politics and the sexual subjugation of women.", "The response from Japanese rightists determined the conflict's subsequent historiographical battlelines. Since the late 1990s, rightists have denied any direct involvement by the Japanese military and the Japanese state in the organized sexual coercion of women during wartime.", "this shift to heritagization has also involved appeals to UNESCO, which through its role in certifying heritage as of 'universal' significance has emerged, in effect, as an international court for commemorative justice.", "Memorialization efforts have typically prioritized affective impact over historical complexity, homogenizing the past into a recognizable and digestible package where the diversity of historical experience is largely erased."

This webpage from the Comfort Women Resource Center (hosted at UCLA's Center for Korean Studies) presents an overview of a primary sources collection documenting the Japanese military "comfort women" system during the Asia Pacific War (1930s-1945). The collection is introduced by Dr. Jimin Kim, a historian specializing in Korean history.

The "comfort women" system is described as one of the largest known institutions of state-sponsored human trafficking and sexual slavery in the 20th century, involving Imperial Japan's systematic use of sexual and gender-based violence to further imperial expansion.

The primary sources fall into two categories:

1. **Japanese Military Documents** - These include documents that escaped destruction at the end of WWII. Key documents confirm that the Japanese military supervised, regulated, and controlled comfort stations. The documents are sub-grouped into: (a) Establishment of the comfort station system, (b) Conscription and recruitment of women, (c) Transportation of women, and (d) Management of the comfort stations. Notably, the documents refer to "comfort women" as military supplies or objects, not human beings. A key document (JS-13) discovered in the 1990s forced the Japanese government to reverse its denials and admit military involvement.

2. **U.S. and Allied Forces Documents** - These include battlefield reports, interrogation reports, and intelligence documents that provide perspectives from victims and witnesses. Key documents include the 1945 ATIS report (US-2), the 1944 OWI Prisoner of War Interrogation Report No. 49 (US-11) containing interviews with 20 Korean "comfort women," and OSS memos confirming women were recruited through deception and coercion. Allied intelligence agencies also used this information for psychological warfare against Japanese troops.

The documents irrefutably establish that the Japanese imperial government, police, and military commanded and authorized the system, using force, fraud, and bureaucratic machinery. The collection notes that survivors' testimonies have been essential to revealing the full history, and the survivors hope the history serves as a reminder to prevent future atrocities.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

This article by Jordyn Haime and Lily Ottinger explores Taiwan's complex and contested relationship with its World War II legacy. While China used the 80th anniversary of Japan's surrender to showcase military might and assert its claim over Taiwan, Taiwan's DPP-led government under Lai Ching-te took a "softer approach," framing the war as a struggle for freedom and democracy against dictatorship.

The article highlights the Kaohsiung War and Peace Memorial Park, the only museum in Taiwan commemorating Taiwanese soldiers who fought under Japan. These veterans—conscripted, forced, or misled into service—were later denied recognition. After the ROC took over in 1945, the KMT regime "politically forgot" their service, and they were treated as "traitors to the Han race." Under martial law (1949-1987), only the Chinese victory narrative was allowed. Democratization enabled Taiwanese to study their own history for the first time.

Veterans' rights activist Khou Chiau-eng self-immolated in 2008 to protest government neglect, leading to the memorial park's opening in 2009. However, advocates say recognition remains incomplete. The "comfort women" issue has been undermined by politicization, with the Ama Museum in Taipei struggling to stay open.

The article critically notes that the Kaohsiung memorial ceremony avoided mentioning Japanese atrocities or the role of Taiwanese soldiers as both victims and victimizers. The museum's director, Lee Wen-huan, stated the focus is on how people were "inexplicably drawn into" war, not revisiting questions of right and wrong. --- SOURCE 21: Mapping the Gap: Translation and Dissemination of China’s War of Resistance Historical Documents in the Anglophone World (Since 1937) ---
URL: https://www.scirp.org/journal/paperinformation?paperid=144777

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper systematically investigates the translation and dissemination of China's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression historical documents and publications in the English-speaking world, primarily in major Anglophone countries since WWII. Using bibliographic/documentary analysis, the study examines books, academic research, periodicals, and audiovisual materials.

Key findings: (1) Translated works related to China's War of Resistance have increased from about 50 new translations in 2010 to roughly 80 in 2015 and over 150 by 2023, with growing diversity in types. (2) Despite this growth, significant gaps remain in translation achievements, contributing to insufficient international recognition of China's wartime contributions. (3) There is a notable lack of translation regarding the Chinese Communist Party-led resistance contributions and the national spirit reflected in these struggles. (4) Major historical facts such as the Nanjing Massacre are also insufficiently translated and disseminated.

The paper analyzes how China's War of Resistance is marginalized in Western WWII historiography, history textbooks (Germany, UK, Australia, France, US), and media coverage. It examines translations of literary works (both wartime and post-war), mass media (songs, movies, documentaries), and commemorative activities.

The study identifies several challenges: imbalance in translation quantity and coverage with over-reliance on classic works by a few authors (e.g., Lao She, Xiao Hong, Ai Qing), underrepresentation of regional narratives and local resistance memories, translation quality issues including cultural misinterpretation and political rewriting, and limited dissemination channels that struggle to reach broader public audiences.

Recommendations include expanding translation content and communication channels, building trust mechanisms, establishing multilingual translation resource databases, promoting a dual-track "academic translation + commercial communication" model, leveraging digital platforms and short video platforms, and constructing interpretive systems framed by the "community of shared future for mankind" to maximize recognition of China's historical wartime status.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

Gail Hershatter discusses her book "The Gender of Memory: Rural Women and China's Collective Past," which examines the lives of 72 elderly women in rural Shaanxi province during the revolutionary decades of the 1950s and 1960s. The book explores how Party-state policy became local and personal, affecting women's agricultural work, domestic routines, marriage, childbirth, parenting, and notions of virtue. Hershatter explains that she wrote the book because there was insufficient material for teaching about the 1950s beyond a list of government campaigns. She wanted to understand the connection between state policy in Beijing and what happened on the ground for rural women far from power. The research was conducted in Shaanxi due to existing contacts there. Hershatter found that women were eager to share their stories but often didn't register 1949 as a significant event. Key concepts include the distinction between "campaign time" (organized around state campaigns) and "domestic time" (personal/emotional time organized around family). For example, women remembered the Great Leap Forward through daily life changes like eating in communal dining halls rather than through state narratives. --- SOURCE 1: Collaboration in Japanese-occupied China (1937-1945): Old and New Questions | Occupation Studies ---
URL: https://fasos-research.nl/occupationstudies/collaboration-in-japanese-occupied-china-1937-1945-old-and-new-questions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by David Serfass (Inalco-IFRAE, Paris) surveys the historiography of collaboration in Japanese-occupied China (1937-1945), focusing on the collaboration regimes established after Japan's invasion of Chinese provinces from July 1937 to October 1938. Key collaboration governments included the Provisional Government in Beijing (Dec. 1937), the Reformed Government in Nanjing (Mar. 1938), and most notably the Reorganized National Government (RNG) chaired by former Premier Wang Jingwei (Mar. 1940), which claimed legitimacy as the successor to the pre-war National Government. Over 200 million people lived under Japanese occupation.

The historiographical debate revolves around three questions: Who were the collaborators? Why did they collaborate? How was collaboration conducted? These questions have been approached from two opposing directions: one viewing collaboration as a historical anomaly to be denounced, and another contextualizing it within broader historical developments.

**Who were collaborators?** The term "hanjian" (traitors) has been politically charged, with the CPC historically using it to delegitimize the KMT. Western historians like John Hunter Boyle (1972) and Timothy Brook (coining "collaborationist nationalism") have offered more nuanced assessments, while Chinese historians have moved from class-based denunciations to more complex analyses post-1980s.

**Why collaborate?** Explanations range from teleological (looking for warning signs in collaborators' pasts) to circumstantial (contextual choices). Political factors include anti-communism, Asianism, and KMT internal rivalries, while sociological factors include studying in Japan or Japanese marriages. Chinese historians have shifted from class-based explanations to psychological determinism and more recently to complex causal analyses.

**How was collaboration conducted?** Scholarship has moved from viewing collaboration regimes as mere "puppets" to recognizing their autonomy and internal negotiations. Historians now examine the concrete functioning of pro-Japanese institutions and the collaborators' agency vis-à-vis Japanese occupiers. Brook argues collaboration regimes should be studied as part of China's modern state trajectory.

**New research perspectives** include: cultural history (visual culture, music), spatial expansion beyond the Lower-Yangzi region and North China, trans-war approaches (post-1945 continuities), prosopography of middle/low-level administration, study of the Japanese adviser system, puppet armies, and connections within Japan's broader colonial empire. The author calls for bridging gaps between studies of occupied and free China, and between occupation studies and other historical fields.
</summary>

He thus makes the point that pro-Japanese collaboration deserves to be studied as one side of the Chinese elites' common effort to 'save the nation'.", "Against a tendency among earlier Chinese historians to address the former as historical anomalies, Timothy Brook placed them as an integral part of China's modern state trajectory by arguing that 'our disdain for forced ideology produces its opposite, confirmation of the natural legitimacy of state sovereignty' (Brook 2005, p. 223).", "Future research on Japanese-occupied China should not only further explore collaboration in all its aspects, but also attempt to better bridge the gap with other historical fields and broader questions emanating from the comparative field of occupation studies."

--- SOURCE 6: Second Sino-Japanese War ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The webpage is the Wikipedia article on the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945), a major conflict in East Asia that was part of the Pacific Theater of World War II. The war began with the Marco Polo Bridge Incident on July 7, 1937, and concluded with Japan's surrender on September 2, 1945, resulting in a Chinese victory. The conflict involved China (Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek and Communists under Mao Zedong, with a United Front against Japan) fighting against the Empire of Japan and its puppet states (Manchukuo, Wang Jingwei regime, Mengjiang).

Key background includes Japanese expansion, the Warlord Era, Nationalist reunification, and the start of the Chinese Civil War. Pre-war events included the 1931 invasion of Manchuria and sporadic Japanese encroachments. The war progressed through phases: 1937 outbreak (Marco Polo Bridge, Battle of Shanghai, Fall of Nanjing and the Nanjing Massacre); 1938 strategic retreat (Xuzhou, Wuhan, Yellow River flood); 1939–1941 stalemate (Chinese counter-offensives, Japan's Three Alls Policy, United Front collapse); 1942–1943 Allied entry (foreign aid, Burma campaign); 1944 renewed Japanese offensives (Operation Ichi-Go); and 1945 conclusion (final Chinese offensives, Japanese surrender).

Casualties were enormous: Chinese military casualties of approximately 3.85 million, Japanese military casualties of 1.5~ million, and 12,000,000+ civilian deaths. The war involved widespread use of guerrilla tactics, chemical and biological warfare by Japan. The aftermath saw the resumption of the Chinese Civil War. The legacy includes commemorations, controversy over historical revisionism, and implications for the political status of Taiwan.
</summary>
