## 2. RESEARCH PERSPECTIVES (Dominant Paradigms)

### 2.1 Communist Party Narrative ("CCP as Mainstay")

The official CCP narrative positions the Party as the "中流砥柱" (mainstay/pillar) of the nationwide war of resistance. The China Victory over Anti-Japanese War website presents the central argument that "中国共产党是全民抗战的中流砥柱" (The CCP is the mainstay of the nationwide war of resistance), claiming the CCP established the anti-Japanese national united front, implemented comprehensive popular warfare, proposed the strategy of protracted war, and led guerrilla warfare in enemy-occupied rear areas. "持久战的方针丰富了反法西斯战争的军事理论，人民战争的伟大实践提供了弱国战胜强国的范例" (The protracted war strategy enriched the military theory of the anti-fascist war; the great practice of people's war provided an example of a weak nation defeating a strong nation). "敢不敢动员人民、武装人民、依靠人民，能不能充分激发蕴含在广大军民中的最深厚伟力，是决定抗日战争前途和命运的重要因素" (Whether one dares to mobilize, arm, and rely on the people, and can fully unleash the deepest strength of the armed forces and civilians, is a key factor determining the fate of the war) [19].

**Zhang Hongzhi's** interview argues: Mao Zedong first used "中流砥柱" in May 1941. The CCP provided political leadership throughout the war while the KMT was passive: the CCP called for resistance the day after the September 18 Incident; it established the anti-Japanese united front; it promoted peaceful resolution of the Xi'an Incident; it proposed the protracted war strategy during the KMT's crisis of defeatism and defections; and it took on the toughest fighting under the most difficult conditions, with no CCP unit defecting to the enemy while killing hundreds of thousands of Japanese and over a million puppet troops. The CCP's mass-line policy—combining national liberation with people's liberation through reforms like reasonable taxation (合理负担) and rent reduction (减租减息)—created a "human mountain" (人山) of popular support. He concludes that the different performance of the two parties on the two battlefields determined the people's hearts and the transition from old to new China [17].

**Zhang Haipeng's** macro-theoretical framework argues "中国共产党的正确主张和对抗日民族统一战线的主导作用是抗日战争取得胜利的基本原因" (The CCP's correct propositions and dominance in the anti-Japanese national united front were the fundamental reasons for the victory of the War of Resistance). He argues there were TWO leadership centers during the war—Yan'an (CCP) and Chongqing (KMT/Chiang). Both were indispensable. Japanese assessments confirmed the CCP's strength as "the number one enemy" and that "whatever happens, China's war of resistance will follow the CCP's track" [20].

### 2.2 Nationalist/Taiwanese Perspective

**President Ma Ying-jeou's** 2015 speech at the "War History and Memory: International Academic Conference on the 70th Anniversary of Victory in the War of Resistance" made three main points: (1) the ROC's war contributions were largely forgotten internationally due to the post-WWII Chinese Civil War, Korean War, and Cold War; he detailed the scale of the war: 22 major campaigns, 1,100 major battles, and 39,000 minor battles; 3.22 million ROC soldiers were casualties, including 268 fallen generals (7 full generals, 56 lieutenant generals, 205 major generals); over 20 million civilians died. The ROC pinned down 800,000 modern Japanese troops, preventing them from fully engaging in the Pacific theater. (2) He traced the legal chain of documents — the 1943 Cairo Declaration, the 1945 Potsdam Proclamation, and the Japanese Instrument of Surrender (Sept 2, 1945) — arguing these have legal force as a unified set (evidenced by their inclusion in the UN Treaty Series). He noted Japan's forces in China surrendered in Nanjing (Sept 9, 1945) and Taipei (Oct 25, 1945), after which the ROC began exercising sovereignty over Taiwan. (3) He stated his principles of "judge matters on their merits, put oneself in others' shoes, and clearly distinguish gratitude from grievances," emphasizing, "The error of aggression may be forgiven, but the truth of history cannot be forgotten" ("侵略的錯誤或可原諒，但歷史的真相不能遺忘") [4].

**Li En-han (李恩涵)**, a research fellow at the Academia Sinica's Institute of Modern History, wrote a review/preface for Zheng Lang-ping's (鄭浪平) book "Immortal Glory: History of the Second Sino-Japanese War," which surveyed post-war Chinese historiography. He noted that early official KMT works include He Yingqin's "Eight Years of War of Resistance" (1946), Bai Chongxi's works (1946), Chen Cheng's (1946), and the Defense Ministry's works (1966, 1978). CCP works like "History of the People's Liberation Army During the War of Resistance" (1953) were similarly limited or more distorted. The catalyst for new research was the autumn 1982 Japan textbook screening incident, when "Japanese militarists denied atrocities including the Nanjing Massacre, even changing 'invasion of China' to 'advance into China,' sparking strong protests from China, Korea, and Southeast Asia and prompting intensified study of the war." Taiwan academic responses included the 1984 "Pre-War Ten Years of National Construction Conference" (Academia Sinica IMR), 1985 "Anti-Japanese War and National Building Conference," 1987 "Anti-Japanese War and National Building Academic Conference," and KMT party history conferences. Private works include Liu Feng-han's collection (1987) and Li En-han's "Research on Japanese Military Atrocities" (1994) [1 of search 2].

### 2.3 "People's History" / History from Below

Diana Lary's "The Chinese People at War" tells the war's history "from the perspective of those who went" through it [6][8]. The Diaries symposium emphasized that "Diaries can restore the 'human' subject that has long been buried in historical research," noted Professor Jiang Pei [11].

The 2015 Renmin University conference consensus called for "combining macro-narrative with micro-empirical research, and top-down with bottom-up perspectives" [9].

### 2.4 Revisionist/Transnational Perspectives

**Yangyang Cheng's** LA Review of Books review notes that Mitter's "China's Good War" explores "not the war itself but how it is remembered in China and whom that memory serves. The Chinese government has embraced more diverse remembering of the war to 'command devotion at home and respect from abroad.'" The 2019 film "The Eight Hundred" about the 1937 Battle of Shanghai faced controversy and was edited after the Chinese Red Culture Association condemned its favorable portrayal of KMT soldiers and the Nationalist flag [11][15].

The 2004 Harvard conference convened by Ezra Vogel revealed critical divergences: "Chinese participants insisted the war was one of aggression and framed discussions in moral terms, frustrating Japanese and Western historians. Japanese participants felt the moral emphasis alienated sympathetic Japanese, while Western historians noted the war had little impact on the Pacific theater's outcome and was considered a 'peripheral theatre.' Chinese historians also avoided debating Chiang Kai-shek's priorities during the war, insisting all Chinese united in times of crisis" [8].

**Zhang Baijia** urged greater use of foreign observers' records and noted that "China's research on war trauma lags behind international WWII studies" [10].

**Zang Yunhu** (Peking University) analyzed the "hot and cold" cycles of resistance war studies, noting that before the 1980s the field was "cold," but has since become "gradually hot," though many areas remain under-researched (e.g., the "14-year resistance war" concept, China's wartime economy, society, and culture, occupied territories, Japanese invasion studies) [10].

### 2.5 Japanese Perspectives

**Qi Jianmin** (Nagasaki Prefectural University, Japan) traced the shift in Japanese research from "Tenno-system fascism theory" to "total war system theory," noting that the latter, emerging after the Cold War, tends to downplay war responsibility and even legitimize wartime policies by linking them to postwar development [10].

**Liu Yuebing** (Nankai University) analyzed the ideological logic of Japan's modern invasion of China, focusing on the kokutai (national polity) theory and Nihon seishin (Japanese spirit) theory [10].

**Tang Liguo** (Peking University) examined Japan's "thought war" (ideological warfare) as a propaganda campaign and a framework for understanding how Japanese elites, intellectuals, and the public accepted the war [10].

**Yin Yanjun** (Kanto Gakuin University, Japan) discussed disagreements between Chinese and Japanese scholars on whether the Marco Polo Bridge Incident was planned, concluding that while the timing and location may have been contingent, Japan's invasion of China was inevitable [10].

**Song Zhiyong** (Nankai University) traced three periods in Japanese scholarship on the Tokyo Trials, noting that political rightward shifts since the 1990s have significantly affected research [10].

**Ji Chen** (Sun Yat-sen University, Zhuhai) examined the compilation of the official Japanese war history of the First Sino-Japanese War (1894-95), noting that after 1903 its editorial policy shifted to beautify Japan's war initiation, avoid military critique, and reduce length, with lasting influence on later official war histories [10].

**Zhao Qingyun** (CASS) examined the exchanges between Japanese leftist historian Inoue Kiyoshi and Chinese academia [10].

## 3. RESEARCH METHODS

### 3.1 Archival Research

The 2015 Renmin University conference noted "extensive archival materials from both Chinese and international sources (including Japan, the US, UK, France, Germany, and Russia)" as a key advance. However, scholars identified as a problem that "能够熟练利用外文文献、具有国际视野的学者还很少" (scholars who can skillfully use foreign-language literature and have international perspectives are still very few) [9].

The CASS War of Resistance Research Office undertakes "overseas collection of rare resistance war materials" as part of the National Social Science Fund Special Project [5].

The 15 digital resources compiled for the 80th anniversary of China's victory (2025) include: Academia Sinica's Institute of Modern History Archives Search System (Taiwan); Academia Historica Archives System (Taiwan) — includes "Anti-Japanese War Historical Materials"; National Archives Information Network (Taiwan); Anti-Japanese War and Modern Sino-Japanese Relations Literature Data Platform (CASS) — massive open-access postwar archive including newspapers, journals, books, photos, and audio-visual materials; JACAR (Japan Center for Asian Historical Records); Japanese Military "Comfort Women" Related Official Documents; Biographical Dictionary of Occupied China (BDOC) (France - INALCO and Aix-Marseille University); Open Library - Sino-Japanese War 1937-1945 (Internet Archive) — 7,011 Chinese, English, and Japanese books; Japan at War and Peace, 1930-1949 (Archives Unbound/US National Archives); Warfare in China, 1839-1945: British Perspectives (UK National Archives); Political, Economic, and Military Conditions in China, 1918-1941 (US Military Intelligence Division); Political Relations and Conflict between Republican China and Imperial Japan, 1930-1939 (US National Archives). The guide emphasizes that "digitization has enabled researchers to transcend national boundaries and construct multi-perspective historical interpretations" [3 of search 2].

The Oxford programme involved "publications, fieldwork, and international collaborations" [2].

### 3.2 Diary-Based Research (Microhistory)

The "Diaries and the History of China's War of Resistance Against Japan Academic Symposium" (November 3-5, 2023, Nankai University) was co-organized by Nankai University's History Department, the Center for Chinese and Foreign Civilizations, the CASS Institute of Modern History's War of Resistance Research Office, and the journal *抗日战争研究*. Over 30 scholars participated, presenting 20 papers across five sessions:

1. **Diaries and Anti-Japanese Base Areas:** Papers examined CCP cadre diaries (e.g., Gao Lu) to explore rural investigation, party-building, and the evolution of the party-state system.
2. **Diaries and Nationalist-Controlled Areas:** Papers utilized diaries of Chiang Kai-shek, Chen Bulei, Chen Kewen, and Zhang Xueliang to analyze high-level politics, military strategy (e.g., the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign), diplomacy (Sino-German relations in 1940), and the publication of Chiang's *China's Destiny*.
3. **Diaries and Occupied Areas:** Papers examined ordinary people's diaries (e.g., engineer Sun Shoushan, village intellectual Lü Shunxiang, Peking opera actor Xun Huisheng) to reveal daily life, mentalities of fear and survival, and local military integration under Japanese occupation.
4. **Diaries and Wartime Intellectuals:** Papers focused on the diaries of Zheng Tianting, Mei Yiqi, and other scholars to examine the restoration of Peking University after the war, field investigations by scholars in the rear areas, and the spread of wartime information.
5. **Foreign-Language Diaries:** Papers explored diaries of Western residents (e.g., Bertrand Beitler in Shanghai) and Japanese Prime Minister Hara Takashi's diary.

Key methodological debates: "Diary as a type of historical material has irreplaceable significance for deepening the study of the history of the War of Resistance," said CASS researcher Wang Jianlang and Professor Jiang Pei. "Diaries should be cross-referenced with archival materials, and emotional expressions in diaries should be stripped as much as possible," suggested Associate Researcher He Jiangfeng. "People's limitations determine the limitations of diaries; in the current era of explosive growth in historical materials, more attention should be paid to the interpretation of historical materials," stated Professor Li Xiang. The consensus was that diaries are crucial for deepening War of Resistance research but must be used critically and in combination with other sources [11].

### 3.3 Oral History

The Anti-Japanese War Memorial Web (Changsha, China) includes "veteran interviews, oral histories, and large book series" [3 of search 2]. The People's Daily article notes "over 10 volumes of chronicles and interview records" were published [25].

### 3.4 Quantitative Methods

The 2004 Harvard conference and various Chinese sources cite detailed casualty statistics. President Ma cited: 22 major campaigns, 1,100 major battles, 39,000 minor battles; 3.22 million ROC soldiers casualties including 268 fallen generals; over 20 million civilians died [4]. Wang Jianlang cited: front battlefield killed/wounded about 850,000 Japanese troops; enemy-rear battlefield killed/wounded over 500,000; Eighth Route Army suffered over 340,000 casualties including 700+ officers above regimental commander level; CCP forces grew to about 1.32 million troops and 2.6+ million militia; base areas totaling nearly 1 million square kilometers serving nearly 100 million people [16]. Zhang Haipeng cited: In 1938, 94% of Japanese forces were in China; in 1941, 69% (35 of 51 divisions); China always pinned down ~1 million Japanese troops; Japan suffered 1.98 million deaths in China vs. only 890,000 in the Pacific; China suffered 35 million casualties [20].

### 3.5 Comparative History

Li Bingkui called for "comparative studies across CCP base areas, KMT areas, occupied territories, and overseas Chinese communities" [10]. The Wuhan symposium covers "Regional, National, and Global Perspectives" [28].

### 3.6 Digital Humanities

The Pan Xun project developed "replicable and promotable methodologies including school-institute-local collaboration, digital humanities, and multidisciplinary approaches" [26]. The CASS project includes "construction of a digital data platform for resistance war and modern Sino-Japanese relations literature" [5].

### 3.7 Prosopography

David Serfass calls for "prosopography of middle/low-level administration" as a new research direction [1]. The Biographical Dictionary of Occupied China (BDOC) provides biographies of key figures in Japanese-occupied China (1937-1945) [3 of search 2].

## 4. THEORETICAL APPLICATIONS

### 4.1 Total War Theory

**Qi Jianmin** traced the shift in Japanese research from "Tenno-system fascism theory" to "total war system theory" [10]. The Second Sino-Japanese War has been described as a total war where China fought for survival against Japanese aggression [1 of search 2].

### 4.2 Modernization Theory

Rana Mitter's Oxford programme argues "China's conflict with Japan in the mid-twentieth century must be brought to the forefront of our understanding of the wider path of Chinese modernity" [2].

### 4.3 Nationalism Theory

Mitter's "China's Good War" frames "China's radical reassessment of its own past is a new founding myth for a nation that sees itself as destined to shape the world" [12]. The Asian Review of Books notes that "China's international relations have been significantly shaped by its attempt to change the collective memory of the war, particularly in the twenty-first century" [15].

### 4.4 Colonialism/Postcolonialism

The Li En-han article describes the pre-war era as "半殖民地、半封建性" (semi-colonial, semi-feudal) [1 of search 2]. Japanese colonial rule in occupied areas is characterized by "integrated military-political-economic-cultural control" [21].

### 4.5 Trauma Studies

**Zhang Baijia** noted that "China's research on war trauma lags behind international WWII studies" [10]. The LA Review of Books review describes China as "a society in post-traumatic distress and collective amnesia" [11].

### 4.6 Memory Studies

The Oxford programme and Mitter's works apply memory studies frameworks. The APJJF article analyzes "the development of official discourse of the memory of the Second Sino-Japanese War from 1949 to the present in the PRC" [5]. The National WWII Museum notes Mitter's work shows "how Chinese leaders once tried to suppress memories of their nation's brutal experience during World War II, but now they celebrate the 'victory'" [14].

### 4.7 Gender Theory

Helen Schneider's "Keeping the Nation's House: Domestic Management and the Making of Modern China" applies gender/feminist frameworks to wartime domestic management [2].

## 5. RESEARCH CONCLUSIONS AND KEY HISTORIOGRAPHICAL DEBATES

### 5.1 The "Front Battlefield vs. Enemy-Rear Battlefield" Debate

Wang Jianlang argues both battlefields were indispensable and mutually supportive, criticizing attempts to minimize either side's role. He contests comparisons based solely on victory numbers, noting the KMT army had 1.7 million soldiers at the war's start while the CCP-led Red Army had under 50,000 (plus about 10,000 guerrillas), with vastly different equipment—making absolute number comparisons unreasonable. He argues that as the war progressed, the enemy-rear battlefield became increasingly important, playing a leading and exemplary role, especially after the 1944 failure of the KMT front during the Henan-Hunan-Guangxi campaign [16].

Zhang Hongzhi argues the KMT's 22 major frontal campaigns were mostly defensive, recovering little territory (except the Burma-Yunnan counteroffensive), and the frontal battlefield still lost vast territory in 1944. He dismisses claims that KMT high-ranking casualties exceed the CCP's as "absurd" (荒唐), arguing that casualty counts alone are a poor measure of contribution. He notes that CCP commander casualties appear low only because they are counted on the KMT's restricted wartime establishment (only three divisions for the 8th Route Army), with many generals serving in reduced ranks. Left Quan (左权), deputy chief of staff of the 8th Route Army, held a status higher than any KMT casualty. He also emphasizes the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army's fallen generals must not be forgotten [17].

Zhu Hanguo (Beijing Normal University) discussed Wang Guilin's contributions to resistance war studies, including his views on the "one battlefield vs. two battlefields" debate [10].

The 2015 Renmin University conference noted that "the study of the war was divided into two periods: pre-1995 (focused on exposing Japanese atrocities) and post-1995 (expanded to themes of national rejuvenation)" [9].

### 5.2 The "8-Year vs. 14-Year War" Debate

**Zhang Haipeng** argues these concepts are complementary, not opposing. The 14-year war combines 6 years of local resistance (1931-1937) with 8 years of national war (1937-1945). The concept was originally proposed by Mao Zedong in "On Coalition Government" at the 7th Party Congress in April 1945. He explains the distinctions between local and national resistance: during local resistance (1931-1937), the KMT government prioritized "internal pacification before external resistance" (攘外必先安内), focusing on encirclement campaigns against the Red Army, while accepting successive concessions (Shanghai Ceasefire Agreement 1932, Tanggu Truce 1933, He-Umezu Agreement 1935) [20].

**Chen Qianping** (Nanjing University) proposed a three-stage periodization for the 14-year war: (1) partial resistance before the Marco Polo Bridge Incident (July 1937); (2) China's independent full-scale resistance from July 1937 to Pearl Harbor; (3) international resistance after Pearl Harbor—the most critical stage, which laid the foundation for China's victory and postwar international status [10].

**He Jiangfeng** (Nankai University) re-examined the "He-Umezu Agreement" (1935) controversy [10].

**Li En-han** frames the war as "1931-1937-1945" and describes the ~14 years of struggle ("with US, USSR, UK, and Netherlands") leading to victory and China's rise as a founding member of the UN Security Council [1 of search 2].

### 5.3 The Role of the Nationalists vs. Communists

The 2004 Harvard meeting revealed that "Chinese historians also avoided debating Chiang Kai-shek's priorities during the war, insisting all Chinese united in times of crisis" [8].

**Zhang Hongzhi** argues that the KMT represented the big landlord and capitalist class, feared and suppressed the masses, pursued a one-sided army-only resistance, and made unilateral demands (e.g., Yellow River dike breach, Changsha burning, forced conscription). KMT forces in the rear either fled, disintegrated, or defected to puppet forces. Chiang's KMT concept ("exchange space for time, accumulate small victories into big ones") was a one-sided military strategy that devolved into merely "waiting through time" (以拖待变) for favorable international developments (e.g., declaring war only after Pearl Harbor). Mao's "兵民是胜利之本" (soldiers and people are the foundation of victory) in "On Protracted War" was the only strategy relying on self-reliance and people's war to reverse the balance and reclaim territory [17].

**Mitter's** "Forgotten Ally" (2003) covers China's eight-year war of resistance focusing on three key leaders: Chiang Kai-shek, Mao Zedong, and Wang Jingwei [14]. Mitter's works discuss the "long-taboo Guomindang war effort" being examined by Chinese scholars post-Deng [12]. The "good war" narrative requires the rehabilitation of Chiang Kai-Shek's Nationalists (KMT), whose role was long forbidden in Chinese historiography—mirroring Mao's view that the Japanese were a "disease of the skin" while Communists were a "disease of the heart" [15]. The Asian Review of Books notes: "Still today, the CCP is in a position where it is making several conflicting arguments simultaneously: that (by implication) the Nationalist state was legitimate and sovereign, presumably up to 1949, even though the civil war was based on the premise that it was not... The state has still not found the right balance to enable it to use but also control the memory of the Nationalists" [15].

**Wang Chaoguang's** volume argues "The rise and fall of leadership between the Kuomintang and Communist Party not only concerned the development of wartime Chinese politics but also laid the groundwork for the direction of postwar Chinese politics" [13].

### 5.4 The Question of Collaboration

David Serfass frames the debate around three questions: Who were the collaborators? Why did they collaborate? How was collaboration conducted? These have been approached from two opposing directions: one viewing collaboration as a historical anomaly to be denounced, and another contextualizing it within broader historical developments. Timothy Brook's "collaborationist nationalism" concept "makes the point that pro-Japanese collaboration deserves to be studied as one side of the Chinese elites' common effort to 'save the nation.'" Explanations for collaboration range from teleological to circumstantial; political factors include anti-communism, Asianism, and KMT internal rivalries, while sociological factors include studying in Japan or Japanese marriages. Chinese historians have shifted from class-based explanations to psychological determinism and more recently to complex causal analyses [1].

Yu Zidao's review notes the re-evaluation of theories about Chiang Kai-shek and Wang Jingwei's alleged "double act" (双簧) [21].

### 5.5 The Nanjing Massacre Historiography

The 1982 Japanese textbook screening incident—in which "Japanese militarists denied atrocities including the Nanjing Massacre, even changing 'invasion of China' to 'advance into China'"—sparked intensified study of the war in both Taiwan and mainland China [1 of search 2]. Iris Chang's 1997 "The Rape of Nanking" is a key work cited by President Ma [4]. The Library of Congress guide lists "The Nanjing Massacre and the making of mediated trauma" [3]. The 2015 Renmin University conference discussed debates on Japanese war crimes including the Nanjing Massacre and the Tokyo Trials [9].

### 5.6 The "Comfort Women" Issue

The 2015 Renmin University conference discussed the "comfort women" issue as part of debates on Japanese war crimes [9]. The CASS Institute of Modern History undertakes a research project on the "comfort women" issue under the National Social Science Fund Special Project [5]. The digital resources guide lists the Japanese Military "Comfort Women" Related Official Documents database with over 1,700 documents [3 of search 2].

### 5.7 China as the "Eastern Main Battlefield" of WWII

**Zhang Haipeng** presents eight arguments establishing China as the Eastern main battlefield: Key data: In 1938, 94% of Japanese forces were in China; in 1941, 69% (35 of 51 divisions). Chinese forces always pinned down ~1 million Japanese troops. Japan suffered 1.98 million deaths in China vs. only 890,000 in the Pacific. China suffered 35 million casualties. China's war began two years before the European theater's start in 1939. The article criticizes Eurocentrism in WWII historiography [20].

The 2015 Renmin University conference emphasized "the war should be viewed as a pivotal turning point in China's national rejuvenation and as the Eastern main battlefield of the global anti-fascist war" [9].

President Ma stated the ROC pinned down 800,000 modern Japanese troops [4].

By contrast, the 2004 Harvard conference noted "Western historians noted the war had little impact on the Pacific theater's outcome and was considered a 'peripheral theatre.' The critical determinant in the allied victory over Japan was a shortage of ships: even if one million imperial soldiers had not been tied down on the mainland, they could not have stopped the allied march" [8].

### 5.8 The War's Impact on Chinese Society and Postwar Legacy

The Oxford programme states: "The Second World War in China was the single most wrenching event in modern Chinese history. When Japan was finally defeated in 1945, China was on the winning side, but lay devastated, having suffered some 15 million deaths, massive destruction of industrial infrastructure and agricultural production, and the shattering of the tentative modernization begun by the Nationalist government" [2].

**Zhang Haipeng** argues the victory was "a pivot of national rejuvenation" — the first complete victory against foreign invasion in modern Chinese history, reversing national decline to rise; contributing to the CCP's maturity and Mao Zedong Thought; the united front's role; the forging of anti-war spirit; formation of Chinese national community consciousness; recovery of Taiwan (validated by the Cairo Declaration and Potsdam Proclamation, with "One China" as both international and domestic legal principle); paving the way for the PRC's founding; and proving the CCP's full maturity and alignment with historical correctness [20].

**Wikipedia** provides casualty figures: Chinese military casualties of approximately 3.85 million, Japanese military casualties of 1.5~ million, and 12,000,000+ civilian deaths, 14,000,000–22,000,000 total deaths. Official Nationalist data: 1,319,958 killed, 1,761,335 wounded, 130,116 missing, 3,211,409 total casualties. Japanese medical data: 455,700–700,000 military dead, 900,000 wounded, 1.5~ million total casualties. The war began with the Marco Polo Bridge Incident on July 7, 1937, and concluded with Japan's surrender on September 2, 1945. Key phases: 1937 outbreak (Marco Polo Bridge, Battle of Shanghai, Fall of Nanjing and the Nanjing Massacre); 1938 strategic retreat (Xuzhou, Wuhan, Yellow River flood); 1939–1941 stalemate (Chinese counter-offensives, Japan's Three Alls Policy, United Front collapse); 1942–1943 Allied entry (foreign aid, Burma campaign); 1944 renewed Japanese offensives (Operation Ichi-Go); and 1945 conclusion [6].

The Asian Review of Books notes: "Over 10 million Chinese died between 1937 and 1945, mostly civilians killed by the Imperial Japanese Army, and China tied down more than half a million Japanese troops" [15].

### 5.9 War Memory, Nationalism, and the "Good War" Narrative

Mitter's "China's Good War" explores the shift from suppressing memories of WWII to celebrating the "victory" as a foundation of rising nationalism. The book was named a Foreign Affairs Book of the Year and a Spectator Book of the Year. Praise includes: "Insightful…a deft, textured work of intellectual history." —Foreign Affairs; "A timely insight into how memories and ideas about the second world war play a hugely important role in conceptualizations about the past and the present in contemporary China." —Peter Frankopan, The Spectator [12]. China uses the "good war" narrative internationally to claim moral leadership, as evidenced by Xi Jinping's 2015 speech calling for international recognition of China's contribution to the antifascist war. "The book suggests the dispute with Japan is really an internal Chinese debate about national identity, not a conflict between nations" [15].

**Yangyang Cheng's** critical review argues the title "China's Good War" is problematic—while Studs Terkel used "the good war" ironically, "in Mitter's book 'good' is literal, presenting the Chinese government's position without sufficient refutation." The review criticizes the book's omission of China's borderlands and ethnic minorities and its state-centric framework accepting Beijing's definitions of "China" and "Chinese-ness" without interrogation [11].

**De Giorgi's** 2014 article (JSTOR 26372424) states: "New scholarly research on China's resistance against the Japanese invasion has grown considerably in recent years, serving to place the event at the" center of scholarly attention [4].

## 6. INSTITUTIONAL INFRASTRUCTURE AND MAJOR PROJECTS

The University of Oxford's "China's War with Japan: The Persistence of Conflict" (1931 to the Present) was funded by a Leverhulme Trust Research Leadership Award (2007-2012), directed by Professor Rana Mitter. Key personnel included Research Associates Dr Sherman Lai and Dr Helen Schneider; Research Assistant Dr Annie Hongping Nie; Affiliated Researchers Dr Matthew Johnson, Dr James Reilly, Dr Federica Ferlanti, Dr Aaron William Moore, and Dr Tehyun Ma; Graduate Students Lily Chang, Sha Hua, and Elina Sinkkonen. Publications include Rana Mitter's "China's War with Japan 1937-1945: The Struggle for Survival" (published in North America as "Forgotten Ally: China's World War II, 1937-1945"), Aaron William Moore's "Writing War: Soldiers Record the Japanese Empire," and Helen Schneider's "Keeping the Nation's House: Domestic Management and the Making of Modern China" [2].

### 6.2 CASS Institute of Modern History — War of Resistance Research Office

Established in May 2019 following a decision by the CASS Party Leadership Group, with Gao Shihua (高士华) as its first director. The office has 6 research staff: Director Wu Minchao (吴敏超), Deputy Director Feng Miao (冯淼), and members Liang Xinlei (梁馨蕾), Peng Peng (彭鹏), Hao Zhaoli (郝昭荔), and Wang Zhao (王钊). In 2023, the discipline was selected as a key discipline under CASS's "Summit Strategy" (登峰战略). The office was established to implement President Xi Jinping's July 30, 2015 speech stating "同这场战争对中华民族和世界的影响相比，我们的抗战研究还远远不够，要继续进行深入系统的研究" (compared to the impact of this war on the Chinese nation and the world, our resistance war research is far from sufficient, and deeper systematic research must continue). Three platforms: the China Society for the History of the War of Resistance Against Japan (established January 1991), the journal *抗日战争研究* (War of Resistance Against Japan Research, started September 1991), and the WeChat public account (launched January 2019). The institute undertakes 7 projects under the National Social Science Fund Special Project on War of Resistance: construction of a digital data platform; international cooperation research; joint cross-strait compilation of Chinese resistance war history; overseas collection of rare materials; development of special bibliographies and databases; research on the "comfort women" issue; and translation of Japan's "War History Series" (战史丛书) [5].

### 6.3 The 2019 Nankai "Seventy Years of Resistance War Studies" Symposium

Held November 30-December 1, 2019, co-hosted by Nankai University's History Department, the editorial board of *抗日战争研究*, and the War of Resistance Memorial Network. Chaired by Gao Shihua, with opening remarks by Wang Jianlang (Director of the Institute of Modern History, CASS), Tang Zhixuan, and Jiang Pei (Dean of Nankai History Department). Wang Jianlang noted "among all periods of modern Chinese history, resistance war studies is the most popular, and the recent National Social Science Fund 'Special Project on War of Resistance Studies' with nearly 30 approved projects has further boosted its热度, yet beneath the popularity there remain many insufficiently studied areas." Gao Shihua concluded that "the field of resistance war studies, as a mature discipline, should have the capacity for self-summary and self-reflection, and must maintain a sense of crisis; the younger generation should master at least one foreign language and strengthen their grasp of Japanese research information and use of Japanese materials" [10].

### 6.4 The 2015 Renmin University Symposium

Held April 12, 2015, co-organized by Renmin University's Institute of CPC History and Theory and the CASS Institute of Modern History's Revolutionary History Research Office, bringing together over 100 scholars. Key advances identified: (1) rich, diverse research output with hundreds of books and thousands of papers annually; (2) extensive archival materials from both Chinese and international sources; (3) growing international academic exchange. Problems identified: (1) inadequate use of foreign sources and limited international perspectives; (2) interference from nationalist sentiment and political considerations, particularly in popular/sensationalist writing; (3) weak research on actual military/war history; (4) insufficient academic study of occupied areas and puppet regimes, which remains at a superficial, condemnatory level. Consensus for future development: (1) greater use of overseas archives and local Chinese county/municipal archives; (2) strengthening theoretical and methodological frameworks, borrowing from Western and social science approaches; (3) combining macro-narrative with micro-empirical research, and top-down with bottom-up perspectives; (4) balancing national historiography with a global historical perspective [9].

### 6.5 Key Chinese-Language Reference Works

**Du Jidong and Wu Minchao's** "当代中国抗日战争史研究" (Research on the History of the War of Resistance Against Japan in Contemporary China, August 2025) is a comprehensive research survey covering mainland China (excluding Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, and foreign studies). It is structured in three parts: (1) overviewing the development of the topic over 70 years by stages; (2) introducing important themes, developmental context, and innovative research; and (3) identifying existing problems and offering forward-looking thoughts. It contains 15 specific topics [12].

**Mainland China early works** (from Li En-han's survey): Gong Gujin and Tang Peiji's "History of the Anti-Japanese War" (1984), Luo Huanzhang's works (1987), Wang Fu's 3-volume "Japanese Invasion of China War" (1990), the "Anti-Japanese War Research" quarterly journal (launched 1991 by CASS Institute of Modern History), Liu Danian's "Seventy Years of Japanese Invasion of China" (1992, ~600,000 characters), and the Military Science Academy's 3-volume "History of China's Anti-Japanese War" (1992, ~1.5 million characters). By 1992, mainland produced ~400 monographs and ~2,000 papers/memoirs on the war. The Wang Yulin-led "Anti-Japanese War History Series" (1993+, planned 50+ volumes) and the ~10 million character "Anti-Japanese War" documentary compilation (1997, 7 volumes/11 books) were published [1 of search 2].

The People's Daily article (August 19, 2015) notes that from 1978 onwards, "according to incomplete statistics, over 500 specialized works, more than 60 specialized journals, over 30 collections of documents, and more than 10 volumes of chronicles and interview records related to Anti-Japanese War history were published." It calls for research to adopt a correct ideological position, avoid subjective bias toward history, and maintain historical truth. It highlights four future research directions: strengthening the study of cultural history, international history, historical integration, and Taiwan-related history during the Anti-Japanese War period. Regarding Taiwan: "Taiwan was under Japanese colonial rule for 50 years (since 1895)... research on the war should 'appropriately include the Taiwan issue,' as Taiwan's history is an inseparable part of China's overall anti-Japanese history" [25].

### 6.6 The Library of Congress Resource Guide

The "Sino-Japanese War of 1937-1945: A Resource Guide" provides a selected bibliography of secondary scholarship published in Chinese, Japanese, and English. Notable English-language titles include "The Battle for China" (Peattie, Drea, van de Ven), "China's Good War" (Mitter), "Collaboration" (Brook), "Factories of Death" (Harris), "The Nanjing Massacre and the making of mediated trauma," and "The Pacific War, 1931-1945" (Ienaga) [3].

### 6.7 The 2004 Ezra Vogel Harvard Conference

Scholars from China, Japan, and the West were convened to discuss the military history of the Sino-Japanese War. The project aimed "to see if scholars could agree on factual events to provide a foundation for reconciliation." Dr Vogel said: "We want to bring together these scholars to see if they could agree on what actually happened during the war. Hopefully, they can contribute to resolving the history issue. Scholars can't solve political problems, but they can provide a basic message to politicians who want to promote reconciliation and solve these problems." The meeting revealed critical divergences, as detailed above [8].

### 6.8 Wikipedia Overview (Contextual Reference)

The Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945) was a major conflict in East Asia that was part of the Pacific Theater of World War II. The war involved China (Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek and Communists under Mao Zedong, with a United Front against Japan) fighting against the Empire of Japan and its puppet states (Manchukuo, Wang Jingwei regime, Mengjiang). Pre-war events included the 1931 invasion of Manchuria. The aftermath saw the resumption of the Chinese Civil War. The legacy includes commemorations, controversy over historical revisionism, and implications for the political status of Taiwan [6].

### 6.9 Other Notable Resources

- **Wuhan symposium** (October 17-19, 2025): jointly organized by Jianghan University's Urban Research Center, the CASS Sino-Japanese History Research Center, Central China Normal University's Institute of Modern Chinese History, and others. Over 120 papers were submitted; 72 were selected [28].
- **Southwest Associated University exhibition** (September 2025, Nankai news): focused on the university's wartime academic research and field investigations, supporting "the war rear area population resources, economic resources investigation" and providing the basis for "new China's ethnic identification and ethnic regional autonomy policies" [29].
- **The Andrew Rhodes USMCU article** on the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95 analyzes Chinese strategic thinking: (1) the need to inculcate "maritime consciousness" (haiyang yishi); (2) the importance of building strong institutions to sustain seapower; (3) the imperative to employ the navy actively and aggressively in combat [7].
- **De Giorgi's** 2014 JSTOR article (26372424) documents the growth of scholarship on China's resistance war [4].
- **The APJJF article** (2022/11/tian) analyzes official discourse of war memory from 1949 to the present in the PRC [5].

1. RESEARCH FIELDS: What are the major sub-fields of study? (e.g., military history, political history, social history, economic history, diplomatic history, cultural history, intellectual history, memory studies, gender history, local/regional history)

2. RESEARCH PERSPECTIVES: What are the dominant perspectives or paradigms? (e.g., nationalist narrative, Communist Party narrative, "people's history," revisionist perspectives, transnational/global history approaches, perspectives from below)

3. RESEARCH METHODS: What methodologies are commonly employed? (e.g., archival research, oral history, quantitative methods, comparative history, microhistory, digital humanities)

4. THEORETICAL APPLICATIONS: What theoretical frameworks have been applied? (e.g., modernization theory, total war theory, colonialism/postcolonialism, nationalism theory, gender theory, trauma studies, memory studies)

5. RESEARCH CONCLUSIONS: What are the key historiographical debates and conclusions? ## 1. RESEARCH FIELDS (Major Sub-Fields of Study)

### 1.1 Military History

**The "Two Battlefields" framework is central to Chinese military historiography.** During the War of Resistance, China formed two battlefields: the frontal battlefield (正面战场) conducted by the KMT through a unified national government, utilizing national resources and over 2 million regular troops for regular warfare, and the enemy's rear battlefield (敌后战场) conducted by the CCP and its military, which went deep behind enemy lines, established base areas, implemented people's war, persisted in protracted war, and adopted a strategy of basic guerrilla warfare while not giving up mobile warfare when conditions were favorable [18]. The two battlefields resulted from the Anti-Japanese National United Front advocated and promoted by the CPC, representing the most successful military embodiment of that united front. This was the only instance in WWII of a war being fought simultaneously on both frontal and rear battlefields on such a large scale, with the two battlefields being interdependent, mutually responsive, sharing a unified strategic goal yet operating independently — a unique creation of the Chinese nation [18]. Over eight years, the two battlefields conducted 200+ major campaigns and 200,000 battles of various sizes, annihilating over 1.5 million Japanese troops and 1.18 million puppet troops, and accepting the surrender of 1.28 million Japanese and 1.46 million puppet troops [18].

**Wang Jianlang** (Director of the CASS Institute of Modern History) argues that the front battlefield and enemy-rear battlefield were "mutually supportive and interdependent; neither can be missing. Without the enemy-rear battlefield, the front battlefield would have found it difficult to resist the Japanese offensive." Statistics cited: The front battlefield killed/wounded about 850,000 Japanese troops, while the enemy-rear battlefield killed/wounded over 500,000. Over eight years, the Eighth Route Army alone suffered over 340,000 casualties, including 700+ officers above regimental commander level. By war's end, CCP-led forces had grown to about 1.32 million troops and 2.6+ million militia, with base areas totaling nearly 1 million square kilometers serving nearly 100 million people [16].

**Zhang Hongzhi** (Deputy Director of the CPC Central Literature Research Office, interview published August 15, 2015) argues the enemy-rear battlefield ignited the people's war that marked China's turning point from repeated defeats to eventual victory, making it decisive to the war's outcome. He contrasts the "simple army warfare/static defense" of the KMT with the "all-people's war/mobile operations" of the CCP. He notes that the CCP's guerrilla war not only pinned down large numbers of Japanese troops and slowed their advance, but also reclaimed territory and disrupted Japan's "sustain-war-with-war" strategy. By the war's end, most abandoned territories had become CCP-liberated areas, recovering over 100 million people's territory, compressing Japanese occupation into isolated "dots and lines." He refutes claims of "游而不击" (roaming without fighting) and "趁机坐大" (opportunistically growing), explaining that rear-area forces faced extreme Japanese "mopping-up" campaigns including the "Three Alls" (kill all, burn all, loot all) policy and comprehensive political-economic-military operations. He also discusses the KMT's Nanyue Guerrilla Training Class (with Ye Jianying as deputy) and why KMT forces could not replicate CCP guerrilla methods due to their class nature [17].

**The Battle for China: Essays on the Military History of the Sino-Japanese War of 1937-1945** (edited by Mark Peattie, Edward Drea, and Hans van de Ven) "brings together Chinese, Japanese, and Western scholars to provide a comprehensive and multifaceted overview of military operations during the war" [3].

**Su Sheng-hsiung (蘇聖雄)**, Associate Research Fellow and Director of the Archives at the Institute of Modern History, Academia Sinica, Taiwan, specializes in modern and contemporary Chinese and Taiwanese military history, political history, and Cold War history. His military history research covers personnel, intelligence, logistics, training, strategy, tactics, battles, and key military figures. He employs Chinese, English, and Japanese sources, emphasizing recently opened archives and diaries, using global-context research methods combining military, intellectual, and institutional history. His major publications include 《戰爭、制度與思想：近代中國參謀本部的興起》(2023); 《戰爭中的軍事委員會：蔣中正的參謀組織與中日徐州會戰》(2018) [on the Military Affairs Commission, Chiang Kai-shek's staff organization, and the Xuzhou Campaign]; and 《奸黨煽惑——蔣中正對二二八事件的態度及處置》(2013). His PhD dissertation (2016) was "蔣中正與統帥部的組建及運作——以徐州會戰為中心" (232 pp.) [2].

**Su Shengxiong** (Academia Sinica, Taipei) noted at the 2019 Nankai conference that military history research in Taiwan was dominated by the military for the first 40 years, then shifted to academia, with a move from traditional to "new military history" emphasizing war-society relations [10].

**Zhang Haipeng** (张海鹏, research fellow at the Institute of Modern History, CASS) notes that after Wuhan fell (Oct 1938), the enemy-rear battlefield became the main battlefield. By 1943, CCP forces resisted 64% of Japanese troops and 95% of puppet forces. The CCP's forces fought 125,000+ engagements, annihilating 1.714 million Japanese and puppet troops (527,000 Japanese). By 1945, CCP forces reached 1.32 million, with 19 base areas covering ~1 million square kilometers [20].

**Qi Xiaolin** (CCP Central Party School) advocated for studying war history through material factors (food, ammunition, medicine, communications) from an international perspective [10].

**Weakness noted**: The 2015 Renmin University conference identified "weak research on actual military/war history (e.g., guerrilla warfare, battlefield strategy)" as a problem. It was noted that "for the KMT's frontal battlefield troop deployments and the CCP's strategic decisions to advance into the enemy rear... these belong to the category of military history and war history, which cannot be simply summarized by political history" [9].

### 1.2 Political History

**Wang Chaoguang's** volume "The History of China's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression: Wartime Politics" (Volume 3 of an eight-volume comprehensive history published by the CASS Institute of Modern History) examines the political dimensions of China's nationwide war of resistance (1937-1945). Key themes include: the KMT as the ruling party proposing "war of resistance and national reconstruction" while facing organizational deficiencies and corruption; the CCP implementing New Democratic policies in base areas and mobilizing the masses; and the complex KMT-CCP relationship of cooperation and conflict throughout the war. The volume argues that the KMT's leadership declined while the CCP's grew, a shift that shaped postwar Chinese politics. "The center of wartime Chinese politics was how to fully resist Japanese aggression, how to fight to the end, and strive for China's complete victory in the War of Resistance; the protagonists were the Chinese Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party." "The Nationalist Party's detachment from the people, organizational laxity, emphasis on words over deeds, and rampant corruption contrasted sharply with the Communist Party's mobilization of the masses, organizational strengthening, pragmatism, and vigorous governance." [13]

**Li Jinzheng** (Nankai University) discussed the difficulty of writing a comprehensive history of the war, noting three challenges: insufficient attention to foundational social, economic, and cultural forces; the need to address both the anti-Japanese struggle and the CCP-KMT contradictions; and the relative neglect of KMT rear-area resistance [10].

**Guo Yang** (Nanjing University) reviewed 70 years of scholarship on KMT political warfare, calling for new perspectives on party-army relations [10].

**Liang Xinlei's** National Social Science Fund Youth Project covers "Zhu Jiahua and KMT Personnel System during the War of Resistance" [5].

### 1.7 Memory Studies

**Rana Mitter's** "China's Good War: How World War II Is Shaping a New Nationalism" (Belknap Press/Harvard University Press, 2020, 336 pages) explores how China, once reluctant to publicly discuss its war against Japan, has undergone a wide-ranging reassessment of the WWII years as the country grew more powerful—a shift central to its new confidence abroad and mounting nationalism at home. Encouraged by reforms under Deng Xiaoping, Chinese scholars began examining the long-taboo Guomindang war effort, collaboration with the Japanese, and China's role in the postwar global order. Today, museums, TV shows, magazines, and social media present the war as a founding myth for an ascendant China emerging as victor rather than victim. One narrative positions Beijing as creator and protector of the international order—a system many in China now believe is under threat from the US [12].

The Asian Review of Books review notes that during the Mao era, class identity was central to China's self-definition; under Deng Xiaoping, class distinctions were blurred with the restoration of capitalism. "A new form of non-class-based national identity was needed. World War II, with its message of shared anti-Japanese struggle across class lines, proved to be a powerful vehicle for that new nationalism." The review quotes Mitter's final words: "As China becomes more powerful, the world will have to pay more attention to the stories that it wants to tell. Whether we realize it or not, we are all living in China's long postwar." [15]

The LA Review of Books review by Yangyang Cheng praises the book's exploration of divergent narratives, such as writer Fan Jianchuan's "One Person's War of Resistance" (2000) and Cui Yongyuan's 2010 documentary "My War of Resistance," which portrayed Nationalist soldiers sympathetically. The chapter on regional memory comparing Chongqing (Nationalist capital) and Yan'an (Communist base) is called the highlight. The review criticizes the book for omitting discussion of China's borderlands and ethnic minorities, assuming China is a Han nation, and for its state-centric framework. The review quotes Viet Thanh Nguyen: "All wars are fought twice, the first time on the battlefield, the second time in memory" and describes China as "a society in post-traumatic distress and collective amnesia" [11].

The APJJF article (2022/11/tian) analyzes "the development of official discourse of the memory of the Second Sino-Japanese War from 1949 to the present in the PRC" [5].

The National WWII Museum notes: "In 2020, Mitter's 'China's Good War: How World War II Is Shaping a New Nationalism' shows how Chinese leaders once tried to suppress memories of their nation's brutal experience during World War II, but now they celebrate the 'victory'―a key foundation of China's rising nationalism" [14].

### 1.10 Occupied Territories and Puppet Regimes

**Yu Zidao's** (余子道) review, "回眸与展望: 建国以来的沦陷区和伪政权研究" (Retrospect and Prospect: Research on Occupied Territories and Puppet Regimes since the Founding of the Nation), published in *抗日战争研究* 1999 Issue 3, reviews 50 years of research. Key structural findings:

**Three historical stages of research (1949-1999):**
- From 1949 to the Cultural Revolution (first 17 years): A period of slow beginnings, publishing approximately 40+ papers, 5-6 monographs, and 10+ books with relevant chapters.
- From the Cultural Revolution to late 1970s: A period of halt and recovery; research suffered unprecedented devastation during the Cultural Revolution, then slowly recovered after its end.
- From the 1980s onward (20 years): A period of rapid advancement and prosperity. This period produced 500+ papers, 60+ academic monographs, 30+ document collections, and translations of 10+ foreign works—more than 10 times the output of the preceding 30 years.

**Five characteristics of new-era research (post-1980):**
1. Shift toward respecting history and scientific rigor over ideology; e.g., re-evaluation of theories about Chiang Kai-shek and Wang Jingwei's alleged "double act" (双簧).
2. Extensive development of new sources: archives of the Manchukuo government, Wang Jingwei Nationalist Government, and other puppet regimes were opened; trial records of traitors like Chen Gongbo, Zhou Fohai, and Wang Yitang published.
3. Broadened research fields beyond military suppression and political control to include finance, currency, trade, industry, puppet armies and secret agents, culture/education/media, collaborationist organizations (Xiehehui, Xinmin Society, New Asian Reconstruction Movement), and intra-puppet relations.
4. Improved academic quality with works of notable depth.
5. Growth of research institutions at dozens of universities and institutes, with research centers at the CASS Institute of Modern History, Beijing Normal University, Fudan University, and Jilin Academy of Social Sciences.

**Major published works:** "汪伪政权史资料选编" (selected sources on Wang Puppet Regime), "伪满史料丛书" (1993), "日本帝国主义侵华档案资料选编", "满铁史资料", "审讯汪伪汉奸笔录" (1992), Zhou Fohai's diaries (published 1986 and 1991), "伪廷幽影录" (1991), "伪满洲国史" (1980, Jiang Niandong et al.), "伪满洲国史新编" (1995, Xie Xueshi), "历史的怪胎——汪精卫国民政府" (1993, Cai Dejin), "汪精卫汉奸政权的兴亡" (1987, Fudan University), "蒙古'自治运动'始末" (1980, Lu Minghui), "冀东日伪政权" (1992), "抗战时期的伪政权" (1993), "汪伪十汉奸" (1986).

**Debates over causes of Wang Jingwei's treason:** "黄美真等认为:日本的诱降政策是汪精卫集团投敌的外因,汪精卫的抗战失败主义和民族投降主义思想的恶性膨胀是其内因,亦是根本原因;而蒋介石的抗战两面政策则为汪精卫的投降开辟了道路" (Japan's inducement-to-surrender policy was the external cause; Wang Jingwei's defeatism and national capitulationism were the internal and fundamental cause; Chiang Kai-shek's two-sided resistance policy paved the way for Wang's surrender) [21].

**David Serfass** (Inalco-IFRAE, Paris) surveys the historiography of collaboration in Japanese-occupied China. Key collaboration governments included the Provisional Government in Beijing (Dec. 1937), the Reformed Government in Nanjing (Mar. 1938), and most notably the Reorganized National Government (RNG) chaired by former Premier Wang Jingwei (Mar. 1940), which claimed legitimacy as the successor to the pre-war National Government. Over 200 million people lived under Japanese occupation. The term "hanjian" (traitors) has been politically charged, with the CPC historically using it to delegitimize the KMT. Western historians like John Hunter Boyle (1972) and Timothy Brook (coining "collaborationist nationalism") have offered more nuanced assessments, while Chinese historians have moved from class-based denunciations to more complex analyses post-1980s. Brook argues collaboration regimes should be studied as part of China's modern state trajectory: "our disdain for forced ideology produces its opposite, confirmation of the natural legitimacy of state sovereignty" (Brook 2005, p. 223). New research perspectives include cultural history, spatial expansion beyond the Lower-Yangzi region and North China, trans-war approaches (post-1945 continuities), prosopography of middle/low-level administration, study of the Japanese adviser system, puppet armies, and connections within Japan's broader colonial empire [1].

**Xu Yuming's** survey of Japanese research on Wang Jingwei and his regime identifies three characteristics: (1) research is divided into two categories—puppet regime studies placed under modern Chinese history, and occupied territory governance studies placed under Japanese history or colonial governance (the latter being more developed); (2) economic research outweighs political research; (3) attitude toward Japanese militarism is critical, but toward Wang Jingwei's regime is more sympathetic than condemnatory. Major scholars include: Tsuchiya Mitsuyoshi (土屋光芳, Meiji University) who published over a dozen articles since 1988 on Wang's peace movement, anti-Chiang campaigns, democratic political theory, Greater Asianism, and political thought; Tobe Ryoichi's "和平试探者——支那事变和平工作的群像" (1991) which focuses on personnel factors and argues Japanese errors lay in overestimating Wang's power; Liu Jie's "日中战争下的外交" (1995) which argued the "Wang Jingwei work" was from the start strategy to weaken and collapse the Nationalist government; Takahashi Hisashi (Sophia University) researched from the Imperial Army's perspective; Furuya Tadao studied economic aspects, arguing the regime misjudged the strength and direction of Chinese nationalism, and wrote on pacification (清乡) operations; Hatano Sumio (on diplomatic issues under the Greater East Asia policy); Tanaka Etsuko (on Ozaki Hotsumi's views); Baba Akira (secret societies). Two sympathetic non-academic biographies exist — Yamanouchi Tokuo's "和平是卖国吗——汪兆铭传" (1990) and Sugimori Hisahide's posthumous "被人嘲笑称呼汉奸——汪兆铭传" (1998). The author concludes that Japan holds advantages in source materials and urges combining Japanese materials with mainland Chinese and Taiwanese archives while strengthening academic exchange [22].

**Wikipedia on the Wang Jingwei National Government:** A puppet regime established during the war, headquartered in Nanjing, existing from March 30, 1940, until August 16, 1945. Wang Jingwei served as Chairman from 1940-1944; Chen Gongbo succeeded him from 1944-1945 after Wang's death. In 1938, Wang signed the "Chongguangtang Agreement" with Japan via representatives Gao Zongwu and Mei Siping, fled Chongqing to Hanoi, and issued the "Yan Telegram" (艳电) calling for peace talks. The Peace Construction Army grew from 88,000 troops in 1940 to over 400,000 by spring 1945. On January 9, 1943, the Wang Jingwei Government declared war on Britain and the United States. On July 1, 1941, Germany and Italy recognized the Wang government as the sole legitimate government of China; Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Croatia, Spain and Vichy France also recognized it. Only Japan, Manchukuo, and Axis-aligned states recognized the regime; "scholars sometimes compare it to Vichy France." In 1943, it recovered Japanese concessions in Suzhou, Hangzhou, Tianjin and other cities (March); recovered Shanghai French Concession, Tianjin, Hankou, and Guangzhou French concessions from Vichy France (July); recovered Shanghai International Settlement from Japan (August); declared abolition of the unequal "Sino-Japanese Basic Treaty" (October). The regime lasted 5 years and 4.5 months. Most key officials were purged, including executions of Chen Gongbo, Chu Minyi, Liang Hongzhi, Miao Bin, Mei Siping, Lin Baisheng, Fu Shishuo, and Ding Mocun; Zhou Fohai was sentenced to death but commuted to life by Chiang Kai-shek [23].

**《汪伪政权全史》(The Complete History of the Wang Puppet Regime, 2 volumes)** is described as "the first complete work discussing the history of the Wang puppet regime," comprehensively covering the origins and development of the regime, including the pre-war Japanese plots to establish traitor regimes in North and Central China [24].

## 2. RESEARCH PERSPECTIVES (Dominant Paradigms)

### 2.1 Communist Party Narrative ("CCP as Mainstay")

The official CCP narrative positions the Party as the "中流砥柱" (mainstay/pillar) of the nationwide war of resistance. The China Victory over Anti-Japanese War website presents the central argument that "中国共产党是全民抗战的中流砥柱" (The CCP is the mainstay of the nationwide war of resistance), claiming the CCP established the anti-Japanese national united front, implemented comprehensive popular warfare, proposed the strategy of protracted war, and led guerrilla warfare in enemy-occupied rear areas. "持久战的方针丰富了反法西斯战争的军事理论，人民战争的伟大实践提供了弱国战胜强国的范例" (The protracted war strategy enriched the military theory of the anti-fascist war; the great practice of people's war provided an example of a weak nation defeating a strong nation). "敢不敢动员人民、武装人民、依靠人民，能不能充分激发蕴含在广大军民中的最深厚伟力，是决定抗日战争前途和命运的重要因素" (Whether one dares to mobilize, arm, and rely on the people, and can fully unleash the deepest strength of the armed forces and civilians, is a key factor determining the fate of the war) [19].

**Zhang Hongzhi's** interview argues: Mao Zedong first used "中流砥柱" in May 1941. The CCP provided political leadership throughout the war while the KMT was passive: the CCP called for resistance the day after the September 18 Incident; it established the anti-Japanese united front; it promoted peaceful resolution of the Xi'an Incident; it proposed the protracted war strategy during the KMT's crisis of defeatism and defections; and it took on the toughest fighting under the most difficult conditions, with no CCP unit defecting to the enemy while killing hundreds of thousands of Japanese and over a million puppet troops. The CCP's mass-line policy—combining national liberation with people's liberation through reforms like reasonable taxation (合理负担) and rent reduction (减租减息)—created a "human mountain" (人山) of popular support. He concludes that the different performance of the two parties on the two battlefields determined the people's hearts and the transition from old to new China [17].

**Zhang Haipeng's** macro-theoretical framework argues "中国共产党的正确主张和对抗日民族统一战线的主导作用是抗日战争取得胜利的基本原因" (The CCP's correct propositions and dominance in the anti-Japanese national united front were the fundamental reasons for the victory of the War of Resistance). He argues there were TWO leadership centers during the war—Yan'an (CCP) and Chongqing (KMT/Chiang). Both were indispensable. Japanese assessments confirmed the CCP's strength as "the number one enemy" and that "whatever happens, China's war of resistance will follow the CCP's track" [20].

### 2.2 Nationalist/Taiwanese Perspective

**President Ma Ying-jeou's** 2015 speech at the "War History and Memory: International Academic Conference on the 70th Anniversary of Victory in the War of Resistance" made three main points: (1) the ROC's war contributions were largely forgotten internationally due to the post-WWII Chinese Civil War, Korean War, and Cold War; he detailed the scale of the war: 22 major campaigns, 1,100 major battles, and 39,000 minor battles; 3.22 million ROC soldiers were casualties, including 268 fallen generals (7 full generals, 56 lieutenant generals, 205 major generals); over 20 million civilians died. The ROC pinned down 800,000 modern Japanese troops, preventing them from fully engaging in the Pacific theater. (2) He traced the legal chain of documents — the 1943 Cairo Declaration, the 1945 Potsdam Proclamation, and the Japanese Instrument of Surrender (Sept 2, 1945) — arguing these have legal force as a unified set (evidenced by their inclusion in the UN Treaty Series). He noted Japan's forces in China surrendered in Nanjing (Sept 9, 1945) and Taipei (Oct 25, 1945), after which the ROC began exercising sovereignty over Taiwan. (3) He stated his principles of "judge matters on their merits, put oneself in others' shoes, and clearly distinguish gratitude from grievances," emphasizing, "The error of aggression may be forgiven, but the truth of history cannot be forgotten" ("侵略的錯誤或可原諒，但歷史的真相不能遺忘") [4].

**Li En-han (李恩涵)**, a research fellow at the Academia Sinica's Institute of Modern History, wrote a review/preface for Zheng Lang-ping's (鄭浪平) book "Immortal Glory: History of the Second Sino-Japanese War," which surveyed post-war Chinese historiography. He noted that early official KMT works include He Yingqin's "Eight Years of War of Resistance" (1946), Bai Chongxi's works (1946), Chen Cheng's (1946), and the Defense Ministry's works (1966, 1978). CCP works like "History of the People's Liberation Army During the War of Resistance" (1953) were similarly limited or more distorted. The catalyst for new research was the autumn 1982 Japan textbook screening incident, when "Japanese militarists denied atrocities including the Nanjing Massacre, even changing 'invasion of China' to 'advance into China,' sparking strong protests from China, Korea, and Southeast Asia and prompting intensified study of the war." Taiwan academic responses included the 1984 "Pre-War Ten Years of National Construction Conference" (Academia Sinica IMR), 1985 "Anti-Japanese War and National Building Conference," 1987 "Anti-Japanese War and National Building Academic Conference," and KMT party history conferences. Private works include Liu Feng-han's collection (1987) and Li En-han's "Research on Japanese Military Atrocities" (1994) [1 of search 2].

### 2.3 "People's History" / History from Below

Diana Lary's "The Chinese People at War" tells the war's history "from the perspective of those who went" through it [6][8]. The Diaries symposium emphasized that "Diaries can restore the 'human' subject that has long been buried in historical research," noted Professor Jiang Pei [11].

The 2015 Renmin University conference consensus called for "combining macro-narrative with micro-empirical research, and top-down with bottom-up perspectives" [9].

### 2.4 Revisionist/Transnational Perspectives

**Yangyang Cheng's** LA Review of Books review notes that Mitter's "China's Good War" explores "not the war itself but how it is remembered in China and whom that memory serves. The Chinese government has embraced more diverse remembering of the war to 'command devotion at home and respect from abroad.'" The 2019 film "The Eight Hundred" about the 1937 Battle of Shanghai faced controversy and was edited after the Chinese Red Culture Association condemned its favorable portrayal of KMT soldiers and the Nationalist flag [11][15].

The 2004 Harvard conference convened by Ezra Vogel revealed critical divergences: "Chinese participants insisted the war was one of aggression and framed discussions in moral terms, frustrating Japanese and Western historians. Japanese participants felt the moral emphasis alienated sympathetic Japanese, while Western historians noted the war had little impact on the Pacific theater's outcome and was considered a 'peripheral theatre.' Chinese historians also avoided debating Chiang Kai-shek's priorities during the war, insisting all Chinese united in times of crisis" [8].

**Zhang Baijia** urged greater use of foreign observers' records and noted that "China's research on war trauma lags behind international WWII studies" [10].

**Zang Yunhu** (Peking University) analyzed the "hot and cold" cycles of resistance war studies, noting that before the 1980s the field was "cold," but has since become "gradually hot," though many areas remain under-researched (e.g., the "14-year resistance war" concept, China's wartime economy, society, and culture, occupied territories, Japanese invasion studies) [10].

### 2.5 Japanese Perspectives

**Qi Jianmin** (Nagasaki Prefectural University, Japan) traced the shift in Japanese research from "Tenno-system fascism theory" to "total war system theory," noting that the latter, emerging after the Cold War, tends to downplay war responsibility and even legitimize wartime policies by linking them to postwar development [10].

**Liu Yuebing** (Nankai University) analyzed the ideological logic of Japan's modern invasion of China, focusing on the kokutai (national polity) theory and Nihon seishin (Japanese spirit) theory [10].

**Tang Liguo** (Peking University) examined Japan's "thought war" (ideological warfare) as a propaganda campaign and a framework for understanding how Japanese elites, intellectuals, and the public accepted the war [10].

**Yin Yanjun** (Kanto Gakuin University, Japan) discussed disagreements between Chinese and Japanese scholars on whether the Marco Polo Bridge Incident was planned, concluding that while the timing and location may have been contingent, Japan's invasion of China was inevitable [10].

**Song Zhiyong** (Nankai University) traced three periods in Japanese scholarship on the Tokyo Trials, noting that political rightward shifts since the 1990s have significantly affected research [10].

**Ji Chen** (Sun Yat-sen University, Zhuhai) examined the compilation of the official Japanese war history of the First Sino-Japanese War (1894-95), noting that after 1903 its editorial policy shifted to beautify Japan's war initiation, avoid military critique, and reduce length, with lasting influence on later official war histories [10].

**Zhao Qingyun** (CASS) examined the exchanges between Japanese leftist historian Inoue Kiyoshi and Chinese academia [10].

## 3. RESEARCH METHODS

### 3.1 Archival Research

The 2015 Renmin University conference noted "extensive archival materials from both Chinese and international sources (including Japan, the US, UK, France, Germany, and Russia)" as a key advance. However, scholars identified as a problem that "能够熟练利用外文文献、具有国际视野的学者还很少" (scholars who can skillfully use foreign-language literature and have international perspectives are still very few) [9].

The CASS War of Resistance Research Office undertakes "overseas collection of rare resistance war materials" as part of the National Social Science Fund Special Project [5].

The 15 digital resources compiled for the 80th anniversary of China's victory (2025) include: Academia Sinica's Institute of Modern History Archives Search System (Taiwan); Academia Historica Archives System (Taiwan) — includes "Anti-Japanese War Historical Materials"; National Archives Information Network (Taiwan); Anti-Japanese War and Modern Sino-Japanese Relations Literature Data Platform (CASS) — massive open-access postwar archive including newspapers, journals, books, photos, and audio-visual materials; JACAR (Japan Center for Asian Historical Records); Japanese Military "Comfort Women" Related Official Documents; Biographical Dictionary of Occupied China (BDOC) (France - INALCO and Aix-Marseille University); Open Library - Sino-Japanese War 1937-1945 (Internet Archive) — 7,011 Chinese, English, and Japanese books; Japan at War and Peace, 1930-1949 (Archives Unbound/US National Archives); Warfare in China, 1839-1945: British Perspectives (UK National Archives); Political, Economic, and Military Conditions in China, 1918-1941 (US Military Intelligence Division); Political Relations and Conflict between Republican China and Imperial Japan, 1930-1939 (US National Archives). The guide emphasizes that "digitization has enabled researchers to transcend national boundaries and construct multi-perspective historical interpretations" [3 of search 2].

The Oxford programme involved "publications, fieldwork, and international collaborations" [2].

### 3.2 Diary-Based Research (Microhistory)

The "Diaries and the History of China's War of Resistance Against Japan Academic Symposium" (November 3-5, 2023, Nankai University) was co-organized by Nankai University's History Department, the Center for Chinese and Foreign Civilizations, the CASS Institute of Modern History's War of Resistance Research Office, and the journal *抗日战争研究*. Over 30 scholars participated, presenting 20 papers across five sessions:

1. **Diaries and Anti-Japanese Base Areas:** Papers examined CCP cadre diaries (e.g., Gao Lu) to explore rural investigation, party-building, and the evolution of the party-state system.
2. **Diaries and Nationalist-Controlled Areas:** Papers utilized diaries of Chiang Kai-shek, Chen Bulei, Chen Kewen, and Zhang Xueliang to analyze high-level politics, military strategy (e.g., the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign), diplomacy (Sino-German relations in 1940), and the publication of Chiang's *China's Destiny*.
3. **Diaries and Occupied Areas:** Papers examined ordinary people's diaries (e.g., engineer Sun Shoushan, village intellectual Lü Shunxiang, Peking opera actor Xun Huisheng) to reveal daily life, mentalities of fear and survival, and local military integration under Japanese occupation.
4. **Diaries and Wartime Intellectuals:** Papers focused on the diaries of Zheng Tianting, Mei Yiqi, and other scholars to examine the restoration of Peking University after the war, field investigations by scholars in the rear areas, and the spread of wartime information.
5. **Foreign-Language Diaries:** Papers explored diaries of Western residents (e.g., Bertrand Beitler in Shanghai) and Japanese Prime Minister Hara Takashi's diary.

Key methodological debates: "Diary as a type of historical material has irreplaceable significance for deepening the study of the history of the War of Resistance," said CASS researcher Wang Jianlang and Professor Jiang Pei. "Diaries should be cross-referenced with archival materials, and emotional expressions in diaries should be stripped as much as possible," suggested Associate Researcher He Jiangfeng. "People's limitations determine the limitations of diaries; in the current era of explosive growth in historical materials, more attention should be paid to the interpretation of historical materials," stated Professor Li Xiang. The consensus was that diaries are crucial for deepening War of Resistance research but must be used critically and in combination with other sources [11].

### 3.3 Oral History

The Anti-Japanese War Memorial Web (Changsha, China) includes "veteran interviews, oral histories, and large book series" [3 of search 2]. The People's Daily article notes "over 10 volumes of chronicles and interview records" were published [25].

### 3.4 Quantitative Methods

The 2004 Harvard conference and various Chinese sources cite detailed casualty statistics. President Ma cited: 22 major campaigns, 1,100 major battles, 39,000 minor battles; 3.22 million ROC soldiers casualties including 268 fallen generals; over 20 million civilians died [4]. Wang Jianlang cited: front battlefield killed/wounded about 850,000 Japanese troops; enemy-rear battlefield killed/wounded over 500,000; Eighth Route Army suffered over 340,000 casualties including 700+ officers above regimental commander level; CCP forces grew to about 1.32 million troops and 2.6+ million militia; base areas totaling nearly 1 million square kilometers serving nearly 100 million people [16]. Zhang Haipeng cited: In 1938, 94% of Japanese forces were in China; in 1941, 69% (35 of 51 divisions); China always pinned down ~1 million Japanese troops; Japan suffered 1.98 million deaths in China vs. only 890,000 in the Pacific; China suffered 35 million casualties [20].

### 3.5 Comparative History

Li Bingkui called for "comparative studies across CCP base areas, KMT areas, occupied territories, and overseas Chinese communities" [10]. The Wuhan symposium covers "Regional, National, and Global Perspectives" [28].

### 3.6 Digital Humanities

The Pan Xun project developed "replicable and promotable methodologies including school-institute-local collaboration, digital humanities, and multidisciplinary approaches" [26]. The CASS project includes "construction of a digital data platform for resistance war and modern Sino-Japanese relations literature" [5].

### 3.7 Prosopography

David Serfass calls for "prosopography of middle/low-level administration" as a new research direction [1]. The Biographical Dictionary of Occupied China (BDOC) provides biographies of key figures in Japanese-occupied China (1937-1945) [3 of search 2].

## 4. THEORETICAL APPLICATIONS

### 4.1 Total War Theory

**Qi Jianmin** traced the shift in Japanese research from "Tenno-system fascism theory" to "total war system theory" [10]. The Second Sino-Japanese War has been described as a total war where China fought for survival against Japanese aggression [1 of search 2].

### 4.2 Modernization Theory

Rana Mitter's Oxford programme argues "China's conflict with Japan in the mid-twentieth century must be brought to the forefront of our understanding of the wider path of Chinese modernity" [2].

### 4.3 Nationalism Theory

Mitter's "China's Good War" frames "China's radical reassessment of its own past is a new founding myth for a nation that sees itself as destined to shape the world" [12]. The Asian Review of Books notes that "China's international relations have been significantly shaped by its attempt to change the collective memory of the war, particularly in the twenty-first century" [15].

### 4.4 Colonialism/Postcolonialism

The Li En-han article describes the pre-war era as "半殖民地、半封建性" (semi-colonial, semi-feudal) [1 of search 2]. Japanese colonial rule in occupied areas is characterized by "integrated military-political-economic-cultural control" [21].

### 4.5 Trauma Studies

**Zhang Baijia** noted that "China's research on war trauma lags behind international WWII studies" [10]. The LA Review of Books review describes China as "a society in post-traumatic distress and collective amnesia" [11].

### 4.6 Memory Studies

The Oxford programme and Mitter's works apply memory studies frameworks. The APJJF article analyzes "the development of official discourse of the memory of the Second Sino-Japanese War from 1949 to the present in the PRC" [5]. The National WWII Museum notes Mitter's work shows "how Chinese leaders once tried to suppress memories of their nation's brutal experience during World War II, but now they celebrate the 'victory'" [14].

### 4.7 Gender Theory

Helen Schneider's "Keeping the Nation's House: Domestic Management and the Making of Modern China" applies gender/feminist frameworks to wartime domestic management [2].
